World.title: Ukraine Envoy: Russia ‘Not Interested’ in Peace Talks, African States Urged to Reject Recruitment Drive
World.content:
Mr. Oleg Kobzystyi, Chargé d’Affaires of the Ukrainian Embassy in Dakar, Senegal./Credit: Ukrainian Consulate in Dakar, Senegal.

As Ukraine marks its Independence Day on Monday, August 24, the Chargé d’Affaires of the Ukrainian Embassy in Dakar, Senegal, Mr. Oleg Kobzystyi, speaks to the Liberian media on a wide range of issues, including the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and the state of Liberia-Ukraine relations. Below is the full interview.

Q. How do you assess the current state of affairs on the battlefield? Do you have any thoughts on when the war might end?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: The Armed Forces of Ukraine defend our State every day and thwart the enemy’s plans. In particular, the President of Ukraine recently announced the complete liberation of the Dnipro region from the Russian occupiers. In addition, despite the permanent false statements of representatives of the Russian military corps, as of the end of August 2026, the Russian occupiers have not been able to completely capture Donbas.

This indicates Russia’s inability to advance further. They hide this inability behind the daily terror of the civilian population, because they know that there is nothing to catch on the battlefield. Every day, the Russian Federation launches dozens of ballistic missiles at peaceful neighborhoods of Ukrainian cities. What kind of readiness for the end of the war can we talk about?

We will be able to talk about when the war will end, when the fighting will cease. As you know, the Ukrainian side has repeatedly proposed holding negotiations on neutral grounds – in Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Qatar. However, Russia is not interested in negotiations, which is why every time they find new excuses not to accept President Zelensky’s proposals. Russia is only interested in capturing, killing, raping and stealing.

Unfortunately, this is exactly what the documented crimes of the Russian Federation in Bucha, Irpin, Olenivka, Kherson and a number of other Ukrainian cities testify to. People were killed, tortured, raped – all this solely because they are Ukrainians…

Q. How important is the mediation of other countries in the humanitarian issues of this war? Do you see the potential for involving Africa in the negotiation process on the humanitarian track?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: We are grateful to all those who, to varying degrees, are joining in helping Ukraine and its citizens. This applies to both the states located on the same continental shelf with Ukraine, such as the states of the European Union, Norway, North Macedonia and others, and the United States of America, Canada, the states of South America, as well as Qatar, the UAE, Japan, and South Korea.

At the same time, we are convinced that the potential for involving African states in the humanitarian track in this regard is more than significant. First of all, we are talking about assistance in the return of Ukrainian children and the Coalition of the same name – unfortunately, the issue of abduction of children, their loss of ties with their family and homeland – many African states have gone through these trials and their experience in resolving complex humanitarian issues is extremely important right now, when thousands of Ukrainian children were illegally taken away by Russia and placed in foster families in the Russian Federation, which is one of the most egregious crimes of this war unleashed by the Russian Federation.

Q. How do you assess the current state of Ukrainian-Liberian relations?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: Liberia is a friend and ally of Ukraine in the West African region in particular and on the African continent as a whole. Official Monrovia shares the same postulates as official Kyiv – respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, as well as for human dignity and freedom, and this is what allows our countries to develop a mutually beneficial partnership.

At the same time, we are sure that we still have something to offer each other in a significant number of areas. For example, Ukraine remains open to students from African countries and Liberia in particular – the high quality of Ukrainian education is a well-known factor in African students choosing Ukraine as the country where they prefer to acquire new skills and competencies.

Currently, a simplified online system for submitting documents to Ukrainian higher education institutions is operating. We already have a significant number of students from West Africa who have received permits to enter Ukraine and are preparing for the start of the new academic year. We are convinced that the educational component is a solid foundation for the development of further cooperation.

In addition, we believe that the potential for cooperation in the field of agriculture remains untapped. Ukraine has unique experience and expertise, primarily in the context of crop management systems, GPS monitoring of equipment and precision agriculture. Moreover, all of the above is currently functioning during the period of active hostilities on the territory of Ukraine, which indicates the stability of the Ukrainian development system to external factors and the possibility of its implementation in states interested in the development of the agricultural sector.

Another important direction is the digitalization of state databases and systems for providing public services. Ukraine has something to offer in this regard, in particular in the light of the automation of the provision of certain consular services to Ukrainian citizens abroad (approximately 7-9 million people – ed. note), access to online state registers, etc.

Q. How does the Russian Federation operate in Africa? Have you encountered cases of disinformation directed against you?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: The Russian Federation does not have a strategy specifically allocated to the African continent – Russia has always pursued the same policy towards everyone with whom it considers it necessary not to cooperate, but to exploit.

This is exactly how Russia cooperates with African states – it does not offer solutions, it sows discord and, in fact, does not hide it.

For example, almost on a monthly basis, we receive new information about African students who went to the Russian Federation to study, but ended up in the combat zone against their will – they are forced to sign a contract drawn up in Russian, that is, a language they do not even speak sufficiently. If they are lucky, they manage to surrender to the Armed Forces of Ukraine and not die. Unfortunately, such cases are rather an exception to the rule, because for the most part, those whom Russia uses as cannon fodder die in the first days of entering the front line – they are thrown into battle after a week of training.

From open sources, we know about cases of criminal recruitment by the Russian Federation in Kenya, Uganda, South Africa, and Zambia. In our region, citizens of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Ghana have become victims of Russian manipulation. Fortunately, there is currently no information about citizens of Liberia who have become victims of Russian recruitment. We hope that this trend regarding Liberia will continue in the future, because it is very important to make it clear to the Russian Federation that, unlike Russia itself, people are not expendable in other countries.

Citizens of African countries should weigh all the risks when they come into contact with Russians. If there are any doubts, victims of Russian recruiters have repeatedly highlighted the nature of the Russian Federation’s attitude towards people (Malik Diop (Senegal), Richard Kanu (Sierra Leone), etc.). Think twice before signing up for certain death – until a contract with the Russian Armed Forces is signed, you will not find yourself on the battlefield. As soon as the contract is signed, you automatically become a war criminal who violates the territorial integrity and sovereignty of another state and falls under the relevant norms of international law. There is no way back.

As for disinformation, just as Russia hides its inability to advance on the battlefield in Ukraine, Russia hides its crimes behind manipulations and lies in the media. Ukrainian Embassies in Africa are constantly accused of recruiting local citizens, assembling drones right in the Embassies, looking for sorcerers who would poison Putin and his henchmen… This style is nothing new – Ukraine has coexisted and fought against Russia for survival for centuries, so we know very well how Russia seeks to eliminate rivals. But readers should be very careful with such narratives – our African partners have repeatedly debunked Russian lies (for example, in Ghana, when an agent of Russian influence placed Nazi literature on a shelf with Ukrainian books, or in Côte d’Ivoire, when the Russians invented a story about “assembling drones at the Ukrainian Embassy in Abidjan”), which indicates an increasingly better understanding by African countries of the deceitful nature of the Russian Federation.

Q. Turning to the prospects of bilateral relations between Liberia and Ukraine, what, in your opinion, should be the next steps on both sides for the further development of mutually beneficial interstate dialogue?

Mr. KOBZYSTYI: Ukraine and Liberia are partner countries. Countries that value and respect each other. And this is not only within the framework of international organizations, as I said above. In the bilateral direction, among other things, we are working on agreeing on the draft Agreement on the Establishment of a Joint Commission on Economic and Trade Cooperation between the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine and the Government of the Republic of Liberia, on the Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Liberia on cooperation in the field of education, as well as on other equally important draft bilateral documents.

In addition, we continue to work on the possible organization of an official visit of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Liberia, Ms. Sara Beysolow Nyanti, to Ukraine, within the framework of which both states could sign these documents and agree on other specific steps, as you say, of mutually beneficial cooperation between Ukraine and the Republic of Liberia.

These elements of the contractual and legal framework could form the basis, as you ask, of a new stage on the track of Ukrainian-Liberian relations.

World.title: The Inalienable Right to Justice: Embracing a Universal Ethos in Liberia’s Legal System
World.content:
Austin S Fallah: “Justice is not a slogan to be shouted in the streets or a weapon to be used against political opponents. In a nation governed by law, justice requires patience, evidence, due process, and respect for the courts. Liberia must learn to let the law speak louder than empty political rhetoric.”

Austin S Fallah: “The inalienable right to justice belongs to every Liberian, friend or foe, government official or ordinary citizen. We can not demand justice for ourselves while denying it to others. A truly democratic Liberia must embrace one universal standard of justice for all.”

Austin S Fallah: “When allegations arise, responsible citizens should seek truth through lawful institutions, not replace evidence with slogans or judgment with political excitement. Liberia’s strength will not be measured by how loudly we accuse one another, but by how faithfully we allow the law to take its course.”

Austin S Fallah: “Patriotism is not the reckless condemnation of another Liberian before the courts have spoken. Patriotism is respecting the Constitution, trusting due process, and demanding accountability without abandoning fairness. Let justice be pursued with courage, but also with restraint and dignity.“

Austin S Fallah: “A new Liberia cannot be built on rumor, political vengeance, or empty declarations of guilt. It must be built on the universal principle that no one is above the law and no one is beneath its protection. Let us replace slogans with substance, anger with wisdom, and accusations with evidence, and allow justice to take its rightful course.”

In the kaleidoscopic realm of social justice, where the principles of equality and equity contend for dominance, one question reverberates with alarming urgency: If justice is truly impartial, should feminism and gender sympathy inform its execution?

As a resurgent Liberia stands at the proverbial crossroads—with President Joseph Boakai, Vice President Koung, and the coalition government steering the ship —an opportunity looms that must not be squandered.

This moment, situated in the second quarter of the 21st century, is a call to arms for a modern understanding of justice that transcends the constraints of class, gender, and political influence.

It requires a vision of justice that flows unfettered across the vast expanse of our motherland, a vision as relentless and boundless as the Atlantic Ocean itself.

What is justice, if not an unyielding commitment to uphold the rights of every individual, regardless of their societal standing?

It is fundamentally an aporia to assert that laws should only serve the downtrodden.

To segment justice into comfortable compartments risks undermining its very essence.

True justice must be enshrined in the belief that it serves a pluralistic society; it should not be a mere balm for wounds but rather a clarion call for collective responsibility and universal dignity.

Thus, it is not sufficient for justice to cater only to specific groups, be they feminists, the economically disadvantaged, or marginalized communities, while ignoring the broader landscape of humanity.

Justice must resonate with everyone, transcending the divides engineered by economic disparity or social standing.

The contemporary challenges that Liberia faces necessitate a comprehensive re-evaluation of its legal framework.

Under the enlightened leadership of President Boakai, the effort to craft a just society is indeed a salutary ambition that can bear fruit if pursued with sincerity and introspection, as it has been in recent times and will continue.

Laws must be created to encompass all citizens, ensuring that justice does not become a mere playground for tribalism, partisan politics, sectionalism, or countyism.

Such barriers incite division among the citizenry, diluting the purpose of justice and turning it into a vitriolic tool weaponized by political maneuvering and power struggles, as has been done in the past.

The concept of justice as more than a partisan game must be deeply ingrained in Liberian consciousness.

Justice can not simply masquerade as an instrument for political advancement; it must be perceived as a stabilizing force in society.

This idea rejects the notion of selective justice, a concept that appears temporary and transient, more performative than substantive, as Liberians saw in the past.

Liberians must rally around the principle that true justice is devoid of favoritism, empty political slogans, good-for-nothing rhetoric, or partiality, becoming a bulwark against oppression and tyranny in all its forms.

Liberians must examine the dynamic relationship between feminism and justice.

While feminism must amplify women’s voices and address systemic gender inequalities, it must also be framed within universal justice.

A justice system informed by gender sympathy is vital; however, to assign it a singular and exclusive role risks alienating other marginalized experiences that co-exist within the socio-justice landscape.

It is a delicate balance that requires pursuing justice for oppressed demographics while avoiding apathy toward the struggles others face.

Achieving this is no simple undertaking, and it requires courage and commitment from leaders and society at large.

They must act not as arbiters of selective justice but as facilitators of equity for all.

The coalition government under the leadership of President Boakai and Vice President Koung has an invaluable opportunity to establish a judiciary that safeguards the rights of women and men, youths and elders, rich and poor alike, which they are doing.

The winds of change blowing through Liberia’s legal landscape are rife with potential, provided they are harnessed effectively and cascaded through policies and practices that reflect an earnest dedication to neutrality and fairness.

Moreover, the fight against drug trafficking and its criminal networks within Liberia exemplifies the urgency and necessity of an impartial justice system.

The drug cartels that have seeped into the fabric of society are a visceral reminder of the degenerative forces that threaten to undermine the nation; therefore, anyone criminally involved must be held to account.

To confront this challenge, Liberians must collectively confront these entities’ manipulation of justice.

A justice system that is equal for all citizens must approach crime through a lens of unwavering scrutiny.

Drug traffickers and their accomplices must reckon with the full weight of Liberian jurisprudence, uninhibited by questions of social hierarchy or political association.

Liberia stands poised to redefine its narrative, to be something more than a historic victim of division and strife.

By nurturing a contemporary legal framework, one that exists above the fray of commonplace prejudices, Liberians embrace a future rooted in justice that is both restorative and transformational.

Justice should not be an abstract ideal whispered within academic circles; it must permeate citizens’ everyday lives, reinforcing the bonds of community and kinship.

The pursuit of justice in Liberia must also encompass compassion and understanding, recognizing that pontificating ethics can not fill the void created by injustice.

It must push the boundaries of empathy and extend beyond superficial engagement.

The legal system must be as multi-faceted as the challenges Liberians face.

It requires every air-breathing Liberian at home and in the diaspora to engage dialectically, acknowledging and integrating diverse perspectives that repeatedly clash in the society.

In doing so, they cultivate a justice that is informed by the complexities of their lived experiences.

To expound on the notion of dual citizenship, both in terms of legal status and moral obligation, is essential when discussing this new dawn of governance.

Emphasizing mutual accountability encourages each citizen to uphold the civic principles of justice while remaining vigilant and proactive against injustices they witness.

Engaging through community outreach initiatives that foster dialogue among diverse segments of the population can mitigate the fears and grievances that often surface in the collective psyche.

Embracing this new wave of justice under the leadership of President Boakai and Vice President Koung demands more than a superficial commitment; it necessitates action.

Each citizen must also see themselves as a steward of justice, a guardian of their neighbors’ and compatriots’ well-being.

To cultivate a legal environment conducive to true justice requires a long-term investment in education, positive advocacy, and unremitting diligence.

The very fabric of justice in Liberia hangs in the balance.

It can become a tool for selective justice or a profound catalyst for unity and equity.

The opportunity to forge a new path has emerged at a critical juncture in our history.

Let us champion a justice system robust enough to encompass individuals from all walks of life, unraveling the chasms formed by tribalism and systemic oppression and promoting a collective sense of responsibility.

Together, everyone must see justice flow like the bountiful tides of the Atlantic Ocean, limitless, unyielding, and impartial, until it envelops the very essence of the nation and identity.

Only then can Liberians truly dare to call ourselves a society committed to justice for all.

World.title: LAZ Says Closure Timing Threatens Constitutional Rights
World.content:
LAZ Demands Explanation As Court Closures Collide With Election Petition Window

The Law Association of Zambia has raised sharp concern over the closure of courts nationwide, coupled with the presence of heavily armed military personnel around court premises, demanding a formal public explanation for the action. LAZ president Arnold Kaluba said in a statement that the closure carries immediate implications for access to justice, particularly for people requiring urgent judicial intervention, including those with pending criminal proceedings, bail applications and habeas corpus matters.

Kaluba grounded his objection in specific constitutional text. He cited Article 13(3) of the Constitution, which requires that a person arrested or detained on reasonable suspicion of having committed, or being about to commit, a criminal offence and who is not released, be brought without undue delay before a court. He said any disruption to the ordinary operations of courts must be managed in a manner that ensures affected persons do not suffer prejudice and that constitutional rights continue to receive effective judicial protection.

What makes the timing especially significant, Kaluba said, is Article 103(1) of the Constitution, which provides a strict seven-day window within which a person may petition the Constitutional Court to nullify the election of a President-elect following the declaration of results. He warned that closing the courts during this constitutionally prescribed period creates a real risk that persons seeking to exercise that right may be prejudiced by uncertainty over access to court registries, filing facilities and judicial officers.

Kaluba said LAZ is demanding an explanation from the judiciary, arguing it is imperative that the institution immediately clarify the arrangements in place to ensure no person is prejudiced in exercising a constitutional or statutory right because of the closure, including any applicable filing deadline. He was careful to acknowledge that LAZ recognises exceptional circumstances, including genuine and immediate security concerns that may require temporary protective measures for judicial officers, staff, litigants and the public.

However, Kaluba stressed that any such measures must be lawful, proportionate and implemented in a way that preserves access to justice and respects the constitutional independence and autonomy of the judiciary. He demanded the urgent restoration of access to the courts and the resumption of filing, receipt and hearing of matters as soon as it becomes safe and practicable to do so.

Pending full reopening, Kaluba said the judiciary must immediately establish and publicly communicate alternative arrangements for the filing and receipt of urgent and time-sensitive matters, and, where necessary, ensure such matters can be placed before a judicial officer without undue delay. He called for particular priority to be given to matters affecting personal liberty, including habeas corpus and bail applications, as well as constitutional, electoral and other proceedings subject to strict statutory or constitutional timelines.

Kaluba said the judiciary must ensure no person is prejudiced by the closure in respect of any applicable filing deadline, and should issue directions or make arrangements as necessary to preserve parties’ legal and constitutional rights. He further called for prompt communication to legal practitioners, litigants and the public regarding the reasons for the closure, its geographical scope, expected duration and the arrangements for continued access to justice, along with clarification of the legal and institutional basis for the security measures, to the extent such information can properly be disclosed without compromising legitimate security considerations.

LAZ’s intervention adds institutional and legal weight to concerns already raised separately by other bodies, including the Human Rights Commission and civil society organisations, over the timing of the court closures relative to the constitutional petition deadline.

World.title: Former Kanchibiya MP Chanda Says Bill 7 Vote Cost Him His Seat
World.content:
Former Kanchibiya Member of Parliament Sunday Chanda has attributed his election loss to his vote in favour of the contested Bill 7 constitutional amendment, saying constituents turned against him over the decision and that the party subsequently withheld campaign support because he was seen to have defied local sentiment.

Chanda said the practice within his party was for the leadership to consult stakeholders before major decisions, and that outcomes were meant to reflect those consultations. He said he was not deployed to campaign in Kanchibiya during the run-up to the election, a decision he linked directly to how his Bill 7 vote had been perceived among constituents and party structures.

The former legislator’s account offers a rare first-hand illustration of how constitutional reform debates, which dominated parliamentary business well before the election, continued to shape voter behaviour and party dynamics at constituency level. Bill 7 remained a politically divisive issue throughout its passage, with supporters and opponents divided along lines that did not always track neatly with party affiliation.

Chanda’s remarks suggest that his vote was interpreted locally as a break from the wishes of Kanchibiya residents, regardless of the broader political or constitutional justification he may have had for supporting the amendment at the time. He indicated that this perception hardened opposition to his candidacy well before the formal campaign period began.

He also pointed to the absence of campaign deployment as a compounding factor, describing it as a signal that the party itself had distanced itself from his position. Without that support, Chanda suggested, an already difficult path back to the seat became considerably harder to navigate.

The episode highlights a broader dynamic playing out across several constituencies this election cycle, where MPs who supported contentious legislation faced consequences at the ballot box regardless of their standing within party structures. Chanda’s case adds a personal dimension to that pattern, illustrating how quickly parliamentary votes on divisive national issues can translate into local political costs.

Chanda has not indicated whether he intends to remain active in politics or pursue any further role within his party following the loss. His comments, however, are likely to resonate with other legislators who supported Bill 7 and who may be assessing their own standing with constituents in its aftermath.

World.title: Human rights Advocate calls for unity
World.content:
Governance expert and human rights advocate Wesley Miyanda has called on Zambians to protect the country’s long standing culture of peaceful democratic transitions, urging political leaders and their supporters to place national unity above political interests.

Mr Miyanda said Zambia has enjoyed peace since attaining independence and has conducted elections that resulted in changes of government without bloodshed or widespread political violence.

Speaking in an interview with the media, the governance expert appealed to political actors, particularly those dissatisfied with electoral outcomes, to use established democratic and legal processes to address their grievances rather than resorting to actions that could threaten the country’s peace and stability.

“Petitions are very important and they are constitutional. No one can stop them. I think that is the best thing we should do. We need to follow the process and see how the issues are resolved at the end of the day,” said Mr Miyanda.

He cited Zambia’s history of political perseverance as an example of how electoral disputes and defeats can be handled within a democratic framework.

He noted that some political leaders had lost elections several times but continued to participate in the democratic process, reorganising and returning to contest subsequent elections without mobilising supporters to cause unrest.

Mr Miyanda said political leaders should consider the broader interests of the country rather than allowing political disagreements to divide citizens.

“We cannot afford to put this country on fire because of politics. We don’t have any other home apart from this home called Zambia,” he said.

Mr Miyanda urged both winners and losers of elections to demonstrate restraint, peace and unity, saying the responsibility to protect Zambia’s stability rests with every citizen.

He said Zambia should now focus on healing and reconciliation following political contestation and begin rebuilding trust among citizens.

Mr Miyanda further warned that political instability could undermine Zambia’s economic prospects by discouraging potential investors.

He argued that investment could help create jobs and business opportunities while contributing to efforts to address the rising cost of living.

Mr Miyanda called on Zambians to put aside personal attacks and political divisions and work collectively to move the country forward.

He said the responsibility of the current generation is to preserve the peace inherited from previous generations and leave behind a stronger and more united Zambia.

“We should put our heads together and forget about personal attacks. Let us become a picture of this country that we should move forward and even make it better than we found it,” said Miyanda.

World.title: GATBRO International launches solar competition
World.content:
GATBRO International has launched the Doom Win a Solar Competition that is aimed at helping community members to access solar products that protect them from malaria.

Speaking during the launch in Lusaka, GATBRO International Head of Marketing, Kalwa Hackett says that the campaign is aimed at rewarding consumers, while protecting homes.

Ms Hacket said that consumers will have a weekly chance to win power banks and shopping vouchers.

“The campaign is a way of rewarding our consumers while helping families protect their homes.” She added.

And TIGER Brands International – Market Development Manager, Etienne Eksteen committed to enhancing people’s lives through the company’s Social Corporate Responsibility initiatives.

Mr Eksteen also commended ShopRite and other stakeholders for making the competition successful over the past two years.

World.title: LSUC gazetted as higher learning Institution
World.content:
Lusaka South University College (LSUC) has announced that it has been officially featured in the Government Gazette of Zambia, marking a historic milestone in the institution’s journey toward becoming a premier centre for higher learning and innovation.

The Government Gazette is the official legal publication of the Republic of Zambia.

Being gazetted, alongside accreditation by the Higher Education Authority (HEA), grants LSUC the legal mandate to award internationally recognised certificates and degrees, conduct high-level research, and provide expert consultancy and professional short-term training.

Speaking on behalf of the Board of Directors, Peter Chikubula noted that the recognition is a testament to the institution’s commitment to quality.

Mr Chikubala said the recognition is a demonstration of trust in the institution by the Government.

“Our official gazetting is more than just a legal formality, it is a seal of trust from the Government. It enables us to empower our students with qualifications that are respected world-over, ensuring they can compete in the global marketplace,” Mr Chikubula said.

He said over the years, LSUC, also registered under TEVETA, has been at the forefront of addressing national challenges through specialised skills training.

Mr Chikubala said the college has made a significant impact in the renewable energy sector, specifically in solar technology.

“By building local capacity during periods of national load shedding, LSUC has provided Zambians with hands-on skills necessary to achieve a sustainable energy mix and support the nation’s green energy goals,” he said.

Mr Chikubala emphasised that LSUC is dedicated to producing graduates who possess the practical skills required to transform and grow the Zambian business landscape.

World.title: Mambwe district engaged on risk management
World.content:
The Eastern Province Administration through the Provincial Planning Unit has embarked on a risk management technical assessment in Mambwe District.

Senior Planning Officer, Steven Madyabi, says the risk management was introduced with the view of improving performance in the civil service across government departments.

Mr Madyabi observed that providing technical support to districts, is necessary as it enables departments to be able to identify risks, analyse them, profile them and come up with mitigation measures to reduce and possibly, eliminate risks.

He further said after the engagement with the provincial team, the district would formulate a risk management committee.

“Mambwe District does not have a Risk Management Committee. Therefore, it is our hope that after this meeting, the district team will be able to identify Risk Focal Point Persons as well as formulate a Risk Management Committee that will bring all government departments on board,” he said.

Mr Madyabi expressed confidence that with the direction that the government is taking, many risks that various government departments were facing will be attended to.

“After today’s meeting, it is our hope that Mambwe District will be able to come up with risk mitigation measures that they, themselves can implement. We want them to be innovative and come up with solutions to the various risks that are there and where resources can’t allow, there is room for risk transfer from the district level to another level for onward submission at national level,” he added.

Mr Madyabi said government observed that the performance of the civil service was not tallying with the funding disbursed across departments.

Meanwhile, Mambwe District Administrative Officer, Diana Lupiya appreciated the step by the Provincial Planning Unit to bring the district up to speed.

Ms Lupiya said many activities in the district tended to be disrupted due to various risks that were being encountered with no mitigation measures in place.

“The only risk that the district is actively managing well is flood, a quite common situation in the area,” she said.

World.title: ZRA, Astrophysics sign contract for advanced cargo scanner
World.content:
The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) and United States-based Astrophysics Inc. have signed a contract for the supply, delivery, installation and commissioning of an advanced drive through X-ray cargo scanner at the Livingstone Border Post.

The contract was signed today at the United States Embassy in Lusaka by ZRA Commissioner General, Dingani Banda and Astrophysics Inc. Vice President of Human Resources and Organizational Development Vincent Zayek, during a ceremony hosted by U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires, Mich Coker and attended by senior government officials.

Speaking during the ceremony, Mr Banda said the initiative was in line with President Hakainde Hichilema’s call for the use of technology to transform tax administration and facilitate trade, through the implementation of the Non-Stop Border Pass concept.

“Technology, therefore, plays a vital role in facilitating trade and securing the supply chain. This underscores the importance of scanners in trade facilitation,” Mr Banda said.

Mr Banda said physical inspection of cargo without scanners can take up to five hours, while the Astrophysics scanner already deployed at Nakonde Border Post can scan a 30-tonne truck in about five seconds.

He said the Livingstone scanner will be the second scanner supplied by Astrophysics, building on the existing cooperation between the company and ZRA following the commissioning of the Nakonde scanner by President Hichilema in June 2026.

Mr Banda said Zambia’s strategic geographical position as a landlocked country situated along six major trade corridors makes efficient trade facilitation critical to the movement of goods across Southern Africa and the continent.

He said ZRA has implemented several reforms, including Coordinated Border Management, which has reduced the number of government agencies operating at borders from 18 to six, as well as Customs to Customs Data Exchange with Zimbabwe, Botswana and Malawi, with discussions underway with Tanzania.

Mr Banda said ZRA is also applying risk management in customs operations, noting that entries channeled through the Blue Lane, which is earmarked for post-clearance audits, accounted for 59 percent of revenue collected in 2025.

“We are also applying risk management in the operations of customs, meaning that not all goods are subjected to a physical inspection,” he said.

Mr Banda said ZRA looked forward to continued collaboration with Astrophysics in leveraging technology to advance tax administration, enhance domestic resource mobilisation, secure the supply chain and ensure efficient trade facilitation.

And Astrophysics Inc. Vice President of Human Resources and Organizational Development, Vincent Zayek said the agreement represented more than a contract, describing it as a shared commitment to strengthening Zambia’s border security and the continued success of the programme.

He said Astrophysics was proud to provide Zambia with the latest technologies in non-intrusive cargo inspection and looked forward to expanding its presence in the country.

Mr Zayek said the company intends to add more systems and establish a permanent Astrophysics office in Zambia to provide stronger local support.

He thanked the U.S. Embassy and commercial team for organising the ceremony, as well as ZRA for its partnership, cooperation and trust in Astrophysics.

Meanwhile, U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires, Mich Coker, said the project represented a model for modern border security by accelerating legitimate trade while making it harder for those seeking to abuse the border to succeed.

“American companies deliver not just best-in-world technology, innovation, and equipment, but an unrivaled standard of quality, of transparency, and of long-term partnership rather than a one-time transaction,” Mr Coker said.

He said the project supports Zambia’s priorities of strengthening domestic revenue collection, improving the ease of doing business and positioning the country as a reliable and secure hub for regional trade.

The initiative is aimed at strengthening border security and trade facilitation by enabling ZRA officers to inspect cargo more efficiently, accurately and safely, while reducing truck clearance times and making it more difficult to move contraband, smuggled goods and dangerous materials across the border.

World.title: Analyst Simutanyi Brands August Polls Among Worst Managed In Zambia’s History
World.content:
Political analyst O’Brien Simutanyi has described the just-concluded August general elections as among the worst managed in Zambia’s recent electoral history, citing a series of process concerns raised by different stakeholders throughout the campaign and counting period. His assessment adds a sharply critical voice to what has otherwise been a mixed chorus of reaction to the poll, ranging from congratulatory messages for President Hakainde Hichilema to independent verification exercises broadly affirming the outcome.

Simutanyi’s criticism centres on the manner and timing in which key stages of the electoral process unfolded, though he stopped short of alleging that the final result itself was manipulated. He argued that administrative decisions taken by the Electoral Commission of Zambia during sensitive periods, including the counting and declaration phase, created unnecessary uncertainty and left room for competing narratives to take hold among the public.

The Commission has not directly responded to Simutanyi’s specific characterisation, though it has previously maintained that the results reflect the will of voters as expressed at the ballot box. Officials have pointed to endorsement from parallel monitoring exercises, including one conducted by a coalition of civil society organisations, as evidence that the broad outcome was accurately captured despite process concerns.

Different stakeholders, including opposition figures, civil society groups and legal bodies, have separately questioned specific aspects of how the election was administered. Concerns have ranged from the handling of candidate withdrawals and running-mate vacancies to the timing of security-related court closures that coincided with the constitutional window for filing election petitions.

Simutanyi’s remarks land at a moment when public trust in electoral institutions is under close scrutiny. Civil society organisations have simultaneously called for reforms including independent electoral courts and clearer rules for managing disputed nominations, suggesting that Simutanyi’s criticism reflects concerns shared more broadly across the analyst and advocacy community rather than an isolated view.

The analyst’s comments have not been welcomed uniformly. Some political figures aligned with the winning party have pushed back against characterisations of the election as poorly managed, arguing instead that high voter turnout, diverse parliamentary outcomes and broad consistency between independent vote tabulations and official results all point to a credible process.

Simutanyi has previously written and commented extensively on Zambia’s electoral administration, and his latest remarks are likely to feature prominently in ongoing debate as the country works through the constitutional petition period. Whether his assessment gains traction beyond commentary circles may depend in part on whether formal legal challenges to the result proceed and what they reveal about the administrative concerns he has raised.

World.content:
KwaZulu-Natal Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case

A KwaZulu-Natal businessman accused of human trafficking and sexual exploitation is set to apply for bail at the Durban Magistrates Court, reports EWN. The 65-year-old, whose identity is protected by law, was arrested by the Hawks. He is accused of being the ringleader of a trafficking operation in which four women were allegedly lured from Johannesburg to Durban with promises of sales jobs before being forced into prostitution and pornography. His alleged accomplice, a 48-year-old man, is also expected in court. The businessman has also been linked to senior police officers and politicians through testimony at the Madlanga Commission.

A Limpopo lawyer and her Tshwane Metro Police officer husband are set to continue their bail application over allegations that they defrauded three deceased estates of more than R4 million, reports EWN. Charlotte Tibana, who runs a law firm in Polokwane, is accused of unlawfully transferring money from trust accounts. Acting as executor, while Peter "Gagash" Nonyane is alleged to have been involved in the fraud. The State is opposing bail and has expanded the allegations from an initial R1.75 million to more than R4 million. Tibana faces three counts of fraud and two of money laundering. Nonyane faces two counts each of fraud and money laundering. Both deny the allegations.

World.title: Congo-Brazzaville: Congo's Wealth Is Not Yet Power
World.content:
guest column

Across Africa, the decisive economic contest lies between raw material and finished product. For cotton, it is the distance from fibre to fabric. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, it is the distance from mineral and hydropower wealth to electricity, industrial capacity and productive work. The sectors differ, but the development question is the same: who captures the value created between extraction and the final product?

The Democratic Republic of Congo contains a startling share of the raw materials on which the modern economy depends. It is the world’s leading producer of cobalt. It has vast copper deposits, one of the planet’s great river systems and a population of roughly 100 million people, most of them young. On a map of the energy transition, the country appears indispensable.

On a map of lived prosperity, it looks very different. Only about 21 per cent of Congolese people have access to electricity, according to the World Bank. Poverty remains deep, insecurity persistent and the state distant or predatory for many citizens. The country’s most important economic question is therefore not how much wealth lies beneath its soil or runs through its rivers. It is whether that wealth can be converted into power, production and broadly shared opportunity.

That distinction separates endowment from development. Congo has never lacked resources. It has lacked the durable institutions and infrastructure that allow resources to become public value.

An extractive inheritance

The origins of that failure reach back to the formation of the state itself. Under King Leopold II, the Congo Free State became synonymous with forced labour and brutal extraction. Coercive labour practices persisted after Belgium assumed direct colonial rule in 1908, and a genuinely free labour market emerged only slowly before independence in 1960, according to academic research cited in the original manuscript.

The colonial economy was designed to remove value and administer territory, not to cultivate a broad Congolese political, managerial and technical class. At independence, the country inherited immense land and mineral wealth but little indigenous administrative capacity. A World Bank historical assessment cited in the manuscript describes both the shortage of trained Congolese personnel and Belgium’s effort to retain influence through technical advisers placed alongside key officials.

The crisis that followed independence, the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, Mobutu Sese Seko’s long authoritarian rule and the Congo wars deepened those institutional weaknesses. Mobutu did not invent the extractive state, but his personalised system entrenched it: institutions weakened, patronage expanded and public resources served political survival. Later conflicts and regional interventions fragmented authority further and allowed armed groups to flourish.

This history matters not because it condemns Congo to failure, but because it explains why geology alone has proved such a poor development strategy. Resources create possibilities. States, markets and public institutions determine who captures them.

From quarry to factory

The scale of the opportunity is nonetheless exceptional. The US Geological Survey estimated that in 2024 the DRC accounted for about 75 per cent of global cobalt production and roughly 55 per cent of global reserves. It was also the leading producer of tantalum and among the leading producers of copper, diamonds, tin and other strategic minerals.

These materials sit inside the energy, electronics, telecommunications, defence and manufacturing supply chains that are reshaping global commerce. Yet the familiar model remains one in which the highest-value activity occurs elsewhere. Minerals are extracted in Congo; more sophisticated processing and manufacturing take place abroad.

The policy choice is often described as one between exporting minerals and exporting products. But moving from one to the other requires more than declaring an industrial ambition. Copper processing, battery materials, electrical equipment, construction inputs, machinery and chemicals all require dependable electricity, transport, skills, capital, enforceable contracts and access to markets.

The real transition, then, is not simply from “quarry” to “factory”. It is from an extractive system to a productive one. The measure of success is not how many tonnes leave the ground, but how much capability, employment and domestic value are created before they leave the country.

The river and the grid

Congo’s most consequential industrial asset may be the one that flows through it. The Congo River and its tributaries give the country extraordinary hydropower potential. The Inga site alone has an estimated capacity of about 42,000 megawatts, which the World Bank describes as one of the world’s largest hydropower opportunities.

That number is dazzling. The national power deficit is sobering. With electricity reaching only about one in five people, the first claim on Congo’s hydropower future must be domestic: households, schools, clinics, farms and businesses that cannot develop without reliable power. The country’s National Energy Compact aims to raise access to 62 per cent by 2030, potentially reaching about 82 million people, according to the World Bank.

Power is also the bridge between Congo’s mineral base and its industrial ambitions. A processing plant cannot run on geological promise. Mines, smelters, factories and cities need generation connected to functioning transmission and distribution networks. The Inga opportunity therefore cannot be judged only by installed capacity. It must be judged by whether electricity reaches Congolese users reliably and affordably.

Regional trade could extend the value of that system. The DRC participates in the Southern African Power Pool, and electricity from Inga has historically been supplied to countries including South Africa and Zimbabwe. The World Bank has identified stronger transmission links between Inga, Zambia and the wider southern African market as strategically important.

The proposed Inga 3 project illustrates both the promise and the uncertainty. World Bank analysis cited in the manuscript places its possible generation between 2 and 11 gigawatts, depending on the final design. Congo’s position could eventually allow power to move across southern, central and eastern African pools. But “could” is the operative word. Regional electricity trade depends on finance, transmission lines, credible contracts, regulatory alignment and political confidence—not capacity estimates alone.

World Bank/ Ai Generated Congo at the centre. Country and river geometry: Natural Earth.

Europe’s interest, Congo’s choice

The strongest European connection is not a speculative cable from the Congo River to European homes. It is the prospect of a different industrial relationship. Europe seeks secure supplies of critical minerals and lower-carbon industrial inputs. Congo needs energy, jobs and greater value addition.

If renewable power can be combined with copper, cobalt and other minerals, Congo could produce more of the intermediate goods required by the energy transition. That would allow trading partners to buy higher-value Congolese output rather than raw material alone.

But the arrangement will be developmental only if industrial capacity takes root inside Congo. Supply security for foreign buyers is not the same as prosperity for Congolese citizens. The terms of contracts, the distribution of rents, local skills, environmental safeguards and the strength of domestic suppliers will decide whether a new mineral boom merely modernises extraction or changes the structure of the economy.

A young country needs work

The urgency is demographic. A World Bank assessment cited in the manuscript estimates that almost 65 per cent of the population is under 25. About 22 million people were aged 15 to 24 in 2025; that figure is projected to reach roughly 26 million by 2030. About a third of young people are neither in education, employment nor training, while roughly 40 per cent struggle to find work.

A young population is neither automatically a dividend nor inevitably a danger. It becomes an economic advantage when education, electricity, investment and functioning markets allow people to be productive. Without those conditions, demographic scale can intensify exclusion and instability.

This is why Congo’s industrial debate must be about jobs as much as exports. Capital-intensive mining can generate revenue without employing people on the scale the country requires. Processing, construction, energy, logistics, agriculture, services and regional manufacturing offer a broader employment base—but only if skills policy and industrial policy are designed together.

Peace as economic infrastructure

No such strategy can succeed while conflict continues in the east. Violence is first a human catastrophe. It is also a destruction of economic possibility: roads go unbuilt, schools are disrupted, responsible investment becomes harder and informal or illicit systems gain ground.

The IMF has identified governance weaknesses, mineral dependence, youth exclusion, conflict and the regional dimensions of insecurity among the DRC’s drivers of fragility. The implication is that peace cannot be treated as a security file isolated from economic policy.

The DRC and its neighbours have a material interest in replacing the economics of conflict with the economics of connection. Electricity links, roads, railways, ports, digital networks, agricultural value chains and lawful cross-border trade can raise the opportunity cost of destabilisation. Integration is no guarantee of peace. But an economy organised around shared production and exchange offers a stronger foundation than one organised around contested extraction.

Finance, and the test of delivery

Development institutions have begun to finance parts of this agenda. As of September 2023, the African Development Bank’s active DRC portfolio consisted of 27 operations worth about $1.45bn across transport, information and communications technology, energy, water and sanitation, and agriculture. Its 2023–2028 country strategy focuses on industrialisation, employment, infrastructure, agricultural value chains, human capital and the business environment.

The energy commitments cited in the manuscript include $22.4mn in parallel AfDB financing alongside $73.1mn of World Bank support approved in 2014 for Inga-related technical assistance. In December 2024, the AfDB was appointed mandated lead arranger for the $340mn Moyi Power Metro-Grids project, intended to bring cleaner, more reliable electricity to more than one million people in three cities.

These commitments show that Congo’s needs are recognised. They do not, by themselves, prove transformation. Portfolios, strategies and mandates are inputs. The meaningful outputs are functioning grids, reliable transport, competitive firms, transparent institutions and work that pays.

The missing chain

Congo’s agenda is often presented as a list: better mining contracts, more roads and rail, stronger security, technical education, regional power links, a better business climate. Each item is necessary. The more difficult insight is that they are interdependent.

Electricity without transmission cannot power a factory. A railway without predictable freight may not be financeable. Mineral processing without skills and reliable energy will not compete. Investment without accountable institutions can reproduce the very extractive bargain Congo needs to escape. Peace without legal economic opportunities may remain fragile.

The country therefore needs more than projects. It needs a sequence: secure productive regions; improve public institutions and contract transparency; expand electricity access and transmission; connect mines, farms and cities to markets; build technical capabilities; and use mineral and energy policy to support industries that can compete.

None of this is quick. Nor is it guaranteed. The same resources that make Congo strategically valuable also intensify struggles over rents and influence. Large infrastructure can create debt, displacement and governance risks if projects are badly designed. Regional interconnection creates opportunity, but it also requires patient diplomacy and institutions able to enforce agreements.

Yet the alternative is not stasis. Global demand for strategic minerals is placing Congo closer to the centre of the world economy. The country can remain indispensable as a source of raw materials while its citizens remain excluded from the value those materials create. Or it can use this moment to negotiate a more productive bargain.

The real test will not be whether the Democratic Republic of Congo finally “wakes”. Countries are not giants in fairy tales. They are political economies, built through choices and constrained by institutions.

Congo already has the assets. What it has not yet secured is the chain that joins them: peace to investment, power to production, minerals to industry, and national wealth to household prosperity. Building that chain would not merely alter Congo’s fortunes. It could change the economic geography of Africa.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa Dragged to Constitutional Court, Accused of Packing Senate With Zanu-PF Politicians
World.content:
President Emmerson Mnangagwa has been dragged to the Constitutional Court over his appointment of 10 senators, with two applicants accusing him of packing the Upper House with politicians instead of independent professionals as required by the Constitution.

Thamsanqa Ncube and Ibhetshu LikaZulu are seeking an urgent order blocking the nominees from being sworn in and ultimately declaring their appointments null and void.

The respondents are Mnangagwa, the Speaker of Parliament, Justice Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi, the Attorney-General and the 10 nominees, Jabulani Sibanda, Makhosini Hlongwane, Mary Mliswa, Nokuthula Matsikenyere, Kudakwashe Tagwirei, Godwills Masimirembwa, Lucy Chitaga, Gen Gibson Mashingaidze, Brilliant Dube and Iren Mutumbwa.



The applicants argue that Section 120(1)(e), introduced through Constitution Amendment No. 3, requires the President to appoint 10 senators based on their "professional skills and other competencies" and after consultation with the National Assembly.

But they claim the nominees are predominantly Zanu-PF politicians or closely linked to the ruling party, defeating the purpose of the amendment.

The application says the appointments are "the precise opposite" of assurances given by Justice Minister Ziyambi during debate on the amendment.

Ziyambi had told Parliament: "The appointment power is not unbounded. The text requires that these 10 Senators be chosen for their professional skills and competencies."

He said the new senators were intended to bring expertise "in finance, in science, in law, in technology, in public health".

The applicants also challenge the consultation process, saying Mnangagwa's nominees were simply announced in Parliament before the Speaker declared: "Recommendations put and agreed to."

"There was no debate, no question, no point of order, and no opportunity for meaningful consultation," Ncube says in the founding affidavit.

The applicants further argue that there is no legislative or parliamentary framework regulating the consultation process, making the appointments premature and unconstitutional.

They fear the dispute will become academic if the nominees are sworn in and begin voting in the Senate.

"The ten individuals are awaiting swearing-in. Once sworn, they will sit and vote in the Senate with full rights," Ncube says.

The applicants want the court to stop the swearing-in and order that any fresh appointments only be made after proper procedures are established to ensure the nominees have the professional expertise required by the Constitution.

The case comes shortly after Constitution Amendment No. 3 increased the Senate from 80 to 90 members by creating the 10 presidentially appointed seats.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa's Daughter-in-Law Tells Court Alleged U.S.$9.3m Money Laundering Proceeds Were Gifts From Husband
World.content:
Kelsea Tafirenyika will spend more days behind bars after her bail hearing was postponed to Wednesday, as she told the court that the luxury properties and vehicles at the centre of a US$9.3 million money-laundering case were gifts from her husband, Collins, son of President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Tafirenyika, through her lawyers, said her husband can afford the assets because of his vast business empire.

But investigating officer Detective Assistant Inspector Gift Machipisa told the court police have evidence suggesting otherwise, including a Victoria Falls property whose owner allegedly confirmed receiving cash directly from Tafirenyika.

The State alleges Tafirenyika acquired assets worth US$9,353,750 in Zimbabwe using proceeds from alleged dealings in pethidine hydrochloride, morphine sulphate and dagga.



Machipisa said police had secured title deeds, Deeds Registry searches and vehicle registration records for nine vehicles, as well as an alleged forged identity document bearing the name Getrude Badza.

He said about ten witnesses were expected to testify and police were still gathering evidence.

The State is also relying on allegations that Tafirenyika owns 13 properties in Dubai and South Africa, which Machipisa said gave her the means to flee.

Her lawyer Afmire Rubaya attacked the State's affidavit, arguing that it "had not been properly commissioned because the person who signed it did not state his rank."

Tafirenyika was re-arrested last Thursday moments after being released on US$1,000 bail in a separate drug case in which she is jointly charged with her uncle, Isaac Jessub.

Magistrate Francis Mapfumo postponed the matter after Machipisa asked to be excused to attend his father's burial.

Tafirenyika will therefore remain in custody until Wednesday, when the court is expected to continue hearing the case.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Peace Roadmap - Will the Fighting Finally End?
World.content:
Eastern DR Congo has seen repeated waves of violence and displacement. Pictured here, families sheltering at an IDP camp in Ituri province in September 2025.

A new roadmap sets out the conditions toward peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). But disagreements over M23 rebels, Rwanda's role and security concerns remain, and could still derail the process.

Representatives of the Congolese government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed on a roadmap for peace after negotiations in Geneva.

It builds on the US-brokered framework signed in Doha last year, and sets out steps and timelines for negotiations and implementation: a ceasefire monitoring mechanism is also due to receive support from the UN peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO.

The United States, Qatar, the African Union (AU) and Switzerland have all expressed their support for the process as brokers of the push for peace.



However, it is not a full peace plan with bindíng resolutions and terms; rather, many aspects of the push will still need to be fine-tuned.

The new diplomatic initiative could nevertheless be offering fresh hope following years of bloody conflict in eastern DRC; fighting in the region has killed hundreds of civilians and displaced millions since 2022. The M23 rebel group continues to control large parts of North Kivu and South Kivu — two provinces in eastern DRC that are highly coveted for their minerals.

As disagreements remain over key issues, doubts continue to cast a shadow over the prospect of a lasting peace.

From signature to implementation

"There are likely to be many more bumps on the road — disagreements remain over issues including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms. So this remains a very fragile commitment," Alex Vines, Africa program director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told DW.

Conflict analyst Clifton Chifuwe, executive director of the Centre for Peace Research and Advocacy (CPRA), a local NGO that focuses on conflict management, agrees with that assessment, pointing to the presence of multiple armed groups in the area, the deep level of mistrust between DRC and Rwanda, and competition over eastern Congo's mineral wealth.

He believes that the biggest of the challenges across the board is to turn this roadmap into action.

"Signing it is easier than implementing it on the ground," Chifuweexplains.

Chifuwe told DW that independent monitoring mechanisms and the involvement of all key stakeholders will be essential for any peace to hold.

Rwanda's role in the conflict

Rwanda has repeatedly rejected accusations that it backs M23 rebels — though international groups maintain the view that the small neighboring nation is deeply entrechned in the conflict.

Kigali's relationship with the rebel group therefore remains central to the peace process, says Vines:

"Rwanda's good faith and its relationship with M23 is a really key consideration. Kigali's buy-in to any agreement and influence over M23 is key."

Rwandan President Paul Kagame's comments at a press conference on August 24 further underline the complexity of the issue; Kagame rejects the narrative that Rwanda is responsible for the current conflict, blaming factions within the DRC instead.

He links any Rwandan involvement in the conflict to what he describes as a longstanding security threat from the other side of the border, naming the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) armed group — which fights against M23 rebels alongside the Congolese military — as his main target.

Kagame said that "if this problem of the FDLR is not resolved," Rwanda would act to protect itself "at any cost."

Mixed messages of hope and skepticism

There also are signs and reasons for cautious optimism: Chifuwe highlights that the roadmap focuses on a sequenced implementation plan, with monitoring initiatives to be put in place to help identify warning signs before any violence resumes.

These international mediators will also have to maintain pressure on the parties while ensuring regional concerns are heard.

In this context, Vines believes that US and Qatari involvement remains important, while stressing that African input through the AU must not be ignored.

All parties involved have signed off on a pledge to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution" — for now.

Close 

What does peace mean for the displaced?

Ultimately, the roadmap will not be measured by the signatories' attitudes but by results for thousands upon thousands of people in the eastern DRC, who remain displaced.

"The real test is ... whether ordinary Congolese people become safer and better off," Chifuwe says emphatically, highlighting also the restoration of state authority and the management of mineral resources as key objectives that need to be achieved.

For Congolese civilians, the diplomatic language carries a personal meaning: One refugee named Linda Kasongo finds herself stuck in Zambia five years into the conflict.

She told DW that she wants to return home, but can't even entertain the thought, since violence on all sides continues to wreck lives and livelihoods in her war-torn home region.

"I hope it works out because I want to go home," Kasongo says. "I want to be with my people. I miss my people. I miss my home."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Arizona grandpa to undergo amputation after collapsing on scorching sidewalk
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An Arizona grandfather is preparing to undergo an above-knee amputation of his right leg after he tripped and fell while walking outside in Bullhead City during 120-degree heat earlier this month, according to his family.

Grant Siler, 72, fell during a walk on Aug. 3 in Bullhead City, causing his body temperature to rise to more than 105 degrees.

The family’s GoFundMe said Siler was on the ground for an estimated at least an hour before a passerby found him. The fundraiser said he suffered second and third-degree burns in multiple areas of his body, heat stroke and multiple organ shock.

HIKERS FACE URGENT GRAND CANYON HEAT WARNING AFTER TEEN’S DEATH ON POPULAR TRAIL

He was then taken to a burn ICU in Las Vegas, where he has been cared for since the incident. When he arrived at the facility, doctors discovered he was suffering from heat stroke and organ shock.

"He is in constant pain, can barely move, and has undergone two debridements. Also, he will soon need to undergo surgery for amputation, the extent is not yet known," the GoFundMe reads.

During surgery, a surgeon found that tissue in Siler’s right leg was so severely damaged it was unlikely to fully heal, according to an update posted to the fundraiser.

Siler is scheduled to have his right leg amputated above the knee on Aug. 31, according to FOX 10 Phoenix.

ESPN ANALYST MATT MILLER SAYS HE UNDERWENT LIFE-SAVING AMPUTATION OF LEFT ARM AFTER CAR ACCIDENT

"The plan now is to have an above-knee amputation. The Dr's feel he will overall heal faster and have better pain control this way," the fundraiser reads.

"We can all imagine that after any amputation, the road to recovery is long and hard...physically, mentally and emotionally," it continued.

His wife, Vicki, has been traveling one-and-a-half-hours each way to be with her husband as she continuing to work to support the family’s financial obligations. The family said the couple will also soon have to face medical bills to help with Siler’s recovery.

The family is accepting donations to help with home renovations, home medical supplies, prosthetics and other added costs.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Siler's daughter, Heather Crook, recalled an incident in which he dropped an 80-pound cinderblock on his foot but did not even take a Tylenol.

"He's hurting really bad," Crook told FOX 10. "He's the 'get up and walk it off' type."

"So for him to holler out in pain … it’s really hard to hear. That’s not the kind of person that he is," she added.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Postpartum is real, but child killing demands accountability, veteran prosecutor says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

While failures by people, medical professionals and systems around Lindsay Clancy deserve scrutiny, nothing should erase a parent’s responsibility for killing a child, according to a veteran prosecutor who said he's concerned that public support for the Massachusetts mom is overshadowing the killing of her three young children.

Clancy is accused of killing her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

But as the case has drawn national attention, Clancy has also attracted supporters both online and in-person at the courthouse, and experts have warned that that support has taken attention away from the victims.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S THREE CHILD VICTIMS FORGOTTEN AMID CROWDS OF SUPPORT: MOTHER OF SIX

"Nobody who murders children is a victim no matter what they’re suffering through," said Jonathan Hatami, a veteran child abuse prosecutor. "You're never a victim if you murder people because victims don't do something. Something happens to them."

GOT A TIP?

The defense does not dispute that Clancy caused the deaths — but she has pleaded not guilty and is contesting criminal responsibility.

Hatami has spearheaded a number of high-profile cases against child abusers in Los Angeles, California, including the murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, who was tortured and killed by his mother and her boyfriend. Gabriel's killing exposed a series of missed red flags by the county's Department of Children and Family Services and inspired a Netflix docuseries.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE SCORES ‘EXTREMELY HELPFUL’ PSYCHOSIS CONCESSION AS EXPERT FLAGS NEXT HURDLE

"Gabriel Fernandez was tortured and murdered by his mom and her boyfriend — however, there were a lot of other people...that were responsible," Hatami told Fox News Digital. "There were a lot of people that missed signs through the eight or nine months of Gabriel's torture. There were a lot of people in government, in law enforcement, social workers, who missed all these different signs that really could have saved Gabriel — and they didn't do it. However, Pearl Fernandez and Isauro Aguirre were ultimately responsible for the torture and murder of Gabriel and were prosecuted for that and they were convicted of that."

LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

In Clancy’s case, he argued, many of the people and systems around her deserve scrutiny — but that should not turn her into the central victim of the story. In his view, she's been too much of the focus.

"Instead of about the three victims who were innocent kids," he said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

While failures of government and the child welfare system were investigated after Gabriel's murder, that didn't take responsibility away from the killers, he said. And in the Clancy case, he said he sees a risk that the focus on her mental health could eclipse the three children who were killed in their own home.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I didn't see people out in the streets cheering on Pearl Fernandez because there were other people that were somewhat responsible for what happened to Gabriel," he said. "And the same thing plays in this case. Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death. She admitted to strangling them to death with exercise cords."

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Clancy's defense has said she sought help repeatedly as she struggled with depression, sleeplessness, suicidal thoughts and voices urging her to harm herself and the children.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

"If you murder your children, you need to be held accountable and responsible for that," Hatami said. "No matter what the whys are, no matter what reasons are."

SUSAN SMITH ELIGIBLE FOR PAROLE AGAIN AFTER BEING DENIED RELEASE FOR DROWNING HER 2 SONS IN 1994

If convicted of any of the three counts of first-degree murder she faces, Clancy would see a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Your children should be your life. And if you take their life, you should, as a person, want to be punished for that," Hatami said.
