The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Bolt Launches App-Free Ride Kiosks in the Czech Republic
World.content:
Bolt has introduced self-service kiosks in the Czech Republic that allow customers to order a ride without a smartphone, mobile data or the Bolt app.

The first kiosk is now operating at Westfield Chodov in Prague. A second will open at Westfield Černý Most on September 1. The company says it plans to consider other high-traffic locations in the future.



The kiosks use TapBox technology and provide access to the same Bolt driver network, pricing and safety standards available through the app.

Customers can place an order directly at the screen, making the service available to people who do not use smartphones or cannot access their phones at the time.

Both shopping centres have also introduced dedicated parking spaces for Bolt drivers collecting passengers. Customers are directed to these designated areas rather than having to meet drivers at potentially unsafe stopping points such as bus stops.

How Bolt kiosks work

Ordering a ride takes several steps. Customers enter their destination, select a ride category and provide their phone number. The available categories are Standard, Comfort, Premium and XL.

Payment is made by card. Once the booking is completed, the kiosk prints a confirmation and sends an SMS containing the vehicle details, estimated arrival time and instructions for finding the driver.

The kiosks operate around the clock and support Czech, English, German, French and Ukrainian.

Each ride booked through a kiosk carries an additional CZK 25 fee.

Bolt says the system could also benefit drivers by connecting them with customers who might otherwise be unable to use the app. The company expects the kiosks to reduce waiting times between rides at busy shopping centres and create additional opportunities for drivers.

The Czech launch follows the introduction of similar kiosks in Slovakia earlier this summer, including at airports.

World.title: Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Cycle Routes but Cycling Numbers Barely Rise
World.content:
Prague is continuing to expand its cycling infrastructure, but the number of recorded bicycle journeys across the city has remained largely unchanged.

Automatic counters installed on major cycling routes recorded about 5.6 million passages in 2025, roughly 1 percent fewer than the previous year.

After adjusting for counter failures and temporary route closures, however, the Technical Road Administration (TSK) calculated a 0.4 percent increase in cycling traffic.



Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Routes Away From Traffic

The city added 18 kilometers of two-way cycle paths and other cycling routes separated from motor traffic during the year. The total length of marked cycling routes increased by one kilometer to approximately 550 kilometers.

Routes separated from car traffic now account for 263 kilometers of the network, an increase of seven kilometers compared with the previous year.

TSK operates automatic counters at 31 locations on Prague’s main cycling routes. The devices use induction loops or radar to record cyclists and can determine their direction of travel.

The largest increase in two-way cycling routes came over the past year. Their combined length grew from 63 to 81 kilometers. These routes allow cyclists to travel in both directions on streets that are otherwise one-way for motor vehicles.

New two-way routes were added mainly in Prague 7 around Letná, in Prague 5 in Barrandov, and in Prague 6 around Na Petynce, Rozdělovská and Podbaba.

Modřany Remains Prague’s Busiest Cycling Route

The highest number of cyclists was recorded in Modřany, at the intersection of Vltavanů and U Kino streets. The counter registered 578,016 passages during the year.

Another 540,656 cycling journeys were recorded on Povltavská Street south of Troja Castle.

The largest year-on-year increase was recorded on the Barrandov Bridge, where cycling traffic rose following the completion of its more than two-year reconstruction.

World.title: “Upcycling” Prague: Old Offices and Industrial Sites Find New Life as Apartments
World.content:
Former offices, commercial properties and industrial sites in Prague are being converted into apartments rather than demolished, giving developers another option in a city struggling to build enough new homes.

The approach is sometimes described as “upcycling” — adapting ageing buildings for a new purpose while making use of structures and land that are already developed.

One recent example is in Pankrác, near Vyšehrad, where an office building has been converted into the Mo-cha HOME residential complex.



Developed by Cimex, the project opened this spring with 91 fully equipped apartments, most of them in the Czech 2+kk layout, consisting of a living room with a kitchenette and one separate bedroom.

Existing buildings offer valuable locations

Owners of older properties increasingly have to decide whether to renovate them, change their use or demolish them. Many were built for different needs and standards than those expected from buildings today.

Their locations, however, can be a major advantage. Older properties are often close to public transport, shops and other services, making them attractive for residential conversion.

Transforming an existing building can also be faster to prepare than developing a completely new project on a brownfield, although each property must be assessed individually.

The approach can preserve existing structures, reduce demolition and make better use of land that is already developed.

More former offices are becoming homes

Pankrác is not the only part of Prague where old buildings are being converted into housing.

In Holešovice, the former Tesla complex, once used for light-bulb production, has been transformed into a residential project with 149 apartments. The building had stood unused for years, but its main structure remained in relatively good condition.

In Prague 7, another former administrative building near Urania has also been adapted for residential use.

In Prague 3, PSN is preparing the reconstruction of a former telecommunications exchange on Fibichova Street. Built in 1926 and designed by architect Bohumír Kozák, the building is expected to become a rental housing project with 116 units.

One of the largest transformations is planned in Žižkov, where the functionalist former General Pension Institute will be converted into an apartment building with smaller units. The project received a building permit last year.

Not every older building is suitable for conversion. Technical condition, layout, location, project costs and future use all determine whether redevelopment makes economic and practical sense.

World.title: Hungary to reclaim EUR 303 million as government moves to scrap controversial foundations
World.content:
The ministry of science and technology will recover a total HUF 110 billion (EUR 303 million) through the elimination of public interest asset management foundations (KEKVA), Zoltán Tanács, the minister, said on Facebook on Monday.

Tanács said his portfolio would take over the activities of the ZalaZONE and Élvonal foundations, adding that while the “redundant” foundations would be scrapped, the ministry would maintain their activities. He also added that scrapping the system would save the ministry an annual HUF 800 million.

According to Tanács, the two foundations have a combined HUF 62.5 billion on their accounts, while they also have assets worth nearly HUF 50 billion. “That is over HUF 110 billion – from now on in public funds,” the minister added.

Tanács said both Élvonal’s and ZalaZONE’s activities were crucial, the first focusing on the development of young talents and building world-class scientific teams and the latter having an automotive research and development infrastructure, which could provide a test environment for self-driving cars, drones and robots in future. “But all that does not require an unnecessarily expensive, not sufficiently transparent or controlled foundation model,” he added.

World.title: Hungarian FM Anita Orbán names new ambassadors: historians tapped for Paris and Warsaw
World.content:
Prominent historians and specialists are among the latest nominees for key ambassadorial and consular posts. Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has announced several new nominees for ambassadorial and consular positions, including historians selected for key posts in Paris and Warsaw.

Speaking on ATV’s Egyenes Beszéd on Monday evening, Orbán said the government had so far replaced 34 of Hungary’s 138 heads of mission since the change of government. She stressed that most of the new appointments were career diplomats, although several well-known experts from academia and other fields have also been selected.

Among the latest nominees are historian Balázs Ablonczy for Paris, election expert Mátyás Bódi for Barcelona, historian and Poland specialist Miklós Mitrovits for Warsaw, and China expert Tamás Hajba for Beijing.

Historian nominated for Paris

Ablonczy, a historian specialising in Hungarian-French relations, has been asked to serve as Hungary’s ambassador in Paris. He previously headed the Hungarian Institute in Paris between 2011 and 2015. Orbán described him as one of the country’s leading experts on Hungarian-French diplomatic relations, making his nomination one of the most notable among the latest appointments.

The Warsaw nomination has also gone to a historian. Mitrovits, a prominent Polish studies expert, currently teaches at a Polish university and has extensive experience researching Poland and Hungarian-Polish relations.

Election expert to become Barcelona consul general

One of the more unexpected names on the list is Mátyás Bódi, who became widely known in Hungary through his work on electoral geography. Orbán has asked Bódi to become Hungary’s consul general in Barcelona, although the nominees are currently at different stages of the appointment process.

The foreign minister said the government was seeking to select people with relevant professional expertise, language skills and knowledge of the countries and regions where they will serve. “These names also illustrate that we are trying to find the best person for every location,” Orbán said, highlighting professional preparedness and integrity alongside knowledge of the relevant language and bilateral relationship.

China post goes to an experienced China specialist

Tamás Hajba has been selected as Hungary’s next ambassador to Beijing. Unlike some of the other newly announced names, Hajba has a long career in diplomacy and international economic policy. He spent more than a decade working at Hungary’s Foreign Ministry before joining the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in Paris, where he worked as a China specialist.

Orbán said the majority of the newly selected heads of mission were career diplomats, with Hajba among those appointments. She also said the government was trying to match diplomats to posts where their existing knowledge and experience could be put to the best use.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Why has Hungary recalled 34 ambassadors?

Orbán also addressed the government’s decision to recall 34 heads of mission since taking office. She rejected the idea that all of those diplomats had been recalled simply because they were associated with the previous Fidesz government. According to the minister, some were replaced because they had already spent an unusually long period in their posts.

Under previous governments, some ambassadors remained abroad for as long as 10 or even 12 years. Orbán argued that lengthy postings can create a diplomatic problem, as questions may eventually arise over whether a diplomat has become too closely embedded in the interests of the country where they serve.

The new government plans to restore a more traditional rotation system. Under the proposed arrangement, ambassadors and consuls general would spend four years on a foreign posting before returning to Hungary for at least one year.

World.title: Hungarian Gripen crash: Swedish Saab offers support as investigation begins
World.content:
The fighter jet that crashed near Szolnok on Monday was a single-seat Gripen C, not the latest E/F model. Saab says it will assist the Hungarian investigation, while the crash has also briefly affected the Swedish defence company’s share price.

Saab has confirmed that the Hungarian Gripen fighter jet that crashed near Szolnok on Monday was a single-seat Gripen C. The Hungarian pilot ejected from the aircraft and survived the crash. Hungarian authorities are responsible for investigating what caused the accident, while Saab says it will provide technical assistance to the investigation.

“Of course, Saab will assist in the investigation,” Mattias Rådström, the company’s press manager, told Swedish news agency Direkt.

Gripen developed a fault during a training flight

The aircraft was flying alongside another Gripen during a training exercise when a warning indicating a malfunction appeared in the cockpit. The training mission was aborted, and the two aircraft headed towards Szolnok, as the damaged fighter could reportedly no longer reach Kecskemét.

However, another incident occurred during the final stage of the landing. The pilot decided to eject, after which the aircraft left the runway area and caught fire.

The pilot survived the ejection and is currently reported to be in a stable condition.

Hungary’s air force has suspended Gripen training flights until the investigation is completed. The aircraft assigned to alert and operational duties continue to perform their missions. Investigators have already begun examining the crash site, while data from the fighter’s flight recorder – commonly known as its black box – could prove crucial in determining exactly what happened.

Could Hungary ground its Gripen fleet?

Saab has not announced a general flight ban for the Gripen following the accident. Asked whether the aircraft could potentially be grounded while the investigation is under way, Rådström said the company would have to return to the question if such a decision became necessary.

The crash leaves Hungary with 17 Gripen aircraft in service.

Saab said in June that it had completed deliveries under an additional agreement signed by Sweden’s Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and Hungary’s Ministry of Defence in January 2024. Hungary had subsequently operated a total of 18 Gripen C/D aircraft: 16 single-seat Gripen C fighters and two two-seat Gripen D aircraft. Hungary has not purchased the newer Gripen E/F variant.

The Gripen is a single-engine, supersonic multirole fighter designed for missions including air combat, ground attack and reconnaissance.

Saab shares briefly fall after the crash

The accident also had a short-term impact on Saab’s shares on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, according to Világgazdaság. The stock initially reversed an earlier gain of around 0.8% and briefly fell by approximately 0.6% following reports of the Hungarian crash.

The shares subsequently recovered much of the lost ground. By around noon, Saab stock was up approximately 0.1% for the day.

World.title: The Guardian: Hungary is ‘de-Orbánising’ at record speed
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s government has launched Hungary’s most dramatic transformation since the fall of communism, according to a Guardian editorial – but concerns remain over constitutional moves targeting Fidesz politicians and the fate of more than EUR 10 billion in EU funds.

Hungary is undergoing its most far-reaching political transformation since the fall of communism in 1989, according to The Guardian, which says Péter Magyar’s government is dismantling Viktor Orbán’s 16-year political legacy at an “extraordinary pace”.

In an editorial published on Sunday, the British newspaper assessed Magyar’s first three months as prime minister, describing the changes as a “peaceful political revolution”.

The Guardian portrays Orbán’s former system as a “soft autocracy” that flourished on corruption and extended its influence across much of Hungarian society, from religion and culture to the media. Now, it argues, that system is being dismantled at remarkable speed.

New president and a shake-up of state media

One of the most significant developments highlighted by the newspaper is the appointment of András Baka as Hungary’s new president. Baka, a former president of Hungary’s Supreme Court, was removed from his judicial position during Orbán’s rule in a case that was later found to have violated his rights by the European Court of Human Rights.

His appointment stands in stark contrast to the departure of his predecessor, Tamás Sulyok. Magyar had accused Sulyok of effectively rubber-stamping the erosion of the rule of law, while a constitutional amendment brought his presidential term to an early end.

The Guardian also points to the return of news bulletins to Hungary’s main state television channel on 20 August, after a six-week suspension. The newspaper describes ending what Magyar has portrayed as overt political bias in state media as one of his key campaign promises. Magyar won April’s election despite an electoral system that the Guardian says was weighted in Orbán’s favour.

Hungary goes after the legacy of corruption

The government’s efforts to dismantle corruption networks established during the previous administration have also been moving quickly, according to the editorial. The Guardian says well over EUR 100 billion in public funds, including billions in EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during Orbán’s years in power.

Investigators have been given new powers to pursue allegedly misappropriated assets through Hungary’s newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Magyar has also confirmed Hungary’s participation in the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, a move intended to strengthen the protection of EU funds and the investigation of financial crimes.

The next major test could come as soon as this autumn. Brussels has given Hungary until the end of August to demonstrate that sufficient measures have been taken to tackle corruption. More than EUR 10 billion in frozen EU funding is at stake.

The Guardian considers it likely that the vast majority of the money will eventually be released, arguing that this would further cement the rapprochement between Hungary and the European Union after years of conflict.

Concerns over Fidesz and ‘revenge’

Despite its broadly positive assessment of the new government’s direction, The Guardian also raises concerns about some of Magyar’s methods. The newspaper points to constitutional manoeuvring aimed at preventing a number of Fidesz MPs from standing in future elections.

President Baka has himself warned against creating the impression that the new government is seeking revenge against Orbán’s supporters. The Guardian nevertheless argues that a root-and-branch effort to dismantle the former system was necessary, and notes that Magyar’s approach continues to receive strong public backing in opinion polls.

At the same time, the newspaper cautions that rebuilding Hungary as a “normal pluralist European democracy” will take time.

For now, it describes Magyar as a “one-man political whirlwind” at the head of what is effectively a national unity government, supported by voters from across the political spectrum.

From symbolic gestures to a political revolution

The Guardian also highlights the symbolic changes introduced by Magyar. In May, the new prime minister moved his office out of the Carmelite Monastery, the heavily guarded building used by Orbán during his premiership. The building has since been opened to the public.

“I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” Magyar said shortly after taking office, the newspaper recalls.

Three months later, The Guardian argues, that symbolic break with the past has been accompanied by much more substantial changes.

World.title: Hungary begins EUR 275 school-starting support payments to families
World.content:
The first HUF 50,000 instalment of Hungary’s new school-starting allowance has begun reaching eligible families, with the government saying the scheme will support the families of more than 400,000 children.

Hungary has begun paying the first instalment of a new HUF 100,000 (roughly EUR 275) school-starting allowance to eligible families, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Monday.

“Today we began the payment of the first instalment of the HUF 100,000 school-starting support to the families of 400,000 children,” Magyar said in a Facebook post, adding: “We promised it, and we delivered it.”

The first payment amounts to HUF 50,000 (EUR 138) and is being distributed ahead of the new school year to help families cover the costs associated with starting school.

Second HUF 50,000 payment coming in November

The remaining HUF 50,000 will be paid by the end of November in the form of a voucher that can be used for the child’s schooling needs. According to the government, the support is intended to help with significant back-to-school expenses, including school supplies, clothing and other essential items.

The first instalment is being paid by the Hungarian State Treasury in the same way as the family allowance. Families who receive their family allowance into a bank account will receive the school-starting support in the same account, while those who receive it in cash will receive the money through the post.

The school-starting allowance is paid separately from the family allowance. The State Treasury is also bringing forward the payment of September’s family allowance, as well as several other family support benefits, including GYES, GYED, CSED and GYET.

Who is eligible for the HUF 100,000 support?

The new benefit is targeted at families considered to be in greater need of financial assistance. Eligibility depends on several conditions. According to a statement by the Hungarian government, the child must meet at least one of the following criteria:

be eligible for regular child protection benefits;

have a long-term illness or severe disability and therefore qualify for a higher family allowance;

have special educational needs;

participate in the Dobbantó programme or workshop-school training;

be raised by a single parent;

live in the child protection care system; or

receive an orphan’s benefit.

In addition, family allowance must be paid for the child for August, with at least one of the above conditions already applying at that time. The child must also attend a public education or vocational training institution, or be starting their first year of school in September.

No application is required

Eligible families do not need to submit an application for the payment. The government says the payments will be arranged automatically using existing official registers, meaning parents do not need to register, submit a separate request or complete any forms.

The HUF 100,000 benefit is also tax-free and cannot be subject to enforcement proceedings, meaning the full amount is intended to remain available for the child’s needs.

With the first HUF 50,000 now being distributed and the second instalment due by 30 November, the government says the scheme will provide direct financial help to the families of more than 400,000 children as the new school year begins.

World.title: Hungarian spa to close in bid to save millions as town struggles with budget
World.content:
A spa in the Hungarian town of Szerencs will temporarily close from 1 September as the municipality looks to cut costs and save almost HUF 25 million (around EUR 69,000) by the end of the year.

The Szerencsi Fürdő & Wellnessház will remain closed to visitors until at least 17 December, according to an announcement by Szerencsi Hírek and Mayor Attila Kiss. The decision comes as the town seeks to reduce spending across its municipal operations.

Low visitor numbers make spa costly to operate

Szerencs operates two water facilities: the Szerencsi Fürdő & Wellnessház and a municipal swimming pool. While the swimming pool benefits from state support and energy-efficiency improvements, the spa has to be financed from the town’s own resources.

Visitor numbers at the spa have remained relatively low despite efforts to attract more guests, including free entry vouchers provided by the municipality.

The town had previously ordered the Szerencsi Városüzemeltető Nonprofit Kft., which operates the spa, to cut its costs by around 10 per cent because of the municipality’s financial situation. After examining the available options, the company concluded that temporarily closing the spa would deliver the largest savings.

Nearly HUF 25 million in savings expected

Mayor Attila Kiss said the closure between 1 September and 17 December could generate substantial savings across several areas.

The municipality expects to save approximately:

HUF 9.8 million on wages and related contributions

on wages and related contributions HUF 5.2 million on natural gas

on natural gas HUF 6.8 million on electricity

on electricity HUF 2.2 million on water and sewage charges

on water and sewage charges HUF 570,000 on water testing and monitoring

on water testing and monitoring HUF 340,000 on chemicals

Together, these measures could save the town close to HUF 25 million by the end of the year.

The closure will not mean that the entire building becomes unused. Tenants operating businesses there will continue to have access to their premises, while a smaller and more economical heating system will be introduced to heat the necessary parts of the building. Staff working at the spa will, where possible, be reassigned to other duties.

If you missed it: Hungary’s famous Miskolctapolca Cave Bath finally reopens after almost two years

Spa could reopen around Christmas

The municipality says it does not want residents to be left without access to swimming facilities for an extended period. The town’s swimming pool is normally scheduled to close temporarily after 19 December for maintenance and a water change. If Szerencs’ financial position improves and the planned savings are achieved, the municipality may therefore reopen the spa from 18 December until around mid-January.

The aim is to ensure that one of the town’s two water facilities remains available to residents whenever possible. Residents who still have free vouchers for the spa can use them until 31 August. After the temporary closure begins, unused vouchers will be accepted at the municipal swimming pool instead.

The Szerencsi Fürdő & Wellnessház was previously closed in autumn 2022 due to soaring electricity and gas prices and did not reopen until June 2023, according to Borsod24.

World.title: Baby taken from German hospital found on Hungarian motorway
World.content:
A sick baby who was taken from a German hospital without permission has been found safe in Hungary after police tracked the vehicle carrying the child and intercepted it on the M43 motorway.

German authorities issued a wanted notice after the infant was removed from the hospital. Hungarian police were alerted to the case and immediately passed the information to officers on patrol in Csongrád-Csanád County.

Police tracked the vehicle to the M43

According to the Csongrád-Csanád County Police Headquarters, officers were able to determine the vehicle’s expected route by monitoring its movements.

The information enabled police to organise a rapid and coordinated intervention. Officers eventually stopped the vehicle at a rest area on the M43 motorway in southern Hungary. The circumstances surrounding why the baby was taken from the German hospital have not been disclosed.

If you missed it: Breaking: Hungarian Air Force Gripen fighter jet crashes near Szolnok – UPDATE: Video

Baby taken to hospital in stable condition

Police said the infant was found in a stable condition. With the assistance of Hungary’s National Ambulance Service, the baby was taken to hospital to receive the necessary medical treatment. The officers involved in the operation are set to receive official recognition from the deputy national police chief responsible for policing.

The Hungarian police described the operation as a race against time to protect a vulnerable child. Thanks to the swift intervention, the baby was brought to safety.

World.title: Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ
World.content:
Lower new-build property prices in Bucharest and Poland’s major cities may catch the attention of Hungarian buyers, but the success of a property investment abroad is determined by much more than the purchase price and achievable rental income. An analysis by Cordia comparing the Hungarian, Polish and Romanian markets, while also looking at Spain, examines the differences, costs and yields investors should consider when thinking about entering a new-build market in the region or buying a newly built home in a popular holiday destination.

By the end of the first quarter of this year, the average price per square metre of new-build homes in Budapest had risen above HUF 1.9 million, 8% higher than in March 2025. Against this backdrop, Bucharest may look particularly attractive: even using the average exchange rates recorded during the first quarter, the gross average price remained below HUF 1.3 million per square metre despite annual price growth of more than 10%.

Among Poland’s major property markets – Warsaw, Kraków, the Tricity area (Sopot, Gdańsk and Gdynia), Wrocław, Poznań and Łódź – the capital is the most expensive. By the end of March, the average price per square metre of new-build homes in Warsaw, calculated in forints and referring to properties in shell-and-core condition, approached HUF 1.7 million. In Poznań, meanwhile, the average remained below HUF 1.2 million. These figures are among the findings of a regional market comparison prepared by Cordia, one of Hungary’s leading residential property developers.

“These potentially significant price differences may also spark the interest of Hungarian investors. For our projects abroad, we naturally assist buyers who are considering purchasing a new-build apartment either in regional markets or even on the Spanish Riviera,” said Áron Görög, Sales Director at Cordia.

“On the Costa del Sol, where we are now developing our second project, we are seeing significant appreciation. The average price of €7,220 per square metre recorded in March this year – equivalent to around HUF 2.6 million – was almost 9% higher than a year earlier. It is also important to note that developers there traditionally advertise net prices, to which 10% VAT is then added.”

If you missed it: Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

What about rental prices?

For a property investment, achievable rental income and the characteristics of the local rental market are also crucial.

In Poland, for example, lower prices per square metre come with unit rental prices comparable to or higher than the Budapest average. As a result, gross rental yields calculated in euros range between 4.5% and 6%, even after taking into account the additional costs required to bring a property to a fully finished, move-in-ready condition.

It is also worth looking at the differences between individual Polish cities. Poznań, for instance, is a major industrial and logistics hub, with low unemployment and more moderate new-build property prices. In Warsaw, on the other hand, investors can expect relatively high property prices but also stable rental demand, as the capital is the country’s main business centre.

In Bucharest, relatively low new-build prices compared with other regional markets offer an attractive entry point. However, gross rental yields are also broadly in line with the Polish average, at around 5–6%.

“Sales have recently begun at Cordia’s latest Bucharest project, the 274-apartment Centropolitan development. We are seeing significant interest in the project from buyers in Hungary as well,” the expert said.

Double land costs and shell-and-core apartments in Warsaw

It is also worth examining what lies behind the significant differences in property prices across the region.

When interpreting Warsaw’s prices, it is important to bear in mind that, unlike in Hungary and Romania, developers traditionally offer apartments in shell-and-core rather than fully finished condition. This means buyers face substantial additional costs beyond the purchase price before they can move in.

At the same time, construction costs for an average Warsaw or Bucharest development are 25–33% lower than in Budapest. Land prices, however, tell a different story. In Warsaw, land represents a cost more than twice as high in the per-square-metre price of a property compared with the Hungarian or Romanian capital.

Differences in tax systems must also be taken into account. In Hungary, the standard VAT rate for new-build homes is currently 5%, and VAT can also be reclaimed in the case of homes in designated brownfield regeneration zones. In Poland, an 8% VAT rate applies to residential properties smaller than 150 square metres, while the portion above that threshold is subject to a 23% rate. In Romania, following a temporary period with a lower tax burden, the standard VAT rate returned to 21% in August this year.

“Alongside differences on the cost side, prices are also strongly influenced by the complexity of administration, the varying strength of demand and the range of government measures available to support buyers,” Görög emphasised.

Air conditioning is now a basic requirement in Bucharest and Budapest

“The technology used in the buildings we develop is fundamentally similar. There is also no difference in the fact that we build apartments with terraces everywhere, although this is less important to Polish buyers. Efficient floor plans are expected across all markets, but environmental awareness and energy efficiency are less prominent considerations in Poland and Romania.

“As summers become increasingly hot, buyers in both Budapest and Bucharest are placing greater emphasis on effective cooling systems, whereas this is not as common in Poland, particularly in the northern parts of the country,” the expert said.

Interestingly, Poland is introducing energy-efficiency ratings for multi-apartment buildings only this year, making it the last EU member state to do so. Experts believe this could encourage investors to sell older, energy-inefficient apartments and instead seek out newly built, energy-efficient properties.

According to Cordia’s experience, however, there is one common trend across all markets: buyers everywhere are increasingly demanding higher quality, better-equipped homes and additional services, such as communal spaces and facilities, co-working areas, lounges and gastro bars.

Here, the company can draw particularly strongly on its experience in the more developed Spanish market. This gives Cordia a competitive advantage in markets such as Romania, where such extras are still relatively uncommon in projects developed by other companies.

World.title: Romanian unions demand minimum wage increase from January 2027
World.content:
Several Romanian trade union federations will protest outside the Ministry of Labour on August 25, demanding an increase in the statutory minimum wage from January 1, 2027, and the resumption of collective bargaining at sectoral and national levels, according to the National Trade Union Confederation Cartel Alfa, as reported by Agerpres.

The protest will bring together the Federation of Trade Unions, the Federation of IT & Communications Unions and the Federation of Financial Industry Unions, which are affiliated with Cartel Alfa and UNI Global Union, as well as the Insurance and Banking Union Federation, affiliated with the Confederation of Democratic Trade Unions of Romania and UNI Global Union.

The unions said collective bargaining in the private sector is facing blockages, with some companies and employer organisations refusing to participate in negotiations, lacking mandates from their members or rejecting proposals submitted by trade unions.

The organisations also criticised the state for failing to act sufficiently as a facilitator of negotiations at sectoral and national levels. They said the government has not created adequate conditions for effective social dialogue despite the Action Plan for the Promotion of Collective Bargaining 2025-2030.

“The state does not assume the role of facilitator of sectoral and national negotiations. Although the promotion of collective bargaining is provided for in the Action Plan for the Promotion of Collective Bargaining 2025-2030, the authorities fail to create the necessary conditions for an efficient social dialogue and for the conduct of real negotiations,” Cartel Alfa said.

The unions are also seeking an increase in the minimum statutory wage from January 1, 2027, with its new level to be established according to the mechanism provided by Romanian law and following consultations with social partners.

Romania last increased the minimum wage in July 2026. The latest demand comes as the government is negotiating a new wage law for the budgetary sector, while seeking to contain public expenditure amid fiscal consolidation measures.

The unions said the minimum wage decision should be made through a transparent process involving employers and employee representatives, alongside the statutory mechanism for determining its level.

World.title: Romanian minister says there’s still hope for new Wage Law
World.content:
President Nicusor Dan will resume efforts to unblock the talks among centrist parties for the wage Law on August 25, according to sources consulted by Economedia.ro, while G4media.ro cited minister of investments and European projects (MIPE) Dragos Pislaru expressing hopes for a last-minute agreement on the law that needs to be legislated by the end of the month for bringing EUR 770 million under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). Besides the new Law on Integrity Agency (ANI), the Wage Law is one of the two milestones under RRF with the weakest political support.

Sorin Grindeanu, the leader of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), said that it is nearly impossible to have the Wage Law legislated by the end-of-the-month deadline, according to Spotmedia.ro.

Grindeanu said that Romania needs a wage law, but this law must be fair and discussed with all social partners. The initial deadline for the Wage Law as a milestone under the RRF/PNRR was June 30, 2023. The deadline was deferred to December 31, 20024 and later to August 31, 2026. During the entire period of time until May 5, when PSD left the ruling coalition, the Labour Ministry has been supervised by the Social Democrats.

Despite the prolonged period of time dedicated to the drafting of the Wage Law, former PSD minister Florin Manole apparently left no draft when leaving the office at the end of April. Even now, there is very little debate on the structure of relative wages set for individual positions in the budgetary sector – and more for the overall payroll envelope.

Minister Pîslaru said that, following the discussions, two areas were identified where there are problems regarding the social acceptability of the project: Health and Education.

In the case of Health, the minister invoked the results of a salary simulator carried out by the Health Solidarity Federation.

"78% of those who responded (…) have increases," said Pîslaru, adding that 58% of respondents believe the law should pass, while approximately 20% believe it should not be adopted.

World.title: First Romanian companies selected for SME Eco-Tech funding
World.content:
The first Romanian companies have been admitted in principle for financing under the SME Eco-Tech programme, with successful applicants now receiving notifications and being required to contact their selected credit institution within five days, according to interim minister of economy Irineu Darău, cited by Mediafax.

The first stage of the programme, which involved selecting companies seeking financing, has now concluded, while registration remains open for eligible applicants until September 24. The available funding has not been exhausted, the minister said.

“I am happy to announce that we have the first concrete result of the SME Eco-Tech Program. Companies admitted in principle to funding have just started receiving acceptance notifications through the registration platform,” Darău said.

Microenterprises can continue to apply after the authorities removed a RON 2 million turnover ceiling that had previously restricted access to the programme. The change was made following discussions with Swiss partners, according to the minister.

The programme has a total budget of RON 288 million (over EUR 50 million) and is designed to support investments aimed at improving the competitiveness and environmental performance of Romanian small and medium-sized enterprises.

Eligible projects include the modernisation of production lines, automation and digitalisation of business processes, energy-efficiency investments and the adoption of green technologies and recycling solutions.

Funding can also be used to purchase equipment and technologies intended to increase the competitiveness of Romanian companies, according to the Ministry of Economy.

The programme is part of efforts to support companies in reducing energy consumption and adopting cleaner production technologies, while improving productivity through digitalisation and automation.

The ministry said the continued availability of places means eligible microenterprises and other SMEs can still submit applications before the September 24 deadline. Applicants admitted in principle must then complete the required procedures with the credit institution selected through the programme.

World.title: Lukoil’s Romanian refinery files for insolvency “to protect activity and employees”
World.content:
The Petrotel refinery owned by the Russian group Lukoil under US sanctions, under extended supervision by the Romanian state since February 2026, will enter insolvency, according to the decision confirmed on Monday, August 24, in a response to Mediafax. The Petrotel refinery's activity was stopped in October last year for scheduled technical overhaul works, but was not resumed in the meantime, due to the international sanctions.

The Petrotel refinery owned by Lukoil used to provide 21% of the national fuel production and is the only one of the four on Romanian territory (including the smaller Vega refinery owned by Rompetrol Group) that is currently closed.

Petrotel Lukoil officials cited by Profit.ro said recently that they are working with the competent institutions of the Romanian state to restart the refinery as quickly as possible and that the supervisor appointed by the government in the context of the economic sanctions imposed by the US against the parent company has not suspended its payments.

The company explained that the insolvency procedure can provide the necessary legal framework to protect the industrial asset and resume operations, even in the context of OFAC restrictions, officials said.

"Petrotel Lukoil continues all legal and operational steps to restart the facilities and resume the refinery's activity. The company's priorities are to retain its entire workforce and all professional skills, protect relationships with Romanian suppliers and partners, continue its fiscal contribution and maintain a relevant asset for Romania's energy security," the statement said.

According to the cited source, in the current context, the company believes that the insolvency procedure can provide the necessary legal protection to preserve the activity, stabilise commercial relations and prepare for the relaunch of operations. The objective pursued is not to close the refinery, but to maintain its industrial capacity in a stable, predictable formula and compatible with the strategic interests of Romania and its European partners.

Petrotel Lukoil has been under extended supervision by the Romanian state since February 12, 2026.

However, the supervisor's duties are to comply with the imposition of OFAC sanctions. It does not have the power to suspend payments; moreover, it has never done so.

"The refinery must enter the production process as quickly as possible and help Romania overcome this current situation on the fuel market," Petrotel Lukoil representatives told Profit.ro.

In turn, supervisor Bogdan Bugheanu conveyed that "the institution of the special supervisor is to deal exclusively with compliance with all special sanctions imposed by OFAC, and the common interest of all parties involved is for the refinery to restart as quickly as possible to support the fuel market, given the current situation."

World.title: Babiš-linked AdBlue producer Greenchem to acquire Romanian distribution assets
World.content:
Greenchem Romania, an AdBlue producer, part of Greenchem Holding controlled by Czech businessman and prime minister Andrej Babiš, is going to take over the assets of Romanian distribution companies Inovator Smart Choice, STD EST Logistic and AD Complex Logis, according to Economica.net, citing the competition body’s approval. Babiš’ group of companies already entered Romania in 2023 by taking over integrated grain trader East Grain.

Inovator Smart Choice SRL, STD EST Logistic SRL and AD Complex Logis SRL distribute AdBlue on the Romanian market.

“The assets to be taken over concern the customer base that makes regular purchases of AdBlue from sellers based on contracts concluded with them and those contracts, as well as the customer base that places one-off orders of AdBlue from sellers. In accordance with the provisions of Competition Law, this transaction must be authorised by the Competition Council, which will evaluate it to establish its compatibility with a normal competitive environment and will issue a decision within the deadlines provided by law," the competition authority said.

Greenchem Romania SRL is wholly owned by Greenchem Holding BV, one of the largest producers and distributors of AdBlue, a diesel exhaust fluid used to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions from vehicles and industrial equipment, in Europe. It also sells urea used as a raw material in the AdBlue production process.

Greenchem is part of Agrofert Holding, a large Czech company, in fact an industrial holding with activities in several fields, and which counts 32,000 employees. The group, which has seven business divisions – and is the largest agri-food group in Europe- has an annual turnover of over EUR 8 billion.

The Agrofert holding company is owned and controlled by Czech politician and businessman Andrej Babiš, a billionaire and now Prime Minister of the Czech Republic.

This is not Agrofert’s first acquisition in Romania. In 2023, it bought the majority stake in Cluj-Napoca-based East Grain through a capital increase, the most important foreign investment in Romanian agribusiness in the last year. Then, through this company, it bought, last year, the MarAgro farm in Timiș, which cultivates a total area of ​​7,000 hectares, mainly cereals.

Also, at the end of last year, the same East Grain took over, together with a partner, the 45% majority stake held by the Hungarian group UBM in the agricultural company UBM Feed Romania, from Mureș County. UBM Feed is one of the largest feed producers in Romania.

World.title: Drone crashes near home in Romania’s Vrancea County
World.content:
Residents within a radius of approximately 300 meters were temporarily evacuated on Monday, August 24, after a drone was found crashed into a walnut tree near a house in Ciușlea, Vrancea County, Agerpres reported. The Defense Ministry later said the device carried no explosive payload and most likely belonged to a drone that had entered Romania from the Republic of Moldova earlier that morning.

Witnesses heard a loud noise followed by a bang at around 8:30 a.m., Garoafa mayor Laurențiu Diaconu told Agerpres. The owner of the house also noticed a strong smell of fuel.

However, the drone was not discovered until around 1 p.m., when it was spotted in a walnut tree about five meters from the house.

“The area was isolated, and residents within the safety perimeter of approximately 300 meters were evacuated,” Diaconu said.

Police officers, firefighters and other authorities were deployed to determine whether the device presented a danger. According to the mayor, the drone had broken into two pieces, with one remaining in the tree and the other falling to the ground.

“Following the checks, it was established that the drone did not carry an explosive payload,” the Defense Ministry said.

A separate alert was issued later on Monday after the Defense Ministry detected two aerial targets approximately 25 kilometers northwest of Snake Island at 10:37 p.m. The targets were traveling toward Romania’s border.

Two Spanish Air and Space Force F-18 aircraft stationed at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base were deployed to monitor them. An RO-Alert message was sent to residents in northern Tulcea County at 10:55 p.m.

According to the ministry, the targets disappeared from radar three minutes later, while explosions were reported on the Ukrainian side of the border. No unauthorized entry into Romanian airspace was detected during the second incident.

Another aerial target was detected on Tuesday morning, August 25, approximately four kilometers east of Vâlcove, near Romania’s border, according to the Defense Ministry.

Two Spanish F-18 aircraft from Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base were again scrambled to monitor the situation. The National Military Command Center notified emergency authorities, and an RO-Alert warning was sent to residents in northern Tulcea County at 7:31 a.m.

The ministry said further details would be released as they become available.

World.title: Romanian agrifood company DN AGRAR records 40% EBITDA margin, net profit down 49% in H1 2026
World.content:
DN AGRAR Group (BVB: DN), one of the leading integrated agrifood companies in Romania and the largest dairy milk producer in Europe, closed the first semester of 2026 with a turnover of RON 90.3 million, EBITDA of RON 36 million and a net profit of RON 13.7 million.

The EBITDA margin stood at 40%, with the impact of lower milk prices partially offset by higher production volumes. According to the company, the financial results recorded reflect the level of milk prices across Europe compared with the strong levels recorded in the first half of 2025, as well as continued pressure from operating costs and unfavorable foreign exchange movements.

“The turnover recorded a moderate decline, while profitability was lower, primarily reflecting the decline in milk prices by 30% and the unfavorable movements of the exchange rate. We had anticipated this market adjustment when preparing our 2026 budget, considering the volatility of the European dairy market, inflationary pressures and the broader geopolitical environment,” said Peter de Boer, CEO, DN AGRAR Group.

“Nevertheless, we remained focused on the factors within our control: increasing production, improving operational efficiency, maintaining cost discipline and executing our major investment projects. We invested more than EUR 6 million in the first six months of the year and secured approximately EUR 20 million in financing,” he added.

The company’s operating revenue reached RON 158 million, the same level as last year. Revenues from production sold amounted to RON 90 million, down 9% year-on- year, with milk sales remaining the group’s main source of revenue, having also contributions from compost and the sale of young cattle.

Revenues from operating subsidies increased by 49% to RON 22 million, driven by higher support levels for milk production and animal welfare, including a non-recurring component, as well as the inclusion of the Straja farm in the eligible subsidy base.

Operating expenses reached RON 132 million, up 10%, mainly reflecting the expansion of the group’s operations. EBITDA reached RON 36 million, with an EBITDA margin of 40%. Net profit reached RON 13.7 million, down 49%, reflecting a 30% lower milk selling price and a negative impact of RON 8.5 million on the financial result, driven by higher foreign exchange losses arising from the revaluation of the group’s foreign currency-denominated loan balances.

Total assets reached RON 477 million, up by 8% compared to the end of the previous year. Total liabilities amounted to RON 244 million, up by 10% compared to the end of 2025. Long-term liabilities were roughly RON 138 million, up by 4% compared to the end of the previous year. In accordance with IFRS standards, the company reported an EBITDA of RON 41.6 million and a net profit of RON 21.3 million.

During H1 2026, DN AGRAR continued to execute its 2025–2030 Development Strategy, securing approximately EUR 20 million in financing and advancing all major strategic projects. Key milestones included completing the new milk processing facility, securing financing for the CUT 2 farm and two new composting facilities, advancing the vertical wheatgrass farm and Food Cluster initiative, and signing a binding offer for the acquisition of Panorganic Vitavit.

The biomethane project also progressed according to plan, the company said.

World.title: Romania’s leading Banca Transilvania posts 26.8% higher net profit in first half of 2026
World.content:
In the first six months of the year, Romania’s leading bank, Banca Transilvania (BVB: TLV), recorded a net profit of RON 2.5 billion, 26.8% above the level recorded in the same period last year, according to a press release.

The BT Group's assets reached RON 233.3 billion as of June 30, 2026, up 4% from the end of last year and 12.1% compared with the same period of the previous year. Loans and net leasing receivables granted to customers reached RON 115.7 billion, up 8.4% from the end of 2025 and 14.8% compared with the first half of last year. At the same time, the gross loans-to-deposits ratio increased to 68.5%, 3.8% above the level at the end of last year.

“Despite the challenging economic environment, we managed to grow the bank's customer base and operational activity, which is reflected in our results,” said Ömer Tetik, general manager of Banca Transilvania.

Within the Group, Banca Transilvania's own net profit reached RON 2.1 billion in the first half of the year, up 20.7% compared with the same period last year. Net profit in the second quarter was 25.6% higher compared with the first quarter of the year. The evolution was supported by commercial performance and the acceleration of activity in the second quarter.

The bank's assets increased to RON 217.8 billion, 3.5% above the level at the end of 2025 and 11.3% compared with June 30, 2025. Customer deposits reached RON 172.4 billion, up 2.1% from the end of last year and 8.8% compared with the same period of the previous year.

The gross loan portfolio granted to customers reached RON 113.7 billion, up 7.6% from the end of 2025 and 11.7% compared with June 30, 2025. The quality of the loan portfolio remained at a very good level, with the non-performing loan ratio according to the EBA definition falling to 2.41%, 0.24 percentage points below the level recorded in the same period last year.

The gross loans-to-deposits ratio reached 65.9%, an evolution that reflects the transformation of attracted resources into financing for individuals and companies.

BT also reported a strong capital position, with a solvency ratio of 21.96%, which includes the interim net profit for the first half of 2026. Return on equity remained at a solid level of 21.98%. At the same time, basic earnings per share (EPS) stood at RON 1.9389 for the first half of the year, up 24.2% from the value recorded in the same period of 2025.

Net interest income at the individual level reached RON 3.3 billion, up 4.6% from the first half of 2025. Net fee and commission income increased by 13.5% compared with the same period last year, amid an increase in transaction volumes. Net trading income was 4.9% above the level recorded in the first half of 2025, supported mainly by foreign exchange activity and the performance of financial assets held for trading.

Operating income increased to RON 5.3 billion, up 15.9% compared with the same period last year and 6.2% compared with the first quarter of 2026, as a result of increased commercial activity. The bank's operating expenses were influenced by investments in development and the integration into Banca Transilvania of the technology company Code Crafters, which was part of the BT Group. Compared with the first half of 2025, operating expenses increased by 12.9%, while compared with the first quarter of this year, they decreased by 8.9% in the second quarter of the year.

Operational efficiency remained at a competitive level, with a cost-to-income ratio of 44.6%, or 38.3% excluding the impact of the turnover tax. The figures show the bank's ability to support growth through an efficient and scalable business model.

BT provided companies with financing of RON 17.6 billion, RON 5.1 billion above the level recorded in the same period last year, while it provided RON 7 billion in financing to individuals, of which 31% were real estate/mortgage loans and 67% loans for current needs. The Large Corporate segment was the main driver of growth in financing granted to companies, contributing more than 80% (RON 4.2 billion) to the increase in lending compared with H1 2025, particularly through financing investment projects and working capital needs.

The outstanding balance of gross loans granted to companies increased by 10.1% compared with the end of 2025 and by 14.8% compared with June 30, 2025.

The number of transactions carried out by all customers through all the bank's channels was more than 17% higher than in the first half of last year.

World.title: Planned Amazon Warehouse in Czechia Faces Local Resistance, Again
World.content:
August deadline

Now being developed by investors Accolade and Garbe, the land of the Borsov Economic Development Zone I was purchased in 1998, with initial zoning plans banking on the construction of a large shopping centre.

This never materialised, and in 2020 developers received zoning approval for the construction of four smaller, separate industrial halls – two of which already have building permits – for a total built area of over 148,000 square metres. Now, the modalities have changed again.

Accolade and Garbe redesigned the entire project into a single, larger building (77,000 square metres in size, about 500 metres long and 15 metres high) specifically for a single tenant – Amazon – on an expected 20-year-lease agreement. About 2,500 people could be employed there, working on a two-shift rotation running almost non-stop from 06:30 to 04:30.

According to Borsov nad Vltavou’s mayor, Romana Rycova, the municipality was only informed about the change at the end of April. And in a video posted on August 13, Mayor Rycova stated that the municipal council must now approve the new variant by the end of August or the investors will redesign the project so they can bypass the municipality’s approval – despite an earlier promise made to residents to “wait as long as you need”.

Representatives for the investors tell BIRN that their earlier communication might have been misconstrued. “When we said that there would be no time pressure, we meant that we would not push municipal council members towards a particular decision or influence how they vote,” says Tomas Mile, project manager at Accolade.

“It did not mean that the project itself had no commercial timetable,” he says, adding that the municipality had been informed since late 2025 about the changes. Rather than a sudden change, Mile describes the new single-building option as “the gradual development of a new option in response to a specific requirement from a prospective tenant”.

Furthermore, he says that while “we understand the concerns raised by residents”, he makes the case that developers have shown goodwill and transparency over the past several months to explain the differences and varying impacts to local residents.

Amazon did not respond to BIRN’s requests for comment.

However, Horakova says she has attended all the public meetings held over the past several months and describes the communication there from developers as “misleading at best”.

Considering the new parameters of the project, she also believes that fresh independent studies should be conducted to upgrade now-outdated environmental impact studies and properly evaluate the impact of such a massive distribution centre on traffic, air-quality, noise pollution and local landscape preservation – just a few of the main concerns expressed by both residents and city officials over the past several months.

“We’ve found no evidence that these studies have been updated for the new design, including in the investor’s own newest technical documentation,” Horakova explains.

Echoing the thoughts of other locals, Horakova accuses the developers of “not being a trustworthy party”. Case in point, Veronika Zacha – who became Garbe’s senior manager for business development for Czechia after moving from Panattoni in 2022 – promised during an August town hall meeting: “We don’t want to pressure the municipality, we also understand that you need to familiarise yourself with all the information, so you have time.”

Yet shortly afterwards, city councillors received an SMS clarifying that developers expect a decision by the end of the month – or else they will move ahead with the four-hall format, according to information from iRozhlas.cz and other local outlets.

World.title: Across the Balkans, Foreign-Backed Luxury Developments Cause Local Anger
World.content:
Since Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’ protests began in May, they have attracted worldwide attention and sparked debate within and outside the Balkans about high-profile investors’ mega-projects.

The protests began in response to the proposed luxury tourism projects on Albania’s Sazan Island and the Zvernec protected coastline. The 1.4 and 4.7 billion euro investments are being led by Affinity Partners, an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Kushner and his wife Ivanka Trump first visited Albania in 2021 and announced plans for the development in 2024.

There has been much to anger locals about the projects, including comments Ivanka Trump made on a podcast where she referred to “discovering” Sazan Island and called the state-owned land a “private island”.

Another more substantive issue is that the Albanian government amended the laws on protected areas on February 22, 2024, allowing five-star hotels to be built inside protected areas. This occurred a month before Kushner’s Albanian projects were announced.

World.title: As Turkey Makes Peace, Kurdish Villagers Who Fled Conflict Contemplate Return
World.content:
“It was the biggest breaking point in my life,” said Aydin Kurdis, remembering the day he and his family left their village 32 years ago.

In the early 1990s, the village of Golord, known officially as Bostancik, was home to around 200 families. Its stone houses sat among hills covered with walnut and fruit trees. Villagers made a living raising livestock, while the orchards provided much of what families needed.

“Before we left the village, I didn't know what pain was. I didn't know what poverty was,” Kurdis said, sitting in front of the house where he was born and eating cucumbers just pulled from the garden down the slope on an August afternoon. “Life was hard on us after we moved to the city.”

Kurdis, 52, lives in Yuksekova, the largest district in Turkey’s southeastern Hakkari province, near the Iranian border. Golord is only a 45-minute drive away, but the final 10 kilometres are unpaved, with potholes dotting the dusty mountain road.

World.title: Experts Warn Proposed Limits on Serbian Officials Campaigning Will Be Ineffective
World.content:
Serbia’s parliament began a debate on amendments to the Law on the Prevention of Corruption on Monday – changes the government says will regulate political campaigning by public officials.

But the anti-corruption watchdog Transparency Serbia claims the measures are unlikely to be effective.

Transparency Serbia said the amendments “create the appearance that restrictions are being introduced, while in practice they will have virtually no effect”.

The watchdog pointed out that the OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) has identified campaigning by public officials as “a key element in blurring the line between the party and the state” in Serbia.

It noted that restrictions would apply only after the publication of electoral lists, and focus solely on the conduct of officials who have been nominated as candidates. As a result, the period before this remains unregulated.

It said this allows officials to use “pseudo-events” like school, hospital and construction site tours to campaign, as long as visits were arranged “before the elections were called”.

With advance notice of election dates, government candidates could schedule events “precisely for the period leading up to the elections, even though these events serve no purpose other than promotion.”

Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic has yet to name the precise date for early parliamentary elections, though he has said they will be held in October.

In the meantime, he has embarked on a prolific schedule of visits around the country. Videos from those events appear on media outlets and social networks, showing local people asking the president about infrastructure works and job opportunities. Vucic has also announced numerous giveaways for Serbian adults, alongside a range of subsidies.

This is precisely what Transparency Serbia has in mind with its definition of “promotional activity” by a public official. It says the draft amendments also fail to address ODIHR delivered recommendations on restricting “extraordinary spending by state institutions ahead of elections”.

The watchdog claims that this “helicopter money” – including various measures planned by the government, such as salary increases, lower medicine prices and one-off payments to various different sectors of society – will amount to almost one billion euros by the time the elections are held.

World.title: Translation Cutbacks Limit International Access to North Macedonia’s Literature
World.content:
For a small country of just under two million people, with a small language and an even smaller literary market, getting books translated and published abroad can be crucial to keeping its literature visible beyond its borders.

But for the past two years, Macedonian authors and publishers have had one fewer tool to help them do that. A government programme that provided grants to foreign publishers willing to translate and publish Macedonian books has been suspended since 2024.

The good news is that the Culture Ministry told BIRN there is a “real possibility” it will relaunch a redesigned translation programme later this year. But the bad news is how many excellent books have been denied a wider readership over the last two years.

The Ministry says it typically allocated between one to four million denars [16,000- 65,000 euros] a year for the programme. In 2024, around 84,000 euros was distributed through 31 contracts with foreign publishers. Foreign publishers interested in Macedonian literature could apply to North Macedonia’s Culture Ministry for funding to cover translation costs, reducing the financial risk of publishing authors who are largely unknown in their markets.

Without that incentive, publishers say, some potentially valuable translations simply do not happen. “Our success at international book fairs, such as Frankfurt, is diminished,” says Bojan Sazdov, editor-in-chief of the publishing house TRI and president of the Macedonian Association of Publishers.

“When there is interest in translating a Macedonian book, we can no longer point publishers to the programme as a way of obtaining funding for the translation.”

World.title: Hanging Out: Serbia’s Ruling Party Funfair is About Suppressing Voter Turnout
World.content:
Without Novi Sad’s EXIT Festival, this year’s summer entertainment in Serbia was provided by the ruling Progressive Party funfair.

After a long day visiting factories, inspecting schools, roadworks and parks, government ministers, advisers, and local authorities hung out with people under white tents.

The show included music, dancing, feasting, and live television broadcasts.

Just in the first 18 days of August, President Aleksandar Vucic made 64 live appearances on Serbian TV, according to the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability, CRTA.

Not quite a formal election campaign, if you ask Vucic. Something between a ‘presidential tour’ and a prequel to the actual election campaign that everyone expects in the autumn.

Such media domination is familiar to those who follow populism; party leaders skip formal institutions and speak directly to the people.

When this media takeover combines with the atmosphere of a village fair, people tend to ask private questions publicly. Here’s where the media literacy classes provided by Serbia’s tabloids begin paying off.

World.title: Seven Days: Ukrainian Recalls Captivity at Hands of Bosnian Serb
World.content:
Mykola said he spent most of his captivity in a forest pit between the villages of Shybene and Krasny Rih. He said his hands were tied and there were rats in the pit. When he killed one after it bit him, he said a soldier hit him in the head with a rifle butt. The soldier told him: “Kill another one and I’ll shoot you.”

Mykola said he saw other captives being tortured.

According to the Ukrainian Media Initiative for Human Rights, MIHR, which inspected the site, the pits were some 90 centimetres deep; those inside had to sit in water; they lost feeling in their legs; and they had to urinate and defecate in the same spot.

Lidiia Tarash, a journalist and head of the documentation department of MIHR, said the researchers were led to the site by Mykola. A dead body was found in one of the pits, as well as the remains of Russian military rations, fortifications and ammunition boxes.

MIHR identified five locations in the area where civilians were held and documented the capture of 43 individuals. Its findings helped lead to the indictment of Savicic. Multiple interlocutors said Serbs were among the Russian forces. Everyone named Savicic as being in charge, Tarash said.

In late May last year, the X account of Milorad Dodik, then the president of Bosnia’s predominantly Serb-populated Republika Srpska entity, published a photo of himself visiting the representative office of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Russia. Savicic was in the photo.

Britain imposed sanctions on him in November 2024.

Mykola said Savicic and his unit are the reason he still has trouble sleeping at night. His back was damaged during his captivity and he said he is haunted by the word ‘liberation’, which he heard over and over again from his captors.

“They kept saying: ‘We came to liberate you.’ But liberate me from what? From a normal life?”

Savicic’s trial is a matter of justice and responsibility, he said.

“None of them can say: ‘I was just following orders’ and to think they aren’t responsible for it,” Mykola told BIRN. “Someone gave you an order, but it was still your choice whether to execute it.”

World.title: August 25th 1991 – The Battle of Vukovar Begins
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – On August the 25th, 1991, the battle of Vukovar began, marking the start of one of the most devastating chapters of the Croatian War of Independence.

The most harrowing episode of the Homeland War began on this day in the eastern Croatian city of Vukovar when members of the JNA from the barracks in Vukovar joined Serbian paramilitary units. After doing so, they jointly launched an attack on both Borovo and Vukovar. Index writes that the siege lasted 87 days and transformed Vukovar into a symbol of Croatian resistance and heroism during the Homeland War.

the initial conflicts begin

Slobodan Milošević – NATO

After Croatia declared independence on the 25th of June 1991, local conflicts in eastern Slavonia had already begun. For centuries Vukovar had been a city where Croats, Serbs and Hungarians lived in peace, but the situation changed at the end of the 1980s with the rise of nationalism and the policies of Slobodan Milošević, who wanted to consolidate power in Belgrade.

On the 25th of August, the JNA left the barracks with six tanks that blocked the road towards Bogdanovci. The very next day a new attack on Borovo began that lasted the entire day. The firing briefly stopped, and already during the following night another offensive started. By the 30th of August, the clashes continued one after another, after which a short ceasefire occurred during which weapons were delivered to the Croats in Vukovar from Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci and Zagreb. At that time Mile Dedaković arrived in Vukovar and organised the army and defensive positions in the city.

the serbs wanted to go all the way to zagreb

The JNA commander in Vukovar was Života Panić, who wanted to capture Vukovar as quickly as possible in order to prevent further mobilisation of the Croatian army. The original JNA plan was to take Vukovar and Osijek, then occupy all of Slavonia so that the road towards Varaždin and Zagreb would be open. However, problems already appeared when fewer than two thousand Croatian soldiers withstood numerous JNA attacks in Vukovar.

The plan was not helped by the fact that only 13% of those fit for military service responded to the call-up. After news arrived of the large number of casualties in Vukovar, many soldiers deserted, and by the end of 1991 there were six thousand open court proceedings against deserters. The failure of mobilisation meant the cancellation of the grandiose conquest of the whole of continental Croatia, culminating with Zagreb.

the fall of vukovar and horrific crimes against humanity

Vukovar endured a three-month siege in which seven thousand projectiles fell daily. On the 18th of November the city fell, although only 10–15% of the buildings actually remained. The rest were entirely destroyed. The army entered the city and the expulsion of the non-Serb population and horrific war crimes and crimes against humanity began. Neighbours accused other neighbours of being a defender, informed on where families were located, and just a few days later more than 250 civilians were brutally killed at Ovčara in one single night.

The sight of the murder of hundreds of innocent civilians – Perun

The total number of victims is measured in the thousands of people, and there are probably other undiscovered mass graves containing those who disappeared during the war. The Serbian government under Aleksandar Vučić refuses to cooperate so that the remaining mysteries from the war can finally be resolved.

The city was returned to Croatia only in 1998 through peaceful reintegration, and the 18th of November is marked in Croatia as the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Homeland War. Vukovar has still not recovered from the war: today it has just over 25,000 inhabitants, while in the years before the war it was home to 45,000 people. As the largest Croatian port on the Danube, Vukovar was a busy centre of trade and transport.

Today. it is only a shadow of what it once was, and Croatian authorities from the 1990s until today have not invested enough in it. It was the fifth-largest city in the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, then larger even than Zadar, while today it is not ranked among the ten largest Croatian cities.
