It brought together the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly (OSCE PA) and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), deploying 339 observers from 43 countries.

The mission said the campaign and election day were generally calm and orderly and that contestants were provided equal conditions to organize campaign activities. It also cited the range of political parties participating, the absence of independent parliamentary candidacies and differences in party resources as factors affecting the level of political competition.

“The elections took place at an important moment for Kazakhstan in the continuation of reforms initiated from 2019, which culminated in this year’s constitutional referendum. After undertaking a constitutional reset of its electoral framework, Kazakhstan’s early parliamentary elections provided an opportunity to see whether these changes opened space for healthy political competition,” said Gábor Hajdu, OSCE Special Co-ordinator and leader of the short-term observer mission. “Despite some positive aspects, there are few genuine opportunities for independent candidacies, limited space for civil society and the independent media, and a lack of a level playing field consistent with OSCE commitments, including for women,” he added.

Political competition and new electoral framework

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary vote under the Constitution that entered into force July 1. The new 145-member Kurultai is elected for five years through closed-list proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency with a 5% electoral threshold.

Seven political parties contested the election with 545 registered candidates. Party platforms addressed a range of social and economic issues, although the mission noted that all contesting parties supported President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s policies.

The mission also examined the position of Adilet, which merged with the former ruling Amanat party ahead of the election. Observers said Adilet drew on Amanat’s organizational structures, networks and resources and ran the most extensive and visible campaign. The mission also reported instances involving the use of administrative resources during campaign activities and said these circumstances affected the balance of competition

Lucija Tacer Perlin, head of the OSCE PA delegation, said the wider political environment was important alongside the administration of the vote.

“The absence of parties representing genuine political opposition and the elimination of the right to stand independently for parliamentary elections limited political participation, pluralism, and electoral competitiveness. While party platforms and campaign messages addressed a wide range of social and economic issues, all contesting parties supported the incumbent president’s policies. We also observed that a number of factors affected the level playing field during the campaign,” she said.

The preliminary assessment also addressed political parties’ role in determining who ultimately receives seats in the Kurultai. Some ODIHR interlocutors from local party branches raised questions about the transparency of how lists are compiled and how parties subsequently determine which candidates take seats.

The law maintains a cumulative 30% quota for women, youth and persons with disabilities both on candidate lists and when mandates are distributed. Some 43.9% of registered candidates belonged to at least one of those groups. According to the mission, the combined quota does not guarantee effective representation of each group separately.

Election administration and voting

The mission assessed the technical administration of the election broadly positively, saying election commissions prepared for the vote professionally and within legal deadlines, conducted nationwide training and voter-information campaigns, and took steps to improve accessibility for voters with disabilities. It also noted that contesting parties generally expressed confidence in the election administration.

Election day was described as calm and orderly. International observers assessed opening and voting as overwhelmingly in line with procedures, with voting receiving a positive assessment in 98% of the 1,327 polling stations observed.

Ambassador Vincent Piket, head of the ODIHR election observation mission, said that while much of election day proceeded well, observers identified shortcomings in voting and counting procedures, including discrepancies between observed voter activity and official turnout data.

“While much went well, observers noted a number of serious procedural shortcomings. For instance, they saw identical signatures of voter lists, they saw a lack of enforcement of proper identification requirements by voters, aspiring voters, they saw a non-respect of the secrecy of the casting of ballots, and photographs were taken of ballots in the ballot box and around it. And there were also marked differences between voter activity on the one hand and official turnout data on the other,” said Piket.

Media and public participation

The mission said voters had access to a wide range of media outlets, while noting limited pluralism in the media environment. ODIHR monitoring found that contestants were generally covered in a neutral tone, though election reporting included relatively little analytical or in-depth coverage.

PACE delegation head Sevilay Çelenk said the assessment went beyond election-day procedures to consider the broader conditions for political participation, including media access, political pluralism and public confidence in electoral institutions.

“The relationship between elections and democracy is more delicate than it appears. No democracy can exist without elections, yet the presence of elections doesn’t by itself guarantee democracy. What matters is not just the ballot box, it is also what surrounds it. Campaigns must be free, media access must be equal, institutions must be independent. Political pluralism must be protected. Citizens must trust that their votes will be counted honestly,” said Çelenk.

Broader international perspectives

Additional international commentary on the election focused on the broader constitutional transition and Kazakhstan’s development agenda.

James Whitney, CEO of Car Park Transformer (CPT), welcomed the constitutional reforms and said the company’s infrastructure projects are aligned with Kazakhstan’s broader development priorities and its position between major East-West trade and transport routes.

Honorary Consul of Kazakhstan in Iceland Sigurður Atli Jónsson described the first election to the unicameral Kurultai as a milestone in Kazakhstan’s political development, saying the new framework could bring greater institutional clarity and predictability for international partners and businesses.

“Constitutional reform of this scale is rare, and carrying it through to a new legislature marks the completion of a process that has been years in the making. Seen from Reykjavík, what stands out is the direction of travel,” said Jónsson.

World.title: Experts See Kazakhstan Emerging as Pivotal ‘Connector State’ in Eurasia
World.content:
ASTANA — As competition between the world’s major powers increasingly reshapes trade routes, energy flows and diplomatic alignments, Kazakhstan’s strategic value may lie not in choosing sides, but in remaining able to connect several sides at once, experts said at a policy discussion in Astana.

The discussion on Aug. 21, organized by the CFive Intellectual Platform and the Hudson Institute, brought together perspectives from the United States, Kazakhstan and Switzerland on the changing dynamics across Eurasia. What made the exchange particularly revealing was that the speakers offered no single interpretation of Kazakhstan’s role. One saw the country as a pivotal swing state in the emerging U.S.-China competition; another warned against viewing Central Asia through the interests of major powers alone; and a third stressed that Kazakhstan’s most valuable asset could ultimately be trust.

For senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and an expert on Greater Asia, Central Asia and the Caucasus Ken Moriyasu, Kazakhstan is not simply another strategically located middle power. He described it as the “most important swing state in the world,” noting that Central Asia, the Caucasus and Türkiye could become an increasingly important arena in the competition between the U.S. and China. Moriyasu’s argument rests on the view that China is seeking to reduce its vulnerability to maritime chokepoints by expanding alternative routes across the Eurasian landmass, including pipelines and railways connecting China with Central Asia, the Caspian region, Russia and Europe.

“What will happen, I think, is a two-step. First, China will try to establish alternative routes through the Eurasian landmass, so pipelines and railroads. These are insular from the U.S. Navy,” he said.

In his assessment, the more China can secure access to energy and trade through routes that are less vulnerable to maritime disruption or sanctions, the greater its strategic confidence will become. That makes Kazakhstan important not simply because of its size or energy resources, but because of its position at the intersection of several of these routes. Moriyasu went further, saying Washington does not need to replace Russia or China in Central Asia to affect Beijing’s calculations.

“The beauty for the U.S. is that all it has to do is create doubt in China’s mentality. China needs to be absolutely confident, 100% confident, that it can continue its trade with Europe and continue to import energy without being interrupted by the U.S. Navy after a Taiwan invasion. All America has to do is reduce the 100% confidence to 99% confidence, because if it’s 99%, Xi Jinping will not do it,” he said.

It was an intentionally provocative framing of Kazakhstan’s importance: not as a country that would choose between Washington and Beijing, but as one whose infrastructure, geography and foreign-policy choices could indirectly affect the calculations of much larger powers.

But that approach immediately raised another question: is Kazakhstan really a “swing state” in somebody else’s contest, or does that description itself miss what Central Asian states are trying to achieve? Bulat Sarsenbayev, a career diplomat and former Kazakh ambassador to India and Jordan, pushed back against viewing the region primarily through the prism of great-power competition.

“You were talking on behalf of a big power, America, and different interests. And you did not mention about the interests of our countries, Central Asian countries,” Sarsenbayev said.

For Kazakhstan, the logic of connectivity is first of all practical. As a landlocked country bordering two major powers, it cannot afford to isolate itself from either Russia or China while also seeking access to other markets and partners.

“Though we are a landlocked country, but we have two oceans: one is Russia, one is China,” Sarsenbayev said, recalling a phrase he had used in his diplomatic career.

He said Kazakhstan’s geography should not be interpreted solely as a source of strategic leverage for others. It also imposes its own constraints and creates its own incentives: maintaining relations with major neighbors, expanding transport links, keeping trade routes open and preserving diplomatic flexibility.

Sarsenbayev also challenged the suggestion that Central Asian connectivity with India should be dismissed because of geography. The Himalayas may make modern infrastructure difficult, he said, but they did not prevent centuries of trade between Central Asia, China and India along the historical Silk Road and caravan routes. He pointed to existing transport links through the Caspian and Iran as another reminder that connectivity is often less a question of whether a route is geographically possible than whether political conditions allow it to function effectively.

“The problem is the political problem,” he said, referring to sanctions on Iran, while stressing that the infrastructure itself exists.

That distinction between connectivity as a geopolitical weapon and connectivity as an economic necessity ran through much of the discussion.

A third perspective came from Muise Wahabdeen, a Swiss human rights advocate, journalist and editor-in-chief of The Geneva Times, who shifted the conversation away from the map itself.

“Kazakhstan has many strengths. Its geography, its natural resources, its location, its economic potential. But I believe there is another strength, perhaps an even more important one. That is trust,” Wahabdeen said.

His question was not where Kazakhstan stands, but what it can connect.

“Not simply to stand between interests, but connect these interests: to connect economies, markets, institutions, to connect people, and perhaps most importantly, to connect dialogue,” he said.

That idea offers perhaps a third way of understanding Kazakhstan’s role. Rather than becoming a country that belongs to one geopolitical camp, Kazakhstan could seek influence by remaining useful to several of them at the same time.

Wahabdeen compared it to Geneva, where countries with competing interests continue to use diplomacy and dialogue to manage disagreements. Kazakhstan, he suggested, could develop a similar role in Eurasia, building on President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s own experience in Geneva and on the country’s broader efforts to position itself as a venue for international dialogue. But he also placed a condition on that ambition.

“Strategic autonomy must create strategic credibility, and credibility is not built by words alone. It’s built through institutions, through predictability, through education, through human capital, through openness and through international cooperation,” he said.

That may be the harder part of Kazakhstan’s proposition. Geography cannot be changed, and its value as a bridge between major markets is obvious. But being strategically useful to several competing powers requires more than simply occupying the space between them. It requires the ability to remain predictable enough that different partners continue to trust the country’s commitments.

The discussion therefore pointed beyond the familiar description of Kazakhstan as a transit corridor linking China with Europe. Transport and energy infrastructure remain fundamental to the country’s strategic importance, but the more ambitious vision is to turn connectivity itself into a broader form of influence. Kazakhstan, Wahabdeen said, should think beyond being a transit hub and become “a “knowledge, diplomatic, investment hub, a place for international dialogue, a place where different sides can meet.”

The competing arguments presented in Astana ultimately suggest that Kazakhstan’s strategic relevance may be growing precisely because the world around it is becoming harder to navigate. For Washington, it can be a pivotal state in a wider Eurasian contest. For Kazakhstan itself, it is a country pursuing its own economic and political interests while maintaining relations with multiple powers. And for observers looking from Geneva, its potential strength lies in becoming a place where those interests can still meet.

Those roles are not necessarily contradictory, but they point to a delicate balance. Kazakhstan cannot compete with China, Russia, the U.S. or the European Union in scale. Its potential influence comes from something else: remaining connected to all of them without becoming dependent on any single one. In a world where major powers increasingly ask smaller and middle-sized states where they stand, Kazakhstan’s more consequential question may be the one raised during the discussion: what can it connect?

World.title: Kurultai Vote Raises Stakes for Parties, Parliament and Foreign Policy, Experts Say
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s first election to the new Kurultai is reshaping more than the country’s parliamentary architecture, said experts at an Aug. 24 meeting in Astana organized by the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies (KazISS). They pointed to voter turnout, a bigger role for political parties and growing geopolitical competition around Central Asia at a moment when Kazakhstan is seeking to translate constitutional reform into a more durable political system.

The Adilet party secured 71.17% of the vote in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai, according to preliminary results announced by the Central Election Commission (CEC) on Aug. 24. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party received 6.26%, followed by Respublica with 5.56%, the Aq Zhol Democratic Party with 5.21%, and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party with 5.11%.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 3.11%, while the Baytaq Green Party received 1.07%. The against all option received 2.51% of the vote. Under Kazakhstan’s electoral legislation, political parties must secure at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats in the Kurultai. Based on the preliminary figures, five parties crossed the threshold.

The Aug. 23 election marked the first test of Kazakhstan’s new constitutional architecture, moving changes adopted earlier this year from legal design into political practice, said KazISS Director Zhandos Shaimardanov. He pointed to turnout of more than 74% and the preliminary indication of five parties above the 5% threshold as two features likely to shape the new legislature: a dominant political force alongside several smaller parties represented in the Kurultai.

“The task now is to understand how this electoral choice will translate into the work of the new Kurultai, its legislative priorities and the parties’ day-to-day activities,” he added.

Election is only the beginning

Domenico Palmieri, director of the Italian Institute for Asia, said the election is just the beginning of a long path because the election itself cannot tell whether institutional reform has worked as that will be determined based on Kurultai’s performance.

“Yesterday was a very important day for Kazakhstan, but it’s only the start of a new path. All these changes, all these reforms must be implemented and followed in the coming months and years,” said Palmieri, who has followed Kazakhstan’s presidential election in 2022, the constitutional referendum in March and the parliamentary vote on Aug. 23.

He described the transition to a unicameral parliament as a potentially more efficient model but said its effectiveness could only be assessed once the newly elected lawmakers begin legislating.

“I think we must wait six months just to see how the new parliament and new deputies will do their job,” he added.

From a technical perspective, the election proceeded smoothly, he said. What particularly stood out to Palmieri and what differs from the situation in Italy was the willingness of Kazakh citizens to vote and express their views on the country’s development. Citing nearly 75% of eligible voters casting ballots in Kazakhstan, the expert said in Italy, turnout of 50% would be considered a success.

Parties have to meet voters’ demands

Andrey Kazantsev, doctor of political sciences and a professor at the Almaty-based Narxoz University, placed Kazakhstan’s turnout in a broader context of declining political engagement in many countries, which he linked partly to growing individualization and weaker public interest in conventional politics.

However, he said the high turnout should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that voters have become more interested in party politics itself. Instead, he noted, it may reflect a broader concern about the country’s direction at a time of growing international uncertainty.

“This is an indicator of a strong interest of the society, probably not in politics as much. I am not sure that if you talk with ordinary people, they are specifically interested in party politics. But what they are interested in is the future: what will happen to them, what will happen to their children and they see every day on TV information about what is going on in the world,” he said.

This could become increasingly important under Kazakhstan’s redesigned political system. As Kurultai deputies are now elected through party lists rather than territorial constituencies, Kazantsev said political parties will assume greater responsibility for translating public expectations into legislative priorities.

“The demand is high. Now the parties have to provide the supply side,” said the expert, noting that it will require parties to modernize the way they operate, understand voters’ concerns more closely and offer a clearer vision of the country’s future, he said. Whether they manage to do so could become an early indicator of whether the new constitutional model is functioning as intended.

Implications beyond Kazakhstan

According to Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Washington D.C.-based Hudson Institute, the implications of Kazakhstan’s political transition extend beyond its domestic institutions.

Addressing the meeting, he pointed to growing international attention to Central Asia’s resources, trade routes and geopolitical position.

He said interest in the region has risen sharply in Washington D.C. as the United States seeks to reduce its reliance on China for critical minerals, while Beijing looks increasingly to overland Eurasian routes that are less vulnerable to disruptions along maritime trade corridors.

“Both China and the U.S. are trying to escape each other, and they’re meeting each other in Central Asia. That’s why there is so much interest,” he added.

In this context, Moriyasu described Kazakhstan’s political transition as part of a broader consolidation underway across Central Asia, where states have increasingly sought greater regional coordination and a stronger collective role internationally. The expert cited the Kyrgyz Republic’s election to the United Nations Security Council in June as one sign of that trend, stressing that greater regional backing helped Bishkek secure the seat.

“I think there is gradual integration in the region. I think it started in 2016 when Uzbekistan had a new president [Shavkat Mirziyoyev], and I think this consolidation of power and stability in Kazakhstan is a part of this big process,” he added.

According to him, greater clarity in Kazakhstan’s domestic political system could also strengthen the country’s ability to navigate intensifying competition among larger powers and continue implementing its balanced foreign policy.

What comes next

The institutional transition is already moving into its next phase. On Aug. 24, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev reappointed the heads of the National Bank, National Security Committee and Supreme Judicial Council, as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights, as Kazakhstan begins implementing changes under the new constitutional framework.

According to the country’s Constitution, once the election results are formally announced by the Central Election Commission, President Tokayev is expected to convene the first session of the Kurultai, which by law must take place within 30 days of the publication of the final results.

The sitting government will then be required to resign after the new Parliament begins its work. Under the new Constitution, the President will nominate a candidate for prime minister after consultations with the factions of political parties represented in the Kurultai. Once appointed, the prime minister will have 10 days to propose the structure and composition of the government, while cabinet members will be appointed by the President following consultations with the Kurultai.

The Constitution also envisages the office of vice president. Tokayev said the decision will be announced soon. The President must appoint the vice president with the approval of the Kurultai within two months of the opening of the new legislature’s first session. The vice president may not serve as a lawmaker or belong to a political party, and would assume presidential powers if the head of state leaves office before the end of the presidential term.

World.title: ASEAN Summer Festival Brings Southeast Asia Closer to Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – The ASEAN Summer Festival brought Southeast Asia closer to Kazakhstan on Aug. 22, turning the Kazakh capital into a showcase of the region’s cultures, traditions, food and tourism while underscoring growing people-to-people ties.

Organized by the Astana ASEAN Committee (AAC), comprising the Embassies of Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam, with the support of the Honorary Consul of Singapore in Kazakhstan, the festival featured traditional music and dance performances, a food bazaar and cultural presentations showcasing the diversity of Southeast Asia.

Held under the theme Navigating Our Future, Together and focused on ASEAN culture, the festival was part of broader efforts to strengthen engagement between Kazakhstan and the ASEAN.

Speaking at the event, Ambassador of Indonesia to Kazakhstan and Tajikistan Mochamad Fadjroel Rachman noted that ASEAN Day is an opportunity to strengthen relations between Kazakhstan and Southeast Asian countries.

“This is the second year we are celebrating ASEAN Day, and hopefully it could be yearly here in Kazakhstan, so we could strengthen the relation between Kazakhstan and ASEAN countries,” he said.

Representatives of Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore participated in the celebration, reflecting the growing presence of ASEAN countries in Kazakhstan and the expanding scope of cooperation between the two regions.

Visa-free travel to boost tourism

Tourism and connectivity were among the key themes highlighted during the event. Rachman noted that Indonesia introduced a visa-free travel for Kazakh citizens on July 9, allowing them to travel to Indonesia without obtaining a visa in advance.

“Indonesia granted visa-free to Kazakhstan to go to Bali, just buying a ticket and then flying to Indonesia,” he said, noting the popularity of Bali among Kazakh travellers.

The ambassador expressed hope that the new arrangement would contribute to a significant increase in tourist flows, estimating that around 50,000 Kazakh people could visit Indonesia in 2026.

He also pointed to the wider opportunities for travel within Southeast Asia.

“If you buy a ticket, you could go not only to Indonesia, but also to Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and other ASEAN countries,” he said.

According to Rachman, improved connectivity can help deepen relations between Kazakhstan and ASEAN not only through tourism but also through broader cultural and economic exchanges.

Connecting people through travel, education and business

Talgat Chinikeyev, honorary consul of Singapore in Kazakhstan, said relations between Kazakhstan and Southeast Asia have become increasingly people-oriented in recent years.

“Over the past several years, I have personally seen a significant change in the way Kazakhstan and Southeast Asia engage with each other. Our relations are no longer limited to official diplomacy or government-to-government contacts. They are becoming much more people-oriented,” he told The Astana Times.

He noted that improved connectivity has made Southeast Asia more familiar and accessible to Kazakh citizens, with growing numbers travelling to Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore for tourism, education, business and healthcare.

At the same time, interest in Kazakhstan and Central Asia is growing in Southeast Asia, with more business delegations, investors, professionals and visitors exploring opportunities in the region.

Chinikeyev said he has observed these trends particularly in Kazakhstan-Singapore relations, with Singapore increasingly recognized in Kazakhstan not only as an Asian economic success story, but also as a center for education, finance, technology, innovation and healthcare.

Business exchanges between the two countries have also become more active, with potential for cooperation in investment, logistics, digitalisation, education and technology.

He highlighted President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Singapore in 2024 as an important push for bilateral relations and stronger people-to-people ties.

“I believe we are now moving into a very interesting stage where Kazakhstan can become a natural gateway for Southeast Asia into Central Asia, while Singapore can serve as an important gateway for Kazakhstan into ASEAN,” said Chinikeyev.

Celebrating ASEAN’s diversity

The festival also provided an opportunity for the public to learn more about the cultural diversity of ASEAN, a region of more than 680 million people comprising 11 member states. The region is also home to hundreds of ethnic groups, more than 1,000 languages and diverse religious traditions.

According to the festival organizers, ASEAN’s ability to maintain unity amid such diversity is one of the region’s defining characteristics. For Chinikeyev, cultural events can help make Southeast Asia feel closer to people in Kazakhstan.

“My hope is that people who come to the ASEAN summer festival will not simply enjoy the food, music, performances and atmosphere, but will leave with a genuine curiosity about Southeast Asia and a desire to learn more about the region,” he said.

He added that culture has a unique ability to bring people together naturally, particularly when regions remain geographically distant from one another.

Culture as a foundation for long-term partnership

The festival was presented not only as a cultural showcase but also as an instrument of public diplomacy and engagement. Held in Astana, a city with a diverse population and an increasingly active international profile, the event sought to create direct connections between the public and ASEAN through food, music, traditional performances and cultural exchange.

The ASEAN summer festival builds on a broader increase in engagement between Kazakhstan and Southeast Asia, supported by direct air connectivity, growing tourism, business exchanges and high-level diplomatic contacts.

“This is how long-term partnerships are built – not only through agreements and official visits, but through friendship, understanding and genuine human connections,” Chinikeyev said.

World.title: Central Asia Sees FinTech As Next Frontier of Regional Integration
World.content:
TASHKENT – Digital and financial connectivity could become the next frontier of regional integration in Central Asia, as Uzbekistan seeks to accelerate its fintech development and advance greater connectivity within the region’s markets.

Central Bank of Uzbekistan Governor Timur Ishmetov called on global investors and innovators to work on infrastructure and standards that can connect markets across Central Asia and beyond.

“Regional financial connectivity cannot be built by one country alone. Build here. Test new solutions here. Invest here. Develop talent here. With the right partnerships, Central Asia can become a more connected, competitive and internationally integrated financial region,” said Ishmetov at the opening of the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum 2026 on Aug. 24.

The initiative comes as Central Asia, a region of more than 80 million people, has been pursuing stronger economic cooperation while accelerating digital adoption and developing new channels for financial services.

Despite its demographic and economic potential, Central Asia’s share of global fintech investment remains “modest.” According to Ishmetov, in 2025, total venture capital funding across Central Asia amounted to approximately $320 million.

“This demonstrates the scale of the opportunity to convert the region’s young population, growing digital adoption, and developing financial infrastructure into sustainable investment and innovation,” he said.

For Ishmetov, the challenge is not simply to expand fintech within national markets but to create conditions for markets to connect with one another. Regional connectivity is seen as a key element of a sustainable fintech ecosystem along with regulation, infrastructure and investment.

“Efficient regional corridors are of utmost economic importance. There remains potential to strengthen payment connectivity between countries of our region and to expand the range of financial services available across borders. Digital finance changes the economic geography. Physical distance becomes substantially less restrictive and that is a strategic opportunity for our region,” he explained.

The economic foundation for connectivity has also been expanding. The report prepared by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), in collaboration with the Institute for Advanced International Studies (IAIS) of Uzbekistan, highlighted the shift of the region from a peripheral destination into one of Eurasia’s more dynamic economic nodes over the past two decades.

Between 2000 and 2024, the countries of Central Asia significantly increased their accumulated stock of foreign direct investment. The UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Report 2025 indicated that the region’s total inward FDI stock reached $220.5 billion as of 2024.

The growing scale of investment and cross border activity brings a broader question for the region whether financial infrastructure can keep pace with the movement of goods, capital and businesses across connected markets.

Otabek Nasirov, chairman of Central Asian Fintech Association, said the region can and should move toward common standards for digital identity, payments and open banking.

“We do not necessarily need identical regulations in all five countries. What we need is interoperability: compatible digital identity frameworks, common principles for secure data exchange and consent, interoperable payment infrastructure, and APIs that allow financial institutions and fintech companies to work across borders,” Nasirov told The Astana Times.

Central Asian countries are developing their digital financial ecosystems at different speeds. The next challenge is to connect these national ecosystems.

“If we can make digital identity, payments and financial data work across borders, a fintech company should eventually be able to scale across Central Asia much more easily – reaching a regional market of more than 80 million people rather than treating each country as a completely separate market,” Nasirov said.

This will require close cooperation between central banks, governments, financial institutions, fintech companies and industry associations.

“I believe we should start with practical areas where interoperability can deliver immediate value cross-border payments and QR interoperability, digital KYC [Know Your Customer] and identity verification, and common approaches to Open Banking and consent-based data sharing,” he said.

“The goal should not be to create one regulator or one system for Central Asia, but to build a connected regional digital financial infrastructure based on mutually recognised standards. That could become one of the strongest drivers of fintech growth, investment and regional economic integration in Central Asia,” he said.

Tashkent is hosting the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum 2026. The event is supported by the Central Bank of Uzbekistan and Singapore-headquartered Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN), and co-hosted by Ant International on Aug. 24-26.

The event connects more than 6,000 participants from 74 countries in Tashkent. The forum focused on five key themes including digital payments and infrastructure, Islamic finance and new economic corridors, AI and emerging technologies, tokenization and digital assets and cross-border finance and regulation.

World.title: Why Kazakhstan Is Creating Domestic Credit Rating Agency and What Will Determine Its Success
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is preparing to establish a national credit rating agency as part of a broader effort to develop its domestic capital market, but the institution’s success will ultimately depend on more than the creation of a new regulator-approved rating system. Its ratings will have to earn the confidence of investors and become a meaningful part of how companies are financed and risks are priced.

The new Law On Credit Rating Activities, signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on July 23, introduces common rules for credit rating agencies operating in Kazakhstan and provides for the establishment of a Kazakh rating agency, with the National Bank among its founders. The law sets requirements for capital, corporate governance, internal controls, conflict-of-interest management and disclosure.

It also expands the potential scope of rating activities beyond conventional credit ratings to include corporate governance, Islamic finance, sustainable development and other types of ratings, while the legislation is set to take effect on Oct. 21, with some provisions coming into force on July 1, 2027.

But the central question is not simply what the new agency will do. It is why Kazakhstan needs one in the first place, and whether it can change the way capital is allocated in the domestic economy.

The gap in Kazakhstan’s capital market

Kazakhstan already has access to the world’s major rating agencies. The new institution is therefore not intended to replace international players or create a domestic version of S&P, Moody’s or Fitch.

“Creating a national credit rating agency is not an attempt to make a Kazakh equivalent of S&P, Moody’s or Fitch, and certainly not a task of replacing international agencies. International ratings will retain their importance,” Kazakh economist Ruslan Sultanov, who served as Chairman of the Board of the Economic Research Institute from 2019 to 2024, told the Astana Times.

The rationale is instead connected to the structure of the domestic financial market. Kazakhstan has been seeking to develop non-bank financing, corporate bonds and institutional investment. Yet a functioning capital market requires investors to be able to distinguish between borrowers according to their level of risk.

According to Sultanov, this is particularly relevant for medium-sized companies. An international rating may make economic sense for a large corporate borrower seeking substantial financing or access to international capital markets. For a smaller issuer, however, the cost and requirements associated with obtaining such a rating can become disproportionate to the size of the planned issue.

“As a result, a gap arises: there is a potential issuer, institutional investors have money, but there is often no independent and understandable market assessment of credit risk between them. The national rating scale makes it possible to solve another problem – to compare the credit quality of borrowers within a single jurisdiction in much greater detail than the global scale allows,” he said.

The distinction is important. A domestic rating system does not necessarily need to compete with international ratings. Its value could instead lie in providing more granular information about relative credit quality within the Kazakh market.

Ratings do not create liquidity on their own

A rating is an information tool. It can tell an investor how an independent analyst assesses a borrower’s ability to meet its obligations. But it cannot, by itself, create investors, issuers or demand for bonds.

“The creation of the agency itself will not create a capital market. An agency can be registered, methodologies approved and the first ratings assigned. Liquidity will not appear from that alone,” Sultanov said.

According to him, for the reform to have a broader economic effect, national ratings would need to become integrated into the infrastructure of the financial market: the investment decisions of institutional investors, risk-management systems, corporate disclosure and bond pricing. This means the agency’s real contribution could be measured by what happens after a rating is issued.

The potential benefit for companies and investors

For companies, the most immediate potential benefit is access.

“The main potential effect is a reduction in the barrier to entering the public debt market. This is especially relevant for issuers that do not need an international rating but still need to demonstrate their creditworthiness to investors,” Sultanov said.

For investors, the benefit is potentially greater transparency in comparing domestic issuers. The effect could also extend to banks, which occupy several positions within Kazakhstan’s financial system: they are borrowers, investors and major professional market participants. Over time, national ratings could be incorporated into their investment policies and risk-management systems.

According to Sultanov, they could also potentially be used in elements of prudential regulation if regulators determine that the quality and reliability of the ratings justify such treatment.

The National Bank’s role as one of the founders brings both advantages and potential questions. For investors, the key issue is not simply who owns the agency, but who controls the rating decision.

“The presence of the state or regulator among the founders in itself does not indicate the quality of a rating. For an investor, what matters more is whether the owner can influence the methodology, a specific rating decision or personnel decisions concerning analysts,” the economist said.

Sultanov points to several mechanisms that could help preserve independence: an independent board of directors, an autonomous rating committee, transparent methodologies, conflict-of-interest controls, rotation of analysts, internal oversight and disclosure of the reasons behind rating changes.

The real test will come later

The agency’s credibility cannot be established on the day it receives its registration. It will have to be built through a track record. An important part of that track record will be whether ratings actually correspond to the behaviour of the companies being assessed. Over time, investors should be able to see how frequently ratings are upgraded or downgraded and how often companies in different rating categories default.

“After several years, the market should be able to see rating migration matrices, the frequency of defaults in each rating category and compare the actual behaviour of borrowers with the risk that the agency previously indicated. In other words, measurable quality of the rating,” Sultanov said.

For large Kazakh companies seeking international financing, global ratings are likely to remain important. A national agency, meanwhile, could focus on the domestic market and provide a more detailed assessment of companies whose financing needs do not justify the cost or requirements of an international rating. The two levels of the rating system could therefore become complementary rather than competing.

“A rating agency has a rather unusual asset – trust. It cannot be contributed to the charter capital. It emerges gradually and step by step, when investors see that the same risk receives the same assessment regardless of the owner’s name, the size of the company or its relationship with the state,” Sultanov said.

For Kazakhstan, this may be the defining test of the new system.

World.title: Tokayev Makes Senior Appointments Amid Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Transition
World.content:
ALMATY – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has made a number of senior state appointments, reappointing the heads of the National Bank, National Security Committee and Supreme Judicial Council, as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights on Aug. 24.

Timur Suleimenov was reappointed the Governor of National Bank of Kazakhstan. He first became Governor in September 2023, having previously served as Deputy Chairman of the National Bank.

Yermek Sagimbayev was reappointed Chairman of the National Security Committee, a position he has held since January 2022.

Dmitry Malakhov was reappointed Chairman of the Supreme Judicial Council, a position he has held since September 2024. Prior to that, he headed the Agency for Financial Monitoring.

Artur Lastayev was reappointed Commissioner for Human Rights in Kazakhstan. He has held the position since January 2023.

The appointments come after Kazakhstan’s new Constitution took effect on July 1, establishing a new constitutional framework and introducing changes to the country’s political institutions.

The latest appointments also come as Kazakhstan begins implementing a series of institutional changes following the first elections to the new unicameral Kurultai on Aug. 23.

Further changes expected

Earlier, Tokayev said the government’s composition would undergo changes, while stressing that there are currently no grounds for concern about its work. He said personnel changes were a normal part of government work and should be aimed at giving the Cabinet new momentum rather than being made simply for the sake of dismissals.

Tokayev also said the name of the person who will take the newly established post of Vice President is expected to become known within the next seven to 10 days.

The appointments and planned institutional changes form part of the broader political transition following the adoption of Kazakhstan’s new Constitution and the establishment of the unicameral Kurultai.

World.title: Kazakhstan Gains US Recognition as Safe Tourism Destination
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has received the least restrictive travel advisory level from the United States, adding to a series of developments leading to strengthening the country’s position as an international tourism destination.

On Aug. 18, the U.S. Department of State placed Kazakhstan at Level 1, the lowest (safest) of its four travel advisory levels. The advisory says Kazakhstan is generally a safe destination for travelers, while noting that flooding can occur in the country.

The assessment comes as Kazakhstan continues to expand its tourism infrastructure, international connectivity and number of tourists.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan received 15.7 million foreign visitors in 2025, 3.1% more than in 2024. Of these, 11.1 million were classified as foreign tourists. Tourism investment reached 1.26 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion), increasing by 32.6% year on year.

The positive trend continued in the first quarter of 2026, when Kazakhstan welcomed three million foreign travelers. More than two million guests stayed at accommodation facilities, including more than 802,000 visitors to resort areas.

The Almaty Mountain Cluster was the most visited resort destination during the period, followed by the Shchuchinsk-Burabai resort area in the Akmola Region and the Mangystau resort area.

Kazakhstan also improved its position in the World Economic Forum’s Travel & Tourism Development Index, ranking 52nd among 119 economies in the 2024 edition, compared with 66th among 117 economies in the previous edition.

The country is also investing in transport infrastructure to make major tourist destinations more accessible. Kazakhstan plans to open or resume 15 international air routes in 2026, including services connecting the country with Vienna, Rome, Shanghai, Tokyo and Riyadh. Domestic connectivity is also being expanded.

The government is working to complete tourist airports in Katon-Karagai and Zaysan in eastern Kazakhstan and Kenderli in the Mangystau Region in 2026. Road improvements include routes leading to major tourist destinations, while new roadside service facilities are also planned. The Astana Times previously reported on measures to improve safety, transport and resort infrastructure ahead of the 2026 summer season.

Nature-based tourism is becoming one of the country’s key areas for development.

The Almaty Superski project is being implemented as part of the broader Almaty Mountain Cluster. The project is expected to expand access to mountain tourism and create infrastructure for skiing, hiking and other outdoor activities.

Visits to specially protected natural areas increased from 2.8 million in 2024 to 3.7 million in 2025, according to the Ministry of Tourism and Sports. National parks currently offer 179 tourist routes and 42 ecological trails.

Officials have emphasized that tourism development should be balanced with environmental protection, including ecological monitoring and visitor management.

Another indicator of Kazakhstan’s growing integration into international travel is the Henley Passport Index.

In the 2026 Henley Passport Index, Kazakhstan ranked 64th, with its passport providing access to 77 destinations without a prior visa. The Henley Passport Index measures international mobility, the number of destinations that passport holders can access without obtaining a visa in advance. It is separate from travel safety assessments.

Kazakhstan is also expanding opportunities for foreign travelers to enter the country.

Citizens of 105 countries can obtain electronic visas, while Kazakhstan has introduced additional visa mechanisms for certain categories of visitors, including the Digital Nomad Visa for IT specialists and the Neo Nomad Visa.

International arrivals are only part of Kazakhstan’s tourism market. Domestic travel continues to account for the majority of tourism trips by citizens.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan recorded 11.77 million tourist trips by citizens in 2025. Of these, 10.27 million, or 87.2%, were domestic trips.

Astana, the Turkistan Region and Almaty were among the most visited destinations, highlighting the importance of both major cities and regional tourism centers.

The new U.S. travel advisory is one of several developments strengthening Kazakhstan’s international tourism profile. Growing visitor numbers, rising investment, new air routes, improved access to regional destinations, simplified visa procedures and expanding mountain and nature tourism are collectively making the country more accessible to international travelers.

For Kazakhstan, the next challenge will be to ensure that tourism growth is accompanied by reliable services, safety measures and environmental protection.

The combination of a favorable safety assessment and expanding tourism infrastructure could further strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as a destination for travelers interested in nature, adventure, cultural heritage and the wider Central Asian region.

World.title: Why has Georgia’s government revived debate over Treaty of Georgievsk?
World.content:
In recent days, Georgian government officials have made a series of similar statements about the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the agreement with Russia saved Georgia and the Georgian nation. He argues that it laid the foundations for today’s sovereign state and helped preserve its European prospects.

Several days later, other leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party began speaking about the Treaty of Georgievsk in similar terms. They repeat not only the main conclusion but also the same arguments: Georgia faced the threat of destruction, an agreement with Russia was the only option, and that decision saved the Georgian nation, Christianity and Georgian statehood.

This level of coordination suggests that the discussion has moved beyond a spontaneous debate about history. The positive assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk sounds more like a unified political message from Georgian Dream.

But what is the purpose of this message?

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement under which eastern Georgia (the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti) came under the protection of the Russian Empire. The parties signed the treaty in the summer of 1783 at the fortress of Georgievsk. The treaty protected Georgia from external threats but ultimately led to the complete loss of its independence.

Opposition figures say the government is preparing the public for a possible new agreement with Russia. Former president Mikheil Saakashvili, who is currently in prison, has even referred to specific draft agreements.

Other political commentators see the renewed focus on the treaty as an attempt to divert attention from important current issues. Against the backdrop of what they describe as the Georgian government’s increasingly pro-Russian course and anti-Western rhetoric, the Treaty of Georgievsk is a particularly sensitive issue for politically active Georgians and can easily provoke a strong reaction.

According to this view, the government deliberately sparked a historical debate to draw attention away from corruption within the administration. At the same time, the authorities have intensified the charges against former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili. His case goes beyond the actions of an individual official and raises questions about the scale of systemic corruption itself.

Russian media have already described Kobakhidze’s remarks as another sign that Tbilisi’s attitude towards Moscow is changing.

So why has a treaty signed 243 years ago suddenly become one of the main topics of Georgia’s current political debate?

What Prime Minister Kobakhidze said

Irakli Kobakhidze has made several statements about the Treaty of Georgievsk. His main argument is that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation.

On 18 August, Kobakhidze described the signing of the treaty as a “civilisational choice”. He said Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose fellow Orthodox Russia.

“The fact that today we are an independent, sovereign state based on traditional European values and traditional European culture is precisely the result of this pragmatic decision taken by Erekle II,” the prime minister said.

Kobakhidze has also argued that Erekle II’s decision was not only justified, but the “only correct and only possible” choice at the time. In his account, Russia honoured the terms of the agreement during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end. Almost 20 years passed between the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country was effectively saved.”

Kobakhidze presented Russia’s abolition of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti as a process that became possible only after the Georgian king’s death: “When Erekle II died, unfortunately, events took a different course.”

Georgian Dream leaders have also drawn parallels between this historical episode and modern Georgian-Russian relations.

Kobakhidze compared the Treaty of Georgievsk with the August 2008 war and said that “under Mikheil Saakashvili’s leadership, all the agreements, whether signed or unsigned, were torn up over our heads.”

Other party leaders have expressed similar views. MP David Matikashvili, for example, called the Treaty of Georgievsk a “smart and wise” decision.

“Ultimately, despite the many negative consequences, Georgia and the Georgian people managed to survive physically. The genius of King Erekle is obvious here,” he said.

More about the Treaty of Georgievsk

The Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783 between the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. It was not an agreement between a united Georgia and Russia. At the time, the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia were not parties to the treaty.

Under the agreement, Kartli-Kakheti came under Russian protection. In return, Russia undertook to protect its territorial integrity and the Bagrationi dynasty.

Historian Beka Kobakhidze strongly disputes Kobakhidze’s claim that Russia honoured the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime. He writes that the period from 1783 until Erekle’s death was instead one of the most difficult periods of his reign.

In 1785, an army led by Avar ruler Omar Khan invaded Kartli-Kakheti. Beka Kobakhidze says Erekle had warned Russia about the planned attack and requested the assistance provided for under the treaty. Russia did not provide it.

Agha Mohammad Khan’s 1795 campaign had even more devastating consequences. After the Battle of Krtsanisi, his forces captured and looted Tbilisi. Thousands of people were killed or taken captive.

Beka Kobakhidze draws on these facts to write:

“Irakli Kobakhidze is falsifying history. The period from 1783 to 1798, from the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk to Erekle’s death, was the most difficult and destructive period of his reign.”

In 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. The Bagrationi royal family lost power, and some of its members were exiled to Russia. The Russian Empire later conquered and annexed the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia as well.

Was Georgia “on the brink of extinction”?

Another key element of Georgian Dream’s new historical narrative concerns demographic survival. The prime minister says the Georgian nation faced a “real threat of extinction” at the end of the 18th century. MP Matikashvili has also referred to the “physical survival” of the Georgian people.

This view is not new. The Russian imperial narrative, and later the Soviet version of history, often portrayed the annexation of Georgia as a painful but necessary step to save the country.

Historian Giorgi Ugulava wrote in a 2025 article for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that this representation was one of the main products of Russian imperial propaganda. The argument was that Georgia could not survive independently and that Russian protection was the best option available.

Why has Erekle II become a political symbol for Georgian Dream?

Georgian Dream’s political campaign around Erekle II began well before August 2026.

In 2023, literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili criticised Erekle II over the Treaty of Georgievsk. Georgian Dream leaders responded with fierce criticism of the scholar. That same year, the pro-Russian Conservative Movement disrupted one of Berdzenishvili’s lectures. He was later attacked in the street.

At the time, Georgian Dream chairman Irakli Kobakhidze said violence was unacceptable. At the same time, however, he accused Berdzenishvili of acting against Georgian identity.

In August 2024, Kobakhidze announced plans to erect a new monument to Erekle II in Tbilisi. The monument opened on 24 September 2025. At the ceremony, Kobakhidze described Erekle II as a symbol of “patriotism”, “love of the homeland” and “pragmatism”.

Kobakhidze also claimed that foreign diplomats had criticised Erekle II during meetings with Georgian Dream representatives. He did not name any of the diplomats or specify which countries they represented. However, according to his account, criticism of Erekle II formed part of coordinated actions by Western diplomats and the Georgian opposition.

Erekle II has therefore gradually evolved from a historical figure into a symbol of the current political confrontation. On one side stands the “pragmatic” king who reached an agreement with Russia. On the other are his critics, whom the government portrays as agents of Western interests.

“A new treaty”: what do pro-Russian forces in Georgia want?

While Georgian Dream highlights the positive historical significance of the old Treaty of Georgievsk, openly operating pro-Russian forces in Georgia are already calling directly for a “new treaty”.

One of the main figures in this campaign is Russian-Georgian citizen Mamuka Pipia, leader of the Solidarity for Peace party.

In July 2025, Pipia called for the signing of a “Treaty of Georgievsk 2” and an alliance treaty with Russia. His proposals included restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and removing Article 78 from Georgia’s Constitution. The article requires constitutional bodies to take all measures to ensure Georgia’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Pipia said: “Given today’s geopolitical situation, Russia and Georgia need to support each other, and they need to formalise an alliance treaty on equal terms.”

In August 2026, Pipia described Kobakhidze’s statements as a success for his own political agenda.

“I am glad that the country’s leadership now recognises the reality that we have been speaking about openly for the past two years,” he said.

Pipia says his idea of a “new Treaty of Georgievsk” means “a completely new, comprehensive and, most importantly, equal treaty with the Russian Federation”.

“We are working in this direction, and Moscow will make an appropriate statement very soon,” he added.

Georgian Dream denies coordinating with pro-Russian groups. However, Pipia’s political network maintains open contacts with Russian officials. He has appeared in public at various times with Russian State Duma deputies and other senior Russian officials.

In May 2025, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who is under US sanctions, was also in Red Square with Pipia. The US Treasury Department has described Partskhaladze as a Georgian-Russian oligarch and said Russia’s FSB used him to influence Georgian society and politics.

How closely do the two narratives align?

Mamuka Pipia’s and Georgian Dream’s ultimate political demands do not currently coincide. Georgian Dream is not officially calling for an alliance treaty with Russia, a “new treaty” or the repeal of Article 78 of the Constitution. This is a significant difference.

However, the similarities in their rhetoric are clear. In both cases, the main arguments for closer relations with Russia are “pragmatism”, peace, security and national interests. In both narratives, the West is increasingly portrayed not as a security partner but as a source of threats or pressure.

The rhetoric around the “deep state” also overlaps. For years, Pipia has spoken about Western forces allegedly trying to use Georgia against Russia. A similar conspiracy theory has become part of Georgian Dream’s official political messaging in recent years.

Now another important element has entered this shared vocabulary: the interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk as an agreement that saved Georgia.

What does the opposition say about a possible new agreement?

Against this backdrop, Georgian opposition figures suspect that the historical debate may serve to prepare public opinion for a more concrete political decision.

Mikheil Saakashvili said that the government was carrying out “ideological preparations for signing a treaty of betrayal”. He claims that Russia has even given ruling-party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili drafts of several agreements.

Saakashvili referred to restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and separate agreements on Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. He also claims that Irakli Kobakhidze is expected to travel to Moscow in the coming weeks.

There is currently no independent confirmation of this information. Neither the Georgian nor the Russian authorities have officially announced preparations for such agreements.

Former diplomat Ghia Japaridze also sees the government’s rhetoric as preparation for possible changes in foreign policy. He says the government is using the Treaty of Georgievsk to “justify a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course”.

What is the Russian media saying?

Irakli Kobakhidze’s statements have also attracted attention in Russia.

On 21 August, the Russian publication Vzglyad published an article headlined “Georgia has taken an important step towards normality”.

The article links several issues: the Georgian government’s campaign against so-called “Russophobia”, accusations against the West and the new interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The publication places particular emphasis on the “restoration of respect for the Treaty of Georgievsk — an alliance with Russia that saved Georgia”.

In other words, what Georgian officials present in Tbilisi as a historical interpretation and an assessment of Erekle II’s decision is already being read by Russian media as a sign of changing political attitudes towards modern Russia.

A day earlier, even more far-reaching claims circulated in Russian Telegram channels. INSIDER-T, citing unofficial sources, claimed that Tbilisi had offered Moscow a behind-the-scenes deal: “full geopolitical loyalty” from Georgia in exchange for Russia publicly abandoning the annexation of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

These claims are also not supported by reliable evidence.

What matters, however, is the political expectations now emerging in the Russian information space in response to statements by Georgian officials.

A historical dispute or an ongoing political process?

There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence that the Georgian authorities are preparing to sign a “New Treaty of Georgievsk” or another alliance agreement with Russia.

However, it is difficult to describe what is happening as merely a dispute among historians.

On one side is a government that has sharply worsened relations with Georgia’s main Western partners in recent years and has effectively frozen the country’s EU accession process.

On the other are pro-Russian groups openly calling for a political alliance and security ties with Russia. They see the prime minister’s new rhetoric as a victory for their position.

This is accompanied by the reaction of the Russian information space, where Georgian government statements are increasingly seen as a sign that Tbilisi is turning towards the Kremlin.

Against this backdrop, the significance of the Treaty of Georgievsk is no longer confined to the 18th century. The key question now is why the government needs to convince the public that a historical agreement with Russia, which ultimately led to the annexation of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, saved Georgia.

And, more importantly, what modern political choice might this version of history be intended to justify?

Debate over the Treaty of Georgievsk in Georgia

World.title: 750,000 lari bribe and other new allegations against jailed former Georgian PM who turned against the government
World.content:
Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili

New charges have been brought against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili for accepting a large bribe. The charges came shortly after he published open letters accusing the government of persecuting him to prevent his return to politics.

Garibashvili is already serving a five-year sentence for legalising illicit income. The new charges carry a prison sentence of between 11 and 15 years.

🟥 According to the prosecution, then-defence minister Juansher Burchuladze, who is now in prison, illegally transferred 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Garibashvili in cash in several instalments.

What does the prosecution accuse Garibashvili of?

The case concerns the purchase of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to the prosecution, the ministry conducted three secret procurement procedures from late 2022 onwards.

At the time, Juansher Burchuladze served as defence minister, while Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister.

According to investigators, Burchuladze and his relative, Vasil Mcheidze, reached an agreement with a local business and offered it an opportunity to take part in government tenders. With their help, the business was supposed to win the tenders and then pay them 10% of the total contract value.

The businessman demanded additional guarantees.

According to the prosecution, Burchuladze then reached an agreement with Irakli Garibashvili, who was serving as prime minister.

Investigators accuse the former prime minister of protecting the scheme and demanding his share of the proceeds.

According to the indictment, deputy defence minister Giorgi Khaindrava and procurement department head Vladimir Gudushauri then created non-competitive conditions. This allowed selected companies to win the tenders at predetermined prices.

The prosecution says the companies supplied the ministry with goods worth 18,484,960 lari (about $7.5 million). However, the actual value of the goods was 11,499,705 lari (about $4.5 million).

The prosecution estimates the damage to the state at 6,985,255 lari (about $2.6 million).

How was the 1.9 million lari divided?

According to the investigation, the businessman ultimately transferred 1.9 million lari (about $730,000) to Vasil Mcheidze in several instalments. The amount represented roughly 10% of the total value of the contracts.

Vasil Mcheidze kept 400,000 lari (about $155,000);

he transferred 1.5 million lari (about $580,000) to Juansher Burchuladze;

Burchuladze kept 750,000 lari (about $290,000);

he transferred the remaining 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Irakli Garibashvili.

Prosecutors have charged the former prime minister under Article 338 of the Criminal Code. The article covers accepting a particularly large bribe by a public or political official as part of a group.

At this stage, the prosecution is asking the court to schedule a preliminary hearing. It is not seeking a new pre-trial measure because Garibashvili is already in custody.

Who gave investigators new testimony?

According to the prosecution, Vasil Mcheidze decided to cooperate with investigators on 12 August. He provided the authorities with information in his possession.

Juansher Burchuladze is also cooperating with the investigation. The prosecution is relying on their testimony to establish Garibashvili’s role in the new case.

Burchuladze was arrested in September 2025. On 23 April 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison for abuse of power and legalising illicit income.

Burchuladze’s former deputy, Giorgi Khaindrava, and Vasil Mcheidze each received eight-year prison sentences in the same case. Gudushauri reached a plea agreement with the prosecution.

Why does the timing of the new charges against Garibashvili matter?

Just days before prosecutors brought the new charges, Garibashvili made three statements from prison. They were published on 17, 18 and 20 August.

The former prime minister said the ruling party was demanding that he admit to additional acts of corruption. He said the government feared his return to politics.

Garibashvili also said he had received a letter from prominent Georgian Dream representative Mamuka Mdinaradze. According to Garibashvili, a close friend of Mdinaradze delivered the letter to a member of his family.

“You sent me to prison for five years because of false assumptions, fantasies, envy, fears and suspicions created by a certain group within the party,” Garibashvili wrote.

He said the demand that he admit to the new allegations came with a hint that authorities could arrest his father.

“I am not fighting anyone. I am only defending myself and my family. That is why I will have no choice but to respond in kind to everything you do,” Garibashvili said.

The new charges have given the former prime minister’s statements added significance. However, his account has not been investigated or independently verified.

What does Georgian Dream say?

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze suggested that Garibashvili may have had information about the ongoing investigation. In his view, the former prime minister’s statements were pre-emptive.

“Former politicians often use this method, and legal issues are sometimes brought into the political sphere,” Kaladze said.

He said Garibashvili’s safety and rights were protected.

Mamuka Mdinaradze denies Garibashvili’s allegations. He considers the current case against the former prime minister part of the government’s fight against corruption.

Garibashvili family’s response

Garibashvili’s wife’s brother, Alexander Tamazashvili, published an extract from the public registry after prosecutors brought the new charges. He said the document showed a property transaction involving Zurab Tukvadze, a businessman and one of the prosecution’s witnesses.

The prosecution’s public statement does not name the businessman. However, Tamazashvili claims that Tukvadze transferred a country house in the Tskneti settlement to Vasil Mcheidze in 2023. Tamazashvili suggested that the property transfer amounted to a bribe.

The statement can also be seen as an ironic rebuttal of the allegations. However, the published property transaction neither proves nor disproves that anyone may have given cash to Garibashvili.

Garibashvili himself has not publicly responded to the details of the new charges.

Opposition raises two possible concerns

Opposition representatives have highlighted two issues in the case.

The first is possible corruption in defence procurement.

The second is the suspicion that the law may serve as a tool of political pressure.

Levan Samushia, a member of the opposition Strong Georgia – Lelo party, said Garibashvili’s earlier statements give grounds for such suspicions.

“Is the law not being used in this case to exert pressure based on clan interests? Otherwise, how could Garibashvili have known in advance that he might face charges?” Samushia said.

Zurab Japaridze, leader of Girchi – More Freedom, drew attention to the scheme described in the indictment. He linked Garibashvili’s alleged receipt of cash to his previous case.

“He artificially inflated the price, received his share in cash in lari, then exchanged it for dollars and gold and kept the bundles in a safe,” Japaridze wrote.

Garibashvili’s first case

Garibashvili first faced corruption charges in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising a particularly large amount of illicit income.

According to the prosecution, Garibashvili provided false information in his property declarations. In doing so, he allegedly attempted to give illegally obtained income a legitimate appearance.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a deal with the prosecution. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

Garibashvili has not pleaded guilty in the new case. The main grounds for the charges are testimony from Burchuladze and Mcheidze. The court will have to assess the credibility of their statements, along with the other evidence.

The case now brings together two parallel questions.

One concerns possible corruption in secret Defence Ministry procurement procedures.

The other concerns Garibashvili’s claim that the government demanded that he admit guilt in advance.

Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

World.title: $12m dispute and house sold at auction: where has former Georgian PM Nika Gilauri gone? – RFE/RL
World.content:
Nika Gilauri case

At the end of 2024, former prime minister Nika Gilauri became one of the most vocal critics of the ruling Georgian Dream party. Over the following months, he faced serious problems: authorities seized his foundation, while a court ordered him and his companies to pay $12 million in compensation to former business partners. Gilauri himself stopped appearing in public.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty published an investigation into the case. The circumstances described in the report raise suspicions that the legal proceedings against Gilauri may amount to political persecution. Georgian and German lawyers have called the court ruling unfounded.

The material draws on a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation.

Gilauri’s house put up for forced auction

On 16 July 2026, the National Bureau of Enforcement put Nika Gilauri’s house in Tsavkisi up for auction. A 3,368-square-metre plot of land and a 1,157-square-metre villa sold for almost four million lari (about $1.54 million).

The property had an estimated value of 4.876 million lari (about $1.87 million), but bidding started at 10% of that amount. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, businessman Vano Sturua bought the house. He is a former business partner of Nika Gilauri’s brother, Irakli.

Since 2018, this house has remained the only property in Georgia registered in Gilauri’s name. However, court rulings have also ordered the seizure of other assets and his shares in companies.

Gilauri himself has not commented on the situation. He only responded to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty in writing:

“The legal proceedings are still ongoing, and on my lawyers’ advice, I will not make any comments or give interviews at this stage.”

Gilauri’s return to politics

Nika Gilauri served as energy minister and finance minister under Mikheil Saakashvili. He then headed the government from 2009 to 2012. After leaving public service, he founded the consulting company Reformatics and stayed out of Georgia’s public political life for about 12 years.

The situation changed ahead of the 2024 parliamentary election. A few days before the vote, Gilauri and the Reformatics team presented a 100-page document outlining their vision for a “Third Republic of Georgia”. It addressed Georgia’s exit from Russia’s sphere of influence, judicial independence and European integration.

Media reports said Gilauri was financing the opposition Coalition for Change. Several coalition leaders later confirmed that they had worked with him and received campaign donations.

After security forces violently dispersed protests in November and December 2024, Gilauri called the Georgian Dream government illegitimate. He demanded new elections and the release of detained protesters.

Gilauri also called on business representatives to create a fund to support protesters. His Prosperity foundation raised 246,000 lari (about $94,450) in three months. The money was intended to support protesters and people who had lost their jobs because of their political views.

In March 2025, the prosecutor’s office froze the assets of the Prosperity foundation and four other foundations. Authorities opened an investigation into allegations of sabotage, assisting the activities of a hostile foreign organisation and actions against the constitutional order. The investigation remains ongoing, and the foundations remain suspended.

Gilauri has not appeared in public since then.

Dispute over the construction of three hydropower plants

The multimillion-lari legal dispute involving Gilauri began several years before he returned to politics.

In 2015, Aquahydro signed memorandums with the Georgian government and state-owned companies to build three small hydropower plants in the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region: Ipari, Khelra and Nakra.

Black Sea Group took responsibility for the construction work. Under the agreement, the contractor would receive payment for the completed work as well as a 20% stake in the company operating the hydropower plants.

Ipari and Khelra were completed and brought into operation. However, Black Sea Group halted construction of Nakra in 2020. A few months later, Aquahydro terminated its contract with the company and hired another contractor to complete the project.

In 2021, Black Sea Group went to court. The company said it had not received full payment for the work it had completed. It sought several million lari in compensation, as well as damages for lost profits.

Gilauri’s side filed a counterclaim seeking 14.5 million lari (about $5.57 million) from Black Sea Group. They argued that the suspension of construction at Nakra deprived the company of expected revenue for 2020-2022. Their expert assessment found that the contractor had received $600,000 more than the actual cost of the work, according to official documentation.

Black Sea Group rejected the assessment, arguing that it had not received full payment for the work it had completed.

Why was Gilauri held personally liable?

On 12 February 2025, Tbilisi City Court judge Liana Kajashvili ruled in favour of Black Sea Group. The court ordered the former prime minister and companies under his control to pay Black Sea Group more than $12 million in damages.
