World.title: Chinese factory workers accidentally caught on camera glasses
World.content:
Factory workers who helped make a Chinese-brand of camera glasses appear to have been unknowingly filmed by the devices in accidental videos.

7.30 bought a pair of budget glasses made by Shenzhen-based company Oho Sunshine online and found footage already on the device, which appears to be from inside the factory.

The collection of four short videos, dated last year, shows a number of workers sitting at their desks inspecting the glasses, while listening to jaunty electronic music.

Video appears to have been filmed inside a factory while the glasses were being made. (ABC News)

One video clearly identifies a worker lifting a pair and shaking them vigorously.

Another three videos, up to 10 minutes long and dated this year, show only black with atmospheric audio, suggesting the glasses were activated while inside a case or box.

The shoot button on the side of the frames is sensitive and easily switched on.

The workers appear to be filmed unknowingly by the glasses. (ABC News)

7.30 approached Oho Sunshine, with questions about the apparent privacy breach but received no response.

Oho Sunshine was founded in 2009 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in Guandong province, north of Hong Kong, as a smart wearable technologies manufacturer, according to the company's website.

The accidental leak perhaps proves not even the workers who make camera glasses are safe from being filmed and provides a rare insight into the globalised production chain.

Rise of camera glasses

7.30 reporter Jason Om wearing the Oho Sunshine camera glasses that already had footage on them. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Camera glasses are enjoying a surge in popularity as cheap brands flood the market. Oho is just one of numerous companies manufacturing similar devices.

They look like ordinary glasses and allow you to record video and audio, largely without people knowing.

While some models have a built-in light to indicate filming, there are now services that remove the indicator cheaply.

A pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

The glasses can play music and make calls, with more high-tech versions allowing users to live-stream or swipe through messages on a display in the lenses.

Meta's fashionable Ray-Ban smart glasses can cost up to $700 a pair, but basic versions can be bought online for as little as $40.

Kmart Australia's $89 Anko brand of camera glasses recently sold out, prompting an online petition to stop their sale amid concerns about privacy and their use by male content creators recording women without their knowledge and uploading the videos to potentially millions of followers.

While filming in public places is generally legal, the devices have raised new concerns around privacy.

Filmed without consent on 'rizz cam'

Beth Knight was filmed with camera glasses at a train station and later found the video of herself online. (ABC News: Daniel Ioh)

Beth Knight, 18, found herself the subject of lurid commentary from online users after a man filmed her with camera glasses and uploaded it to social media without her knowledge.

At the time of the incident late last year, she was 17 and by herself at London's busy Waterloo station.

"I'd missed my train, so I had 40 minutes to wait in the station," Ms Knight told 7.30.

"Then pretty much immediately a man approached me and opened with, 'I've seen you, I found you attractive,' and I immediately shut him down, and I said I had a boyfriend."

She discovered that their conversation had been turned into content after she heard about other cases.

"I started looking up buzzwords. I was looking up, "picking up girls", "Meta Glasses", "Waterloo", all of those into the TikTok search bar, and that's when I found his page."

She saw a video of her interaction titled, "POV: You approach her instead of walking by".

Beth Knight says she asked the content creator to remove the video of her and he blocked her. (Instagram)

"It was framed as a successful pick-up, like a win, when I know in the moment I was incredibly uncomfortable … because it was a strange man refusing to accept my soft hint of a no," she said.

"He had very much framed it as, 'Look, I've picked her up, I got her Instagram, I've won here,' and over the top of the video he was instructing men watching that when girls say they have a boyfriend they're lying."

Ms Knight was not lying and thought the man would get the message and leave.

The man is a content creator who touts himself as a pick-up artist and advertises male coaching on his social media account.

Digital extremism researcher Milica Stilinovic, from Sydney University, said such content was known as "rizz cam" — rizz being slang for charisma — where women are sometimes filmed without their consent.

"I would find it horrendous to be treated that way and then subjected to a global audience," she told 7.30.

Ms Stilinovic led a study that reviewed more than 350 Instagram videos filmed with camera glasses.

Milica Stilinovic is concerned about the use of camera glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"Pick-up artists are adjacent to the manosphere, or part of the manosphere, and they have a dual purpose to exist," she said.

"One is to build the self-confidence of men, supposedly through the subjugation of women, and the second part is to sell male coaching, which is basically like a multi-level marketing scheme.

"Some of the worst examples included underage girls. Some of [the filmers] approached women who were inebriated. Some of them approached women who were semi-nude at beaches."

Ms Knight said her experience left her feeling angry.

"It's weird to watch it back," she said.

"But the anger definitely came from the fact that it was spun so heavily to look good on his part.

" I went home and sobbed to my parents. "

She said she asked the content creator to take the video down, but he blocked her.

7.30 has contacted the creator for comment, but he did not respond.

Is it legal?

According to Australia's Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind, the use of camera glasses in public is largely legal, with laws varying across states.

"Wearing smart glasses in public to capture images of things that happen in public is generally not illegal under Australian law," Ms Kind told 7.30.

"[But] when you are in a private premises or a private space, and that might include a private home, a vehicle, or potentially a semi-private space like a gym or a workplace, for example, then you're likely going to run up against laws that do prohibit the use of surveillance devices."

Carly Kind is worried about the use of camera glasses in workplaces and around "vulnerable groups". (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

In Victoria, where filming inside a private business is generally allowed, one content creator known as "The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses to review coffee around Melbourne.

He is not a pick-up artist, but his videos feature staff and customers.

"The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses as he reviews coffee around Melbourne. (Instagram)

One 19-year-old cafe worker said she did not consent to being filmed while serving him.

Her aunt, Tara Venn, told 7.30 her niece was upset after seeing herself in a video online.

She was new in the job.

"It was a bit affronting [for her]," Ms Venn said.

She said content creators should consider the ethics of filming someone.

This cafe worker says she did not give consent to be filmed by The Latte Bloke. (Instagram)

"Common sense says you are polite and you ask if you are going to invade a person's privacy by filming them without them knowing," Ms Venn said.

"I just want people to think and to actually use good manners and decency."

The content creator declined to be interviewed but told 7.30:

"Latte Bloke is all about filming the latte experience and having a bit of fun reviewing the coffee. The focus has never been on the staff or customers, and I'd never intentionally want to make anyone feel uncomfortable."

Potential real-world consequences

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked Australia's Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses in Australia.

Ms Kind says she was already worried about them.

The Albanese government has asked the Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"If you think about their use in workplaces, there's a high likelihood that corporate espionage could be permitted through these kinds of glasses without proper control," Ms Kind said.

"I think the theft of personal information through the use of the glasses is also a potential offence that we could see spiralling out here, and [there are] obviously real risks around vulnerable groups, women and children."

In New South Wales it is illegal to create or share sexually explicit videos or audio of someone without their consent.

Last year, new federal privacy laws made serious invasions of privacy an offence; however, the commissioner told 7.30 there was a high bar to prove it was intentional and caused harm.

In the UK, some pubs and restaurants have reportedly banned the devices, while in Germany, rights advocacy group HateAid has lodged a complaint to German prosecutors against Meta and other companies, claiming such devices breach the country's covert recording laws.

Ms Stilinovic wants camera glasses temporarily banned in Australia.

"I would suggest that we stop the rollout of smart glasses until regulation and policymakers have caught up to keep societies safe," she said.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays at 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: 'Significant' fencing safety issues at pool where toddler drowned, inquest hears
World.content:
It is likely a backyard swimming pool where a toddler drowned was never required to be subject to an application for an approval, a coronial inquest has heard.

South Australia Deputy State Coroner Emma Roper is investigating the death of a 19-month-old boy after he drowned in the pool at his family's rented home in Salisbury, in Adelaide's north in November 2022.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

In his opening address, counsel assisting the coroner Darren Evans said on the day of the drowning, the boy — whose name has been suppressed — was with his mother, as well as his four siblings who he had been asking to go outside with him.

Mr Evans said it was about 5:20pm when the boy's siblings noticed he was missing.

"The family looked for him … his sister then found him floating in the swimming pool outside," he said.

Mr Evans said the girl found her brother near the pool's steps, before she "grabbed him by the hands and pulled him out".

"Their mother came and turned [the boy] upside down to drain water from his mouth," Mr Evans said.

"Neighbours heard a commotion and came over to assist, calling triple zero, and then commencing CPR with advice over the phone."

The pool gate was kept shut with a bicycle lock. (Supplied: SA Coroners Court)

The court heard when paramedics arrived, the boy had been moved onto the living room floor, and that after about 30 minutes "a return of spontaneous circulation was achieved".

He was taken to the Women's and Children's Hospital, but died seven days later, as a result of a severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy injury post cardiac arrest.

"There was no further treatment that could reverse the brain injury … it was identified that his condition was not compatible with life," Mr Evans told the court.

Ms Roper said the circumstances of the boy's death were "likely to have had and will continue to have a profound impact upon his siblings".

"It may be that it remains unknown who opened the pool gate on the day of his death, but it appears to be open at the time he's retrieved from the water," she said.

Faulty pool gate

The court heard when police attended the family's home, the boy's mother told officers the pool gate was "usually closed" and that she did not know how it came to be open or how her son got in.

It heard the top hinge on the pool gate was missing at the time, and there was a bicycle lock that had been put around it to keep it shut.

"[The boy's] father says that he noticed this was broken but did not raise it with the landlords, as he thought it was simple enough to fix himself with a new hinge," Mr Evans said.

Police commissioned a review of the pool by Salisbury Council pool inspector Jeff Shillabeer, who gave evidence that he found a number of "significant" issues with the safety of the fencing.

An inspector found several safety issues with the pool fencing. (Supplied: SA Coroners Court)

Mr Shillabeer said the "most notable" of those were the fact the gate did not close by itself, there was a gap greater than 10cm under the fence, and that there were climbable objects around the pool including a rabbit hutch and brick barbecue.

The court heard when he attended the property for a re-inspection in January 2023, all safety issues had been rectified by the property owners.

'Grand-fathered' safety compliance

The deputy coroner will consider whether improvements could be made to the regulation of older pools — particularly where the home is rented out — including whether the state government should implement a regular inspection regime, which is already in place in other states.

The court heard the pool was "likely" constructed prior to 1972, and therefore never required to be subject to an application for an approval or be entered onto the council's records.

Mr Evans said the requirement of pool fencing was only enforced under law after that time.

"The legislative regime continues to allow for grand-fathered safety compliance for pools installed in previous decades," Mr Evans said.

Mr Shillabeer said councils were only required to inspect a pool when a new one was built, and that there was no legislative requirement for an inspection after a transfer of sale.

He also told the court that, in his role as an inspector, he had carried out checks of pools following the death of a child at least five times.

The inquest continues.

World.title: 'She didn't care what anybody thought': Margaret Olley in five paintings
World.content:
In 1945, Margaret Olley — one of Australia's most celebrated painters — graduated from the National Art School, then known as East Sydney Technical College, with first-class honours.

Within two years the Lismore-born artist would win the first-ever Mosman Art Prize and join Sydney's post-war art scene, alongside artists like William Dobell, Sidney Nolan and Donald Friend.

During her life she would hold more than 90 solo exhibitions; influence artists like Cressida Campbell and Ben Quilty; establish a trust to buy paintings for public galleries; and be painted for an Archibald Prize-winning portrait not once, but twice.

Olley — who donated $30-40 million worth of her art to public galleries — pictured in her studio in 2005. (Getty Images: Patrick Riviere)

Now, she's being celebrated with a retrospective at her alma mater, titled Australia Intimiste. The intimism of the title refers to the late 19th-century art movement where artists like Pierre Bonnard and Édouard Vuillard painted intimate, domestic scenes from which Olley gathered much inspiration.

"She loved this place," curator Katrina Cashman says of the National Art School, where Olley began her career.

"She spent her whole life working towards the pursuit of beauty.

"She worked very diligently and worked very hard to maintain [her success]. She had her ups and downs. She had various health struggles over the years. She suffered from depression at times.

"But she was relentless in that pursuit of her primary passion: beauty."

Portrait in the mirror

Olley painted Portrait in the mirror in 1948 when she was just 25, living on Sydney's Lower North Shore with her friend and fellow artist Margaret Cilento.

Cashman says Portrait in the mirror shows Olley's "developing awareness of colour". (Supplied: AGNSW)

Cashman describes it as a turning point in Olley's career: "She's really establishing herself. She's recognising that she needs a space away from the National Art School to create her own work."

While she had graduated three years earlier, Olley was still a regular on campus, attending evening classes until the year she painted Portrait in the mirror.

That same year, Olley held her first solo exhibition, in Sydney, where both the Art Gallery of New South Wales and the National Gallery of Victoria purchased works.

"This painting is so special because it shows us who she is and who she's going to become," Cashman says.

Portrait in the mirror is one of many self-portraits of Olley.

"Her own image was something she could find solace in, and it expressed her interior world," Cashman says.

The dressing room table in the painting is adorned with flowers, fruit and postcards of famous works of art.

"[Portrait in the mirror is] the very beginning of her focusing on objects, on cherished items, and the classic still life study … but putting her own spin on [it]" Cashman says.

"She loved flowers as much as she loved people — they were a visual language in themselves … [And] she's surrounded her image with these beautiful pieces of art that she loves."

Spare bedroom

In 1970, Olley painted Spare bedroom in her family home of Farndon in Brisbane's West End.

"I love this work because it's actually a very rich interior," Cashman says.

In 1980, a decade after Olley painted Spare bedroom, Farndon was destroyed in a fire. (Supplied: Lismore Regional Gallery/Carl Warner)

The room depicted — in a "rusty sienna brown" — was a kind of side room, leading to a sunroom out the back.

"It's a painting of absence, but you get that feeling of presence," Cashman says.

"Even the way the chairs are positioned — you get that feeling somebody's just walked out of the room.

"You've got this beautiful, filtered light coming through from a window, presumably in the next room. You've got this feeling of spaciousness and air, like the space is well-ventilated, with a breeze flowing through it."

Cashman admires the simplicity of Spare bedroom, compared to some of Olley's more densely populated paintings.

"It has a lot to say about the idea of the intimate interior," Cashman says.

It's a style of painting unlike the abstract art or large-scale paintings that were fashionable at the time.

"Still life paintings were not de rigueur," Cashman explains.

"So, I think [Olley] was out of step in some ways with a certain part of the art sector who would not have considered this to be contemporary art with a capital C.

"But she persisted regardless. She didn't care what anybody thought of her work."

Kitchen still life

Olley would often paint in the evening with fellow artist David Strachan, who she met in the 40s.

"[Strachan] believed that the night-time was kind of pregnant with creative possibilities," Cashman explains. "There's something happening in the energy of the night."

After he died in 1970 in a car accident, she got permission from his sister to continue using his Sydney home as a studio, where, in 1976, she painted Kitchen still life.

Cashman says Olley's work asserts the domestic is "just as important as public space". (Supplied: NAS)

"It's a simple image," Cashman says. "We see the pots on the stove, the garlic, the onions, the kale, the salt and pepper, the accoutrements. We've got this beautiful dark blue panel at the back, which is the window to the evening sky outside."

Cashman likes the "strange feel" of the painting. "It's slightly menacing with the knife. They're about to cut up the onions or they're about to do the cooking, but there's something about the way that knife is placed."

The ingredients and utensils also seem to indicate there's a "person in that space" — a presence within an absence as in Spare bedroom.

"I just love the energy of this painting, knowing it's painted at night, the stillness, the quiet, that moody blue sky," Cashman says.

Homage to Manet

Often, Olley would replicate the paintings of famous artists in her work, including 1987's Homage to Manet.

The other figures in Manet's The Balcony are painter Jean Baptiste Antoine Guillemet and violinist Fanny Claus. (Supplied: AGNSW/Mim Stirling)

She painted a bowl of cherries and a jug of blue flowers in her kitchen, where she pinned a postcard of French artist Édouard Manet's 1868-9 painting The Balcony and a poster-size version of the work's seated figure: Berthe Morisot, a painter who married Manet's brother Eugene.

The Balcony itself was inspired by Spanish artist Francisco Goya's Majas on the Balcony.

"It's a self-consciously devotional act to include these works [in her art]," Cashman says.

"It's not a postmodern appropriation with any sense of irony. She's not poking fun. It very genuinely is an homage to these great painters that she knows and loves."

Cashman also admires the painting's "extraordinary" use of colour, "the richness of the patina, the focus on the female protagonist, and the focus on the delicacy of the flowers".

Incorporating famous artworks into her paintings was in some ways a means for Olley to work on her craft.

"Transcription is a part of art teaching," Cashman explains. "It's a deliberate thing to be able to transcribe another person's work and learn from it."

It was also simply a reflection of life. Olley's home was "completely strewn with images by other artists", Cashman says.

"Margaret was continually being replenished and refreshed by [other artists' work]."

The yellow room triptych

Olley continued to paint until the end of her life. She was preparing for an exhibition when she died in 2011, at the age of 88.

In her final years, she painted The yellow room triptych, a living room scene spanning 2.7 metres.

Olley died at her home in Paddington, which was once a hat factory. (Supplied: New England Regional Art Museum)

"She's choosing yellow as the colour to represent sunlight and the colour itself emits this sense of light," Cashman says.

It's that light the curator finds so compelling.

"The sunlight coming through the window is bouncing off that wall on the right-hand side and glimmering across the gold in the Chinese screen, and diffuse light is coming off those lemons.

"The energy and the mastery of colour is what makes [Olley] so special."

The yellow room triptych draws together much of Olley's practice, like the paintings by fellow artists, including Dance by French artist Henri Matisse; and the precious objects meticulously arranged beneath the window.

"We've still got that passage to the garden, just beyond, and that vibrancy of that green and the freshness of the light that's coming through and spilling onto the arrangement," Cashman says. "Then in the background she's got these very muted pinks and browns."

Like so many of Olley's still life paintings, the space also feels lived in — like someone has only just left the room.

"For me, that ripple in the fabric [of the curtains] suggests someone whose hand has just touched that," Cashman says.

Margaret Olley: Australian Intimiste is at the National Art School, Sydney, until October 24.

World.title: Darwin retirees lose home and all possessions in Livingstone fire
World.content:
As he sifts through the debris looking for his glasses and wife's engagement ring, Graham Doyle only finds rubble and dust.

He is back at the place he called home for 32 years, a day after a fire swept through the Livingstone property on Darwin's outskirts on Sunday afternoon.

"We've lost our house. There is nothing left," he said.

Graham Doyle and his wife Margaret lived in their home for more than 30 years. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

Mr Doyle and his wife, Margaret, were at home watching the football and getting ready to prepare dinner when Margaret noticed the smell of smoke.

The last time a fire alert was issued the blaze was moving away from their home. But looking out the back door this time, Mr Doyle saw the flames racing towards them.

The couple had just minutes to act.

Firefighting crews captured the scale of the fire that swept through the rural area, on the outskirts of Darwin. (Supplied: CMC Secure NT )

"It was like the surf coming in on the East Coast. It just flew down … travelled 350 metres in about a minute," Mr Doyle said.

"I've never seen anything move that fast. I don't know how to describe it other than absolutely terrifying."

Mr Doyle said they had no time to save any precious belongings, but managed to race their three beloved dogs outside to safety.

"I came back in abundantly trying to put the fire out," he said.

"The garden hose burnt through, so that was useless.

"I grabbed a couple of buckets and went to the kitchen sink.

"There was a fireball that hit me, and that was basically the last I could do in the house."

The fire burnt through the house leaving only some china cups as survivors in the kitchen. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

High fuel load contributed to fire intensity, Incident Controller says

Bushfires NT Incident Controller Nathaniel Staniford confirmed only one house was severely impacted by Sunday's fire, and said the high fuel load in the area contributed to the intensity and spread of the blaze.

Iconic Top End national park under threat from invasive grass Bringing in more than 250,000 visitors a year, Litchfield National Park has become one of the Northern Territory's star attractions but it's under threat from a near-invisible invader.

"There were several properties where the fire did break containment lines," he said.

"Those properties did contain gamba [grass] on them and that did help the fire to spread rapidly."

He said additional crews were called in to help once it was clear the fire could impact multiple properties, because Bushfires NT crews don't have the training or equipment to enter burning buildings.

While fire trucks turned up to help, Mr Doyle said they ran out of water.

Graham and his wife had to flee their home on Sunday and say they didn't have any time to save their belongings. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

"Watching, it was like the house was the timber inside a wood fire stove and the flames were just jumping up everywhere," he said.

Mr Doyle was taken to hospital with minor burns and smoke inhalation.

While he has lost nearly everything, he said he was lucky to be alive.

He returned on Tuesday to the destruction of his home wearing donated clothes and shoes to search for their irreplaceable items.

"My wife's engagement ring and wedding ring, they are somewhere down in amongst the rubble. She didn't get to get them out and I was trying to put the fire out in her room so I could get those for her," he said.

"My parents' medals … My parents' army discharge certificates, all of my university and TAFE qualifications are gone."

The majority of Graham and Margaret's belongings burnt in the fire. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

While a crowdfunding campaign set up by their grand-daughter has so far raised more than $8,000, the couple now face the daunting task of rebuilding their lives and finding somewhere permanent to live.

Graham also said due to historical storm water drainage issues in the area, the couple was unable to insure their home.

"The only thing we can think of at the moment is to try and get a cheap caravan."

World.title: Richmond denies players 'making light' of Swans scandal on Mad Monday
World.content:
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.

Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.

Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets on Monday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.

The club denied that was the case.

"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering," a statement read.

"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.

"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."

Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony AFL boss Andrew Dillon speaks to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.

The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.

"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.

The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.

"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.

Nick Blakey (left) is one of the Swans suspended for breaching club standards. (AAP Image: Dean Lewins)

"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that.

"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.

"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."

The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".

The Richmond footage emerged hours after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon fronted the media for the first time since the Swans scandal began.

"I have been asked a lot in recent days, what message football should be sending young people and what we should be saying to our kids," Dillon said.

"For me, the answer is straightforward: it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter what you do, whether you're an AFL footballer — the way we treat women says a lot about who we are as people, as a community and as a game.

"Quite simply, respect for women is not negotiable."

Dillon said the actions of the five suspended Swans players had "fallen well short of the standards our game expects and community deserves".

"While there are players involved, we cannot lose sight of the bigger picture. More importantly, there are women who have made a report to police and they should be shown care and respect," he said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Man accused of making deepfakes of students told police it was 'like X-ray vision'
World.content:
A man accused of making sexualised deepfake images of former Brisbane high school students and staff told police he did it because it was "funny" and described it as being akin to "X-ray vision glasses", a jury has heard.

Antonio Rotondo pleaded not guilty in the Brisbane District Court to more than a dozen charges, including 11 counts of stalking and five counts of distributing intimate images.

He is also fighting one charge of distributing child exploitation material.

Crown prosecutor Ben Jackson told the jury in September 2023, when Mr Rotondo was living in the Philippines, he sent an email containing numerous images to several recipients, including two Brisbane private schools.

Mr Rotondo has been charged with 11 counts of stalking and five counts of distributing intimate images. (ABC News)

Mr Jackson told the jury the images depicted current and former female students and staff at one of the schools which had been "altered in a digital way".

"To either remove some of their clothing entirely, or to replace that clothing with very revealing lingerie," he said.

The jury heard he did the same thing with images of various models who had been part of Brisbane Fashion Week and sent those to another woman involved in that event.

He also uploaded 16 of the deepfake images to a website that he ran, the jury heard.

Mr Jackson told the jury the feelings of complainants were not ordinarily relevant to an offence at trial, but in this case, they would be.

He said jurors would only need to determine that the offending would "cause someone in normal circumstances some distress".

"[The complainants] will tell you in their own words how they felt," he said.

The jury heard Mr Rotondo spoke with police in the days after he arrived in Australia in October 2023.

Mr Jackson told the jury he gave them "a full and frank set of statements" in a recorded interview.

"Which the crown says amount to admissions … that would count against him in his criminal trial," he said.

The jury heard Mr Rotondo told police he was the user of the email account and accepted he had sent the images and he controlled the website where they were uploaded.

He also admitted he had altered the images using a website, the jury heard.

Jury hears accused told police 'it's funny'

Mr Jackson told the jury in the police interview, which will be played during the trial, Mr Rotondo told officers making deepfakes was "just a hobby".

He said Mr Rotondo explained he did it because it was "just the type of person" he was.

"I'm at the stage of my life where I really don't care, I think it's funny," he said Mr Rotondo told police.

"I don't know the people … never met them, never will meet them."

Mr Jackson told the jury Mr Rotondo also stated in his police interview "you cannot stop deepfakes" and "everyone should live in fear" of them.

"Every woman on earth should live in fear of a camera," he said Mr Rotondo told police.

"You cannot stop it … I know the laws are trying to stop it in Australia, but it will not stop."

" From a guy point of view, from a practical point of view, it's fun to just press a button and remove their clothes, it's like X-ray vision glasses. "

"If there are services that exist that do it … and there's software that's available that makes it possible, it's acceptable to a percentage of community to make deepfakes."

The trial continues.

World.title: NSW prison officers strike over colleague's alleged assault by inmate
World.content:
New South Wales prison officers have walked off the job in protest after an inmate accused of brutally assaulting one of their colleagues was released from custody.

The union representing corrections officers has supplied a picture which it said showed the injuries sustained by the officer at the John Moroney Correctional Centre near Windsor several weeks ago.

The Public Services Association of NSW (PSA) said the attack left the officer with a broken eye socket, broken nose and missing teeth.

The PSA said the inmate was granted bail on other matters and was initially not charged over the alleged assault.

On Tuesday afternoon, NSW Police said in a statement the 55-year-old corrections officers was allegedly attacked by a 21-year-old inmate on July 25.

The man was arrested at a home on Lloyd Street in Blacktown about 11am on Tuesday.

He was taken to Blacktown police station where he was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to a law enforcement officer.

He was refused bail to appear at Blacktown Local Court on Tuesday.

'Members are livid'

PSA general secretary Stewart Little said prisoners had been locked down in their cells and trucks were bringing prisoners involved in court proceedings back to prison.

"Our members are livid. A corrections officers gets bashed and left with life changing injuries and the guy gets released back into the community without being charged? That's outrageous," Mr Little said before the man was charged on Tuesday.

Stewart Little says union members are "livid". (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

A spokeswoman for Corrective Services NSW said the alleged assault remained a NSW Police investigation.

"Any decisions regarding charges are matters for police," she said.

"Staff are right to expect that inmates who assault them in the workplace will be met with the full force of the law and we encourage staff on duty to remain at work whilst police investigate."

The spokeswoman said the 24-hour walk-out has been referred to the Industrial Relations Commission.

"All correctional centres remain secure and appropriate care and essential services continue to be provided for inmates," she said.

"Corrective Services NSW is continuing to support the injured officer who, like all staff deserves to be safe at work."

World.title: Darwin Woolworths blasts jingle outside store to stop 'loitering'
World.content:
Woolworths is blasting its Fresh Food People jingle at its Darwin city store in the hopes it will stop loitering and anti-social behaviour directed at staff and customers.

The supermarket giant has recently installed several outdoor speakers that play the 20-second song on a loop, which can be heard from across the street.

The supermarket sits across the road from a university campus, near residential apartments and next to a major bus stop with the music also audible there.

The store is located right next to a popular bus stop in the CBD. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Some have described the jingle as "very irritating" and "constant" with one customer saying, "it drives me nuts".

"It's not annoying me but it's on repeat, all the time," another shopper told the ABC.

Music aims to tackle anti-social behaviour

A spokesperson for Woolworths said the system was introduced earlier this month to tackle safety concerns, after the store reported 24 incidents of violent or aggressive behaviour this year.

Woolworths says the jingle is being played on a loop in hopes of discouraging anti-social behaviour. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We've received numerous complaints from the community and our own Woolworths team members about their safety while entering and exiting our Darwin City store," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"This is due to ongoing issues of anti-social behaviour and aggression from individuals loitering outside in the carpark and at the bus stop for extended periods of time.

"We introduced a music speaker system that discourages loitering, helping to increase safety."

The tactic is not being used by any other Woolworths store in the country.

A spokesperson for the City of Darwin said the music was being played "from within the Woolworths premises" and none of the speakers are located on City of Darwin-controlled public land.

Loading...

"Therefore, City of Darwin has no role in authorising the music being played by Woolworths," the spokesperson said.

"As the Woolworths and associated car park are not owned or controlled by City of Darwin, capacity to intervene in that space is limited, however City of Darwin will continue to assist where appropriate and within the scope of its jurisdiction."

Tactic an example of 'hostile' architecture

Woolworths isn't the first to use music as a means of tackling anti-social behaviour or driving away unwanted visitors.

In 2023, the City of Bunbury council in Western Australia came under fire for playing The Wiggles' song Hot Potato on a loop to drive homeless people away from a regularly used shelter and sleeping spot.

Wiggles 'disappointed' by council's weaponisation of Hot Potato The children's music group says the City of Bunbury's decision to play the song on a loop to stop people from sleeping rough at a public bandstand runs counter to the message of their music.

In Melbourne, Coles faced criticism for playing opera from a store in the inner-city suburb of Prahran which could be heard from the street in an attempt to deter crime.

Mark Olweny, an associate professor of architecture at Charles Darwin University, said the use of loud or repetitive music is an example of "aggressive" or "defensive" architecture.

He said while the use of "annoying" audio may be effective in the short term, the tactic could be "counterproductive" in the longer term.

"It has a downside because it doesn't only effect the people you want to move on, but it's also going to affect the people you want in that space as well," he said.

Mr Olweny said people may learn to blank out the sound and while people may be deterred temporarily, they would ultimately return for reasons like shade or transport.

Mark Olweny says the looping jingle is an example of "aggressive" or "defensive" architecture. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"In some instances, it may be called loitering but for the individual it is not loitering, they're there because there is a need that space is fulfilling," he said.

"In this case it could be getting away from the sun so if there's shade people are seeking that's where people will go."

"If we address that in a more nuanced way … or empathetic way we may find that the issue of loitering will be resolved with better outcomes rather than taking an aggressive approach."

Loading...

Northern Territory Police said there were regular patrols of the area.

"The Darwin CBD, including the area surrounding Woolworths and the bus interchange, remains an area of regular police activity due to the high volume of people moving through the location each day," a spokesperson said.

"While some incidents can involve violence, the majority of police interactions are resolved through early engagement and proactive intervention before behaviour escalates."

World.title: Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win
World.content:
Analysis NationalNSWPoker machines Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win Harriet Alexander August 25, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a particular feature of poker machine play that raises the pulses of reform advocates and gamblers alike, known as “losses disguised as wins”. The lights flash and the bells ring and the machine celebrates the spin like a win, but the payout is less than the amount wagered. Depending how far you wind back the time machine on this state’s slow descent into poker machine addiction, the Minns government’s long-awaited gambling reform package could be described as a loss disguised as a win. There is nothing terrible about the measures announced on Tuesday. It’s a grab-bag of things that can’t hurt, things that might work and things that are long overdue. The reforms proposed by NSW Premier Chris Minns gloss over money laundering. Sitthixay Ditthavong But it goes nowhere near addressing the social harms that have emerged as a result of NSW having the highest number of poker machines per person in the world. Starting with that metric, for example, the package includes an increased forfeiture rate when gaming machine entitlements are traded from one in three to one in two, so that for every two entitlements traded, one machine is permanently removed from circulation. This is designed to reduce the number of poker machines over time.



NSW has about 87,000 poker machines. That is just 13,758 fewer than when the forfeiture scheme was introduced 25 years ago. The NSW Audit Office projected last year it would take 55 years to reach parity with the national average. The accelerated forfeiture rate might shave a decade off that timeframe, but only if pubs and clubs do not change their behaviour. They might decide the forfeiture rate is too high and stop transferring their entitlements altogether. Related Article Updated

Poker machines Facial recognition mandatory in NSW gaming rooms under latest pokie reforms The second big item is a state-wide third-party exclusion scheme for people experiencing gambling harm. Gambling harm advocates have long advocated for this. Previously, people could ask to be excluded from particular venues, but there was nothing to stop them going elsewhere to get their gambling fix. Few will object to that loophole being closed, or the new ability for third parties to intervene to place their loved ones on the exclusion register. Similarly, the strengthened protections against harmful gambling advertising, a ban on VIP programs that reward high rollers, a ban on gambling advertising on government-owned buildings and new transparency requirements for influencers can only reduce gambling harm. But when it comes to poker machines being used for money laundering – that is, criminals using them to disguise the origins of dirty cash – the changes fall far short.



A casual observer might forget the NSW Crime Commission’s damning 2023 report into money laundering in pubs and clubs was the original catalyst for gambling reform. That problem has not gone away. The financial crimes watchdog last year launched civil proceedings against the state’s largest club group, Mounties, for allegedly allowing criminals to launder $226 million through its pokies. The independent panel for gaming reform recommended last year the government introduce mandatory account-based gaming, which would require gamblers to provide identification and allow crime agencies to track their transactions. Loading This top-line recommendation has appeared only in ghost form. Under these reforms, the government will upgrade the Centralised Monitoring System over the next two years to allow venues to transition to account-based play, which will give players the option of playing without cash – but it will not be mandatory. Setting aside the fact they could have done this two years ago, a voluntary, ad hoc system will do nothing to reduce money laundering. Instead, the government has committed to introducing mandatory facial recognition technology at the entrance to gaming rooms – the money laundering prevention method favoured by the gambling industry – and this will also support the state-wide exclusion program.



One pundit quipped the most generous thing that could be said about the package was that it was more than any other government has done, but only because the bar was so low. World.title: ‘George will be George’: One Nation MP brushes off order to ‘shut up about immigration’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘George will be George’: One Nation MP brushes off order to ‘shut up about immigration’ Rob Harris Updated August 25, 2026 — 5:17pm ,first published August 25, 2026 — 9:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation’s David Farley has dismissed criticism from former Nationals MP George Christensen that he has repeatedly undermined Pauline Hanson’s immigration message, arguing he is fighting for his electorate. Christensen, a one-time Senate candidate for Hanson’s party who campaigned with Farley during the Farrer byelection, said he warned the new MP more than once during the campaign to “shut up about immigration”. George Christensen, pictured with Pauline Hanson in 2022, has urged MP David Farley to “shut up” and stop undermining the One Nation leader. Nine Christensen said Hanson had also delivered the same blunt warning behind closed doors. Farley again went off message on ABC’s Insiders on Sunday, telling viewers One Nation’s immigration policy could effectively allow net overseas migration of about 230,000 a year – close to the Labor target. The comments forced Hanson to intervene within hours, insisting the party’s target remained 130,000.



Fellow MP Barnaby Joyce was then dispatched to explain the position, dismissing Farley’s comments as a “rookie mistake”. Christensen, a close friend of Joyce, said Farley’s record makes that defence difficult to sustain. Loading “A rookie mistake is getting a figure wrong in your first interview,” he wrote on his Nation First Substack. “Farley had already caused trouble over immigration during the campaign and been spoken to about it. This was the same mistake, only bigger, made on national television after he’d been elected.” Christensen’s criticism carries extra weight because he says he was part of the effort that helped Farley win Farrer. He claimed to have spent weeks advising him on media, messaging and the issues driving voters, and wanted him to win.



But he said he worried even then that Farley would struggle to stick to the party line once elected. That concern, Christensen wrote, has proven to be justified. “During that campaign, I had to give him a single piece of advice more than once: David, shut up about immigration,” he wrote. “Every time he wandered off the reservation, somebody had to pull him back. We managed it during the campaign because people were close at hand and watching what was being said. Once he was elected, I worried that he would go his own way.” Farley told this masthead in response: “George will be George and I will look after the constituency of Farrer and their critical immigration needs.” “I trust the rest of Australia are measuring their migrant and labour demand numbers, as the labour market is about to tighten.”





Christensen, who represented the seat of Dawson in central Queensland for the LNP from 2010 to 2022, also took a swipe at Farley’s comments about Sydney’s Mardi Gras, which Farley described as a “great night of entertainment”. “Pauline said she still didn’t like Mardi Gras. Farley apparently thought that was a good time to reminisce about what a wonderful night he’d had there⁠,” Christensen wrote. He said the problem was not that Farley had views of his own but that he kept turning them into public disagreements with his leader. “Political discipline isn’t complicated,” he wrote. “MPs will have personal opinions and occasionally disagree with their colleagues. They just don’t need to blurt out every thought that enters their head while a journalist is holding a microphone.” Christensen also took aim at Farley’s background in corporate agriculture and his support for migrant labour, writing that the new MP should be putting pressure on labour-hire companies and the supermarkets rather than arguing for more imported workers.



“Farley should start there instead of freelancing on immigration policy,” he wrote. “The voters of Farrer didn’t choose David Farley because they wanted Labor’s immigration numbers administered by a former agribusiness executive. They backed him as Pauline Hanson’s candidate ... For now, the most useful thing he could learn is when to shut up.” But Farley’s position on immigration has won support from one of his key backers, with Griffith-based winemaker Darren de Bortoli speaking out in favour of his local MP. Related Article Political leadership Infighting erupts in One Nation over Farrer candidate’s campaign He said there was a failure among political parties to realise each electorate was different, especially when it came to labour needs.



“As I always remind David Farley, which he fully supports, his first obligation is to the people of Farrer, not to One Nation,” he said. “We the people in Farrer have had enough of brain-dead politics that have sacrificed our region for far too long.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Trainer confident horse ready to find his groove
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Trainer confident horse ready to find his groove Ray Hickson August 25, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A first-up win was a positive sign to co-trainer Sterling Alexiou that Harry’s Evidence is starting to find his groove as a racehorse. The five-year-old heads to Canterbury on Wednesday having scored over a trip Alexiou is confident is right at the bottom of his powers and showing a willingness to stretch the neck to win. Harry’s Evidence steps up to a trip in the Asahi Super Dry Handicap (1250m) where Alexiou and Gerald Ryan feel he is well suited to handle a rise in class. “He’s a bit of a quirky customer but he’s always had plenty of talent,” Alexiou said. “It’s just been getting him to realise it and grow up a bit mentally.



“It’s more mental than anything, he was a bit inclined to overdo things early in his career. “He wanted to go too hard and over race. He’s gone the other way and is relaxing really well, we’re looking forward to getting out over 1400m this preparation.” That ability to relax was on show when Harry’s Evidence dropped into a trailing position in third in his resumption before he knuckled down and chased under 60.5kg. What is noticeable out of that win is jockey Chad Schofield only pulled the whip on one occasion and Alexiou said the horse can often overreact to it so it’s rare a jockey will use the persuader on him. “They went a good gallop, now he’s a bit older the 1100m is just a bit short of his best so I think the step out to 1250m will be good for him,” he said.



“There looks to be good speed engaged, he should get a nice run from a middle draw and he will be a winning chance again.” Meanwhile, talented three-year-old Southend is set to kick off his spring in the group 3 Canterbury Hurlstone Park RSL Up & Coming Stakes (1300m) at Rosehill on Saturday. The colt won his first two, including the group 3 Baillieu, before finishing midfield in the group 1 Champagne Stakes. Alexiou said Southend’s first two starts this campaign are locked in and then a decision on whether he tackles the Golden Rose. “We’ve been really happy with him, he’s had two good solid trials for 1300m first-up,” he said. “He’ll go to the Ming Dynasty then we try and work out where he sits in the pecking order.”

World.title: Prime minister dodges WA byelection dominated by One Nation
World.content:
NationalWAWA election Prime minister dodges WA byelection dominated by One Nation Hamish Hastie August 25, 2026 — 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has insisted he doesn’t campaign in state byelections after his absence from Secret Harbour was mocked by the WA Liberals, who paraded life-sized ‘Where’s Albo’ cardboard cutouts at the pre-polling booth. The byelection, in Perth’s south, will have little impact on the makeup of the WA Parliament, but its political ramifications continue to bleed into national discussions of One Nation’s surging support in outer suburban areas, with its candidate tipped to claim the seat. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Perth on Monday. AAP The state electorate also overlaps senior Liberal Andrew Hastie’s federal electorate, which One Nation has identified as a target. Albanese landed in Perth on Sunday and attended two fundraising dinners and a cabinet meeting during his two-day trip as well as an AUKUS announcement 20 kilometres north of Secret Harbour on Monday.



Both One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor have visited the electorate and Albanese’s failure to make the trip further south prompted WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas and his candidate Ryan Robertson to create the ‘Where’s Albo’ cutouts. Liberal leader Basil Zempilas with his candidate, Ryan Robertson (left) in Secret Harbour on Tuesday. Speaking on ABC Perth radio on Tuesday, Albanese said he did not campaign in byelections and quickly pointed out his appearance at the Rockingham byelection in 2023 following the resignation of former WA Premier Mark McGowan was for the opening of an urgent-care clinic. Asked about the ‘Where’s Albo’ signs, he accused the Liberals of running dead in the campaign and One Nation of not standing for anything. “The Libs are running dead. One Nation don’t know what they stand for. I don’t know who their candidate is, but I’m sure if he was asked about migration policy, if they can’t get that right, they can’t get anything right at all,” he said.



“You know what major serious leaders of major political parties want? They want their party to win. I want my party to win. Does Basil? I don’t think so. “I think it’s rather sad that the Liberal Party, the once great Liberal Party, there were two great parties of government in Australia. One of them has essentially folded themselves into One Nation.” Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has previously labelled One Nation leader Pauline Hanson “MAGA first”. One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen’s prospects for Saturday’s byelection have also led to ructions between Hastie and Zempilas. The byelection is considered a three-way contest between Herdegen, Robertson and Labor candidate Georgia Tree.



Speaking to the Australian Financial Review last week, Hastie lamented the effort put into the campaign by his state colleagues after Zempilas admitted One Nation was a force to be respected in WA politics and that a One Nation win would send a message to Labor. He reiterated those comments on the ABC’s 7.30 on Monday night and said he disapproved of Zempilas’ strategy. Secret Harbour byelection frontrunners: One Nation’s Luke Herdegen, Labor’s Georgia Tree, Liberal candidate Ryan Robertson. Ross Swanborough “I think this is a state election contested on state issues, and I don’t accept this idea that a win for One Nation is a win for the Liberal party,” he said. “Basil Zempilas said a win for One Nation would be an opportunity; I don’t see that at all. I think we should be fighting to win in every contest we enter, or we shouldn’t enter the contest.



“I think we could have signalled to voters that we’re fighting for them, we’re fighting for a better deal for outer-metropolitan Western Australians.” Related Article Breaking

Workplace safety Western Power rocked by second sexual assault claim Zempilas denied his party was running dead and said it had spent more than $100,000 on the campaign, adding it was odd that a talking point by Labor would be reused by Hastie. “That’s really what this is, because those lines don’t match the reality,” he said. “We have worked our backsides off now, and we’re very proud of our campaign.



“We put ourselves in the mix because we’ve got the best candidate, and we’ve been very pleased and proud to stand with him and continue to push the message that people are frustrated by Labor. “This is Labor heartland, and if they lose this Labor heartland, that will be a victory for all of those who are frustrated by this Labor government.” Zempilas said he was not bothered by Hastie’s comments. “I hope we continue to work well into the future. This is a state byelection. Hastie’s right to say that, and the campaign is best left to us, and that’s what we’ve been doing,” he said. WA Premier Roger Cook latched onto Hastie’s 7.30 comments.



“I think Andrew Hastie hit the nail on the head. The Liberals are running scared and running dead in Secret Harbour. They just don’t have the guts to actually stand up for what they believe in,” he said. Related Article Local council Plant, pull, repeat: Cottesloe council to vote on replacing uprooted Norfolk Pines “What they are doing is simply waving the white flag, hoping that One Nation gets elected off the back of their preferences and quite frankly, I’m not quite sure what role Basil’s Zempilas is playing in this state. “He’s either a political leader or he’s a follower, and in this case, he’s following Pauline Hanson.”

World.title: The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before Michael Koziol Updated August 25, 2026 — 4:39pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Scott Bessent gave the game away when he acknowledged the danger in taking the very step he had just told the world he was going to take. When the US treasury secretary was asked why he was not immediately applying sanctions to Chinese banks that finance Iran’s oil trade, he replied: “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks to reporters this week. AP Bessent and his boss, Donald Trump, spent the past week building up Monday’s announcement (US time) of crippling new sanctions against Iran and its enablers. They said it would be “economic D-Day”. An unprecedented campaign of financial pressure. The White House even billed it as the endgame in the US-Israeli war against Iran.



Related Article Updated

Middle East at war US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to isolate Iran from the world But what Bessent presented fell far short of that. As is often the case with Trump’s bombastic administration, the substance did not match the rhetoric. There were fresh sanctions against Iran-linked entities, people and ships, but not the big-ticket blacklisting of banks and financial institutions that enable Iranian commerce. To do that, the US would have to hit clearing houses in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, India and Pakistan. Mostly, they would have to hit China. Most analysts do not believe Trump would take such a measure with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House just weeks away. There is too much on the line for a US president who is wary of a full-blown trade war with China and who may still hold out hope of a grand bargain with Beijing. Daniel Fried, a distinguished fellow at think tank the Atlantic Council and former assistant secretary of state for Europe, said the new sanctions were – in Bessent’s own words – a warning shot, not an “economic death blow”.



“None of the moves was a game-changer. The rhetoric was ferocious, but the punch less so,” Fried said. Going hard, he added, “involves costs and risks that Bessent suggested he isn’t eager to bear”. Once again, these actions point to an administration that wants to end the war in Iran but doesn’t know how. Moreover, it has lacked a clear goal ever since Trump’s ambition of regime change went out the window and is operating within political, economic and military constraints. Donald Trump with Xi Jinping in Beijing in May. To truly inflict economic pain on Iran, the US would have to go after Chinese banks – and that seems unlikely to happen. Getty Images Aaron David Miller, a former State Department negotiator and Middle East expert, wonders if the pain these sanctions are supposed to inflict on Iran will have the desired effect. “What is the desired effect? That’s a core question?” he says. “Is it to break the regime and lay the basis of regime change? Is it to bring the Iranians to the negotiating table so they will somehow give up their leverage and control of the [Strait of Hormuz]? What is the purpose of this?”



Oddly enough, after months of the US trying to engage with the remnants of Iran’s brutal, fundamentalist Islamic regime, Bessent brought the goal of regime change back to the table during his speech on Monday. He appealed to Iranian soldiers to consider why they might not be receiving their pay. “Ask whether your commanders are leading your country to triumph or to ruin,” he said. “And recall that the Berlin Wall fell when ordinary soldiers decided not to shoot at their own people.” Their hardline leaders, however, appear unmoved. Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh declared Tehran was “fully prepared” for its enemies to launch what he described as “an economic terrorist attack”. Neither China nor Russia had “accepted” the US measures, he said, predicting that other countries would resist them.



The reality is that to seriously bring the Iranian regime to its knees, the US will need to target Chinese banks. There’s little evidence that Trump and Bessent are prepared to take that risk. Bessent said he preferred to use quiet diplomacy to that end. But that’s the opposite of the megaphone he tried to deploy on Monday. Scott Bessent: “At dawn begins an economic D-Day – the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary.” AP He likened Operation Economic Outcast to the D-Day landings at Normandy during World War II: a massive Allied effort to confront evil. Except in this case, the US is counting on co-operation from countries that are not allies. And it has spent the past 18 months confronting – sometimes bullying – friend and foe alike. World.title: Mother stabbed, 10-year-old son punched in random attack outside police HQ
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaCrime Mother stabbed, 10-year-old son punched in random attack outside police HQ Alexander Darling Updated August 25, 2026 — 4:35pm ,first published 3:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been arrested after allegedly punching a 10-year-old boy and repeatedly stabbing his mother with a pair of scissors in Melbourne’s CBD. Police said the random attack outside Victoria Police’s headquarters on Tuesday afternoon only ended when several passers-by intervened. A man has been arrested after allegedly punching a 10-year-old boy and repeatedly stabbing his mother with a pair of scissors in Melbourne’s CBD. Nine News Superintendent Zorka Dunstan said the woman’s two other children witnessed the violent assault. The family had been visiting the city from Phillip Island. “The man was walking south, and as he passed them, he randomly punched the 10-year-old then kept walking. He then turned around, grabbed mother in a headlock and started to stab her repeatedly with a pair of scissors,” Dunstan said.



Dunstan said she personally witnessed the incident from her office upstairs. Police were horrified by the attack, and grateful that three people came to the family’s aid before police arrived to arrest the attacker. “We had a citizen immediately intervene, who jumped onto him and just pulled him off the mum, and then the other two added assistance by grabbing him as well,” she said. Loading “Without the intervention, it could have been a lot worse, so we are so grateful for their assistance.” The 10-year-old is recovering at The Royal Children’s Hospital, while his 30-year-old mother is at the nearby Royal Melbourne Hospital with injuries to her back and shoulders. “She was in fairly good spirits given the circumstances,” Dunstan said.



Dunstan said the incident had also traumatised the family. “One of the boys was an 11-year-old, he was crying, I gave him a hug,” she said. The 27-year-old man from Sunshine West will be interviewed by police. Dunstan said while the attack was random, the man was known to police in Victoria, NSW and Western Australia. World.title: Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win
World.content:
Analysis NationalNSWPoker machines Gambling reform package is a loss disguised as a win Harriet Alexander August 25, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a particular feature of poker machine play that raises the pulses of reform advocates and gamblers alike, known as “losses disguised as wins”. The lights flash and the bells ring and the machine celebrates the spin like a win, but the payout is less than the amount wagered. Depending how far you wind back the time machine on this state’s slow descent into poker machine addiction, the Minns government’s long-awaited gambling reform package could be described as a loss disguised as a win. There is nothing terrible about the measures announced on Tuesday. It’s a grab-bag of things that can’t hurt, things that might work and things that are long overdue. The reforms proposed by NSW Premier Chris Minns gloss over money laundering. Sitthixay Ditthavong But it goes nowhere near addressing the social harms that have emerged as a result of NSW having the highest number of poker machines per person in the world. Starting with that metric, for example, the package includes an increased forfeiture rate when gaming machine entitlements are traded from one in three to one in two, so that for every two entitlements traded, one machine is permanently removed from circulation. This is designed to reduce the number of poker machines over time.



NSW has about 87,000 poker machines. That is just 13,758 fewer than when the forfeiture scheme was introduced 25 years ago. The NSW Audit Office projected last year it would take 55 years to reach parity with the national average. The accelerated forfeiture rate might shave a decade off that timeframe, but only if pubs and clubs do not change their behaviour. They might decide the forfeiture rate is too high and stop transferring their entitlements altogether. Related Article Updated

Poker machines Facial recognition mandatory in NSW gaming rooms under latest pokie reforms The second big item is a state-wide third-party exclusion scheme for people experiencing gambling harm. Gambling harm advocates have long advocated for this. Previously, people could ask to be excluded from particular venues, but there was nothing to stop them going elsewhere to get their gambling fix. Few will object to that loophole being closed, or the new ability for third parties to intervene to place their loved ones on the exclusion register. Similarly, the strengthened protections against harmful gambling advertising, a ban on VIP programs that reward high rollers, a ban on gambling advertising on government-owned buildings and new transparency requirements for influencers can only reduce gambling harm. But when it comes to poker machines being used for money laundering – that is, criminals using them to disguise the origins of dirty cash – the changes fall far short.



A casual observer might forget the NSW Crime Commission’s damning 2023 report into money laundering in pubs and clubs was the original catalyst for gambling reform. That problem has not gone away. The financial crimes watchdog last year launched civil proceedings against the state’s largest club group, Mounties, for allegedly allowing criminals to launder $226 million through its pokies. The independent panel for gaming reform recommended last year the government introduce mandatory account-based gaming, which would require gamblers to provide identification and allow crime agencies to track their transactions. Loading This top-line recommendation has appeared only in ghost form. Under these reforms, the government will upgrade the Centralised Monitoring System over the next two years to allow venues to transition to account-based play, which will give players the option of playing without cash – but it will not be mandatory. Setting aside the fact they could have done this two years ago, a voluntary, ad hoc system will do nothing to reduce money laundering. Instead, the government has committed to introducing mandatory facial recognition technology at the entrance to gaming rooms – the money laundering prevention method favoured by the gambling industry – and this will also support the state-wide exclusion program.



One pundit quipped the most generous thing that could be said about the package was that it was more than any other government has done, but only because the bar was so low. Tenenbaum disappointed when $1.22 in the Clarendon on Hawkesbury Cup day, perhaps he was in the wrong part of the track but he was still only fair. Chance to produce something fresh.

Race 3 1. Champagne Hero was a strong winner at Canterbury two starts back and that’s a better pointer than his last start at Randwick. 6. Harry’s Evidence was strong at the end of 1100m when resuming after tracking the speed. He’ll be fitter and the rise in distance is only in his favour. How to play it: Harry’s Evidence each-way. Race 6 5. Melanite was game under big weights on heavy tracks in his first two runs then up to midway level and down in weight he proved too strong at Randwick. Some handy form out of that race. Should get a nice run again from the inside. 1. Ruination was placed behind Attica last spring and took on a group 3 first-up before a handy second at Warwick Farm in March. Fresh for this and trialling well. 12. Taxation is a promising mare that impressively won her first two starts before disappointing a shade before a spell. Cobra Club proved too good leading all the way at Illawarra Grange then far from disgraced up sharply in class behind Avista at Randwick in a good form race. Can put himself on the speed here and if he’s able to control will take some running down. 5. Three Arrows is going well without winning and only has to hold form from his last start second in a similar race to be thereabouts again, albeit a trickier draw here. 11. Red Rags To Bulls broke through with an easy win at odds-on at Newcastle earlier this month and while she is a backmarker if they’re running on she can be in the finish.

How to play it: Cobra Club to win.

World.title: Trainer confident horse ready to find his groove
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Trainer confident horse ready to find his groove Ray Hickson August 25, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A first-up win was a positive sign to co-trainer Sterling Alexiou that Harry’s Evidence is starting to find his groove as a racehorse. The five-year-old heads to Canterbury on Wednesday having scored over a trip Alexiou is confident is right at the bottom of his powers and showing a willingness to stretch the neck to win. Harry’s Evidence steps up to a trip in the Asahi Super Dry Handicap (1250m) where Alexiou and Gerald Ryan feel he is well suited to handle a rise in class. “He’s a bit of a quirky customer but he’s always had plenty of talent,” Alexiou said. “It’s just been getting him to realise it and grow up a bit mentally.



“It’s more mental than anything, he was a bit inclined to overdo things early in his career. “He wanted to go too hard and over race. He’s gone the other way and is relaxing really well, we’re looking forward to getting out over 1400m this preparation.” That ability to relax was on show when Harry’s Evidence dropped into a trailing position in third in his resumption before he knuckled down and chased under 60.5kg. What is noticeable out of that win is jockey Chad Schofield only pulled the whip on one occasion and Alexiou said the horse can often overreact to it so it’s rare a jockey will use the persuader on him. “They went a good gallop, now he’s a bit older the 1100m is just a bit short of his best so I think the step out to 1250m will be good for him,” he said.



“There looks to be good speed engaged, he should get a nice run from a middle draw and he will be a winning chance again.” Meanwhile, talented three-year-old Southend is set to kick off his spring in the group 3 Canterbury Hurlstone Park RSL Up & Coming Stakes (1300m) at Rosehill on Saturday. The colt won his first two, including the group 3 Baillieu, before finishing midfield in the group 1 Champagne Stakes. Alexiou said Southend’s first two starts this campaign are locked in and then a decision on whether he tackles the Golden Rose. “We’ve been really happy with him, he’s had two good solid trials for 1300m first-up,” he said. “He’ll go to the Ming Dynasty then we try and work out where he sits in the pecking order.”
